name: Acoma Pueblo
overview: Acoma is a living Pueblo nation whose histories place Haak’u within an enduring homeland. The mesa village is a cultural center of a wider community, connected to farming settlements, water, language, and continuing institutions. These resources bring Acoma’s own historical interpretation and laws together with primary colonial records, public community testimony, and named artists’ work.

sections.title: Haak’u and different ways of knowing historical time
sections.text: Acoma’s own introduction explains its name through the idea of a place prepared and describes Haak’u as a spiritual homeland known through oral history and emergence. It separately discusses archaeological evidence and continuous occupation from at least about AD 1200. Those forms of knowledge ask different questions; an excavated deposit does not define the beginning of Acoma identity. The Pueblo’s longer historical essay also examines early Spanish descriptions, including accounts of multistory houses and abundant food. Such records reveal what visitors noticed and wanted to report. They should be read beside Acoma interpretation, rather than allowed to make an outsider’s arrival the beginning of the community’s history. A different kind of evidence comes from a 1987 tree-ring study undertaken alongside housing rehabilitation, with meetings involving Acoma homeowners and representatives. Sampled timbers indicated seventeenth-century construction and later roof repairs. The study helps reconstruct the histories of particular buildings; its limited samples and distinctions between cutting dates and incomplete rings prevent it from becoming a simple date for the origin of Acoma itself.

sections.title: The 1599 assault and a colonial account of destruction
sections.text: The Pueblo’s historical account describes a three-day Spanish attack, the burning of the village and provisions, the capture of men, women, and children, and subsequent colonial proceedings. A translated excerpt from Juan de Oñate’s 1599 report offers a primary record from the aggressor’s side. He acknowledges razing and burning Acoma, while presenting it as punishment and a warning to other communities after Spanish deaths. His language of royal obedience and alleged treason is a colonial justification, not this profile’s judgment of Acoma people. Reading the two accounts together makes power and authorship visible. Neither a conqueror’s report nor a short modern summary alone settles every question about casualties, sentences, or their implementation.

sections.title: The Pueblo Revolt belongs to a later regional history
sections.text: The 1599 assault should be distinguished from the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, more than eighty years later. The Indian Pueblo Cultural Center’s account explains the regional uprising through exploitation of labor and resources, hunger, violence, and persecution of Pueblo religious life. It presents cooperation among autonomous Pueblo communities as essential to resistance and cultural survival. This regional account provides context for reading Acoma’s colonial history; it is not a detailed reconstruction of Acoma’s particular actions in 1680 or later encounters with returning Spanish forces. The distinction also prevents a misleading story in which one battle, one leader, or one mission represents the whole history of Pueblo resistance.

sections.title: Landholdings and the work of a continuing nation
sections.text: The Pueblo’s landholding document shows how different legal histories occupy the same present landscape. Its inventory distinguishes the Acoma grant, executive and congressional actions, exchanges, purchases, trust holdings, and leased lands. Entries identify nineteenth- and twentieth-century transactions rather than reducing the land base to one reservation-creation event. These classifications matter: buying a ranch, holding land in trust, and leasing grazing land are different relationships. The document is a historical inventory, with dated entries and supporting records, rather than a current cadastral map. Tribal institutions also speak through their own law: Title 13 assigns responsibilities for language, education, and historic preservation, demonstrating governance over the conditions that sustain community life.

sections.title: Water rights, historical loss, and proposed repair
sections.text: In July 2024, Governor Randall Vicente’s written congressional testimony connected Rio San José water to Acoma farming communities, family life, and cultural continuity. He described the effects of upstream development, diversion, and groundwater pumping, alongside federal failures to protect Pueblo water uses. Historical correspondence and earlier proceedings support the Pueblo’s account of a long-running problem. His testimony advocates legislation approving a negotiated settlement and explains a trade-off between enforcing senior rights and obtaining alternative supplies. This is Acoma’s documented argument for a proposed remedy at that hearing. It should not be mistaken for evidence that the legislation was enacted, all settlement conditions were met, or new infrastructure has delivered water.

sections.title: Preservation means protecting records, places, and skills
sections.text: Acoma’s historic-preservation office dates its establishment to October 1999. Its public account describes collecting photographs and documents for the community, protecting archaeological resources on and beyond tribal lands, and providing guidance in preservation consultation and repatriation. At San Esteban del Rey, a condition assessment led to work involving traditional religious leadership and church caretakers, known as gaugashti. The office connects restoration to opportunities for Acoma people to learn traditional building methods. This places the mission within a larger community responsibility rather than treating the church as the whole of Acoma heritage. Title 13 supplies a complementary legal record of the preservation office and its advisory structure; an institutional description is not proof that every restoration proposal has been completed.

sections.title: Language learning and community authority over materials
sections.text: The H’aakume Dzeeni Language Program describes dictionary work begun in 2017, with fluent speakers editing conversational words and phrases from Acoma, McCartys, and Acomita. Its goals connect learning at home with school curricula. It expressly excludes culturally sensitive vocabulary and seeks member-controlled access to the online resource. The published language policy in Title 13 gives families and households a primary role, alongside tribal and school responsibilities, and supports instruction grounded in Acoma language. These sources document both educational work and the Pueblo’s authority over how knowledge is shared. They do not turn a public program description into permission to reproduce restricted lessons, nor do older project figures establish a current speaker count. Acoma educator Christine Pasqual Sims adds a wider policy perspective in her 2018 Senate testimony. She explains how English-centered testing, teacher credentials, and limited resources can obstruct language efforts, and argues for training and early childhood programs shaped by tribal priorities. Her examples from several communities illuminate shared policy challenges; the Cochiti and Jemez initiatives she describes remain those communities’ programs.

sections.title: Pottery: individual artists within a living practice
sections.text: Sky City Cultural Center’s pottery account describes fine walls, geometric work, functional vessels, and artists’ choices among construction and firing methods. Its emphasis on individual expression makes room for innovation alongside inherited practice. The Smithsonian’s biography of Lucy Martin Lewis provides a named example: she learned by watching Acoma women and experimenting, developed her own interpretations, and helped bring Acoma pottery to wider audiences. Her family continued making pottery across generations. Pairing community interpretation with an artist’s biography avoids treating every pot as an anonymous example of a timeless style. These sources support study of public artistic work; they do not authorize copying designs or seeking the locations of materials the community keeps private.

sections.title: Seeds, farming, and adaptation described by Acoma people
sections.text: A 2024 New Mexico PBS program includes public accounts from Acoma preservation leader Theresa Pasqual and seed keeper Aaron Lowden. Pasqual connects stewardship with care for land, plants, wildlife, and future survival. Lowden describes changing rain and snow patterns, a seed bank developed from work with young farmers, and efforts to bring Acoma seeds back from outside collections. He also discusses exchanges with other Indigenous growers and the value of varieties suited to differing conditions. His account shows adaptation through relationships, repeated planting, and seed saving rather than a single technical fix. The transcript includes speakers from other communities as well; only the Acoma speakers’ accounts are used here to describe Acoma experience.

sources.title: About Acoma: Haak’u and historical time
sources.annotation: Read the Pueblo’s substantive introductory paragraphs on names, emergence, Haak’u, and archaeological dating. Brief but important community framing, rather than a directory-only homepage. Its dating claims are attributed and not used to rank communities by antiquity. Undated; no current demographic claim is derived from it.

sources.title: Archaeology and Legend: How Old is Acoma?
sources.annotation: Despite its title, this is a substantial Pueblo-published account of Spanish exploration, written descriptions, the conquest-era attack, prisoners, trial, and later proceedings against Oñate. Read the complete historical text. Its quoted colonial passages require attention to authorship; precise casualty and punishment totals need comparison with critical editions of the records.

sources.title: The Diversity of Native America: The Southwest — Juan de Oñate, 1599
sources.publisher: Digital History / University of Houston; excerpt from Hammond and Rey’s documentary edition
sources.annotation: Read the complete displayed translated excerpt, including Oñate’s acknowledgement of burning Acoma and his attempt to justify it. Source cited by the university is George P. Hammond and Agapito Rey, eds., Don Juan de Oñate: Colonizer of New Mexico, 1595–1628 (1953), vol. 1, pp. 480–485. This is a colonial report excerpt, not the complete letter, full trial, or an Acoma account.
sources.author: Juan de Oñate; edition by George P. Hammond and Agapito Rey

sources.title: Pueblo Revolt
sources.annotation: August 6, 2021 public educational account by the Pueblo cultural institution. Read “Monthly Feature: Pueblo Revolt” and the Po’pay discussion for regional causes, intercommunity cooperation, and cultural survival. This is broader Pueblo context, not a detailed Acoma chronology. Books and videos recommended on the page were not counted as separately inspected sources.

sources.title: Pueblo of Acoma Landholdings
sources.annotation: Eight-page tribal document. Inspected PDF pp. 1–4, distinguishing grant, statutory, purchased, trust, and leased holdings, with dated entries extending to 2008. This is a historical inventory; its total is not asserted as the current land base. The attached primary legal material is a further reading path, not a full survey of today’s title status.

sources.title: Written Testimony of Pueblo of Acoma Governor Randall Vicente in Support of H.R. 1304
sources.publisher: Pueblo of Acoma / U.S. House Committee on Natural Resources
sources.annotation: July 23, 2024, twelve pages. Read pp. 1–7 on Acoma, hydrology, earlier use, development, and historical correspondence, and p. 12 on the settlement argument. Primary tribal testimony advocating legislation; statements about federal failures are the Pueblo’s documented position. No claim here that H.R. 1304 or a successor bill became law, or that proposed water projects are complete.
sources.author: Randall Vicente, Governor of the Pueblo of Acoma at the hearing

sources.title: Tribal Historic Preservation Office
sources.annotation: Read “Our Journey,” “Preserving the Invaluable,” and “Preservation through Education.” Describes the office’s October 1999 establishment, community archives, archaeological protection, consultation, repatriation guidance, and restoration with traditional leadership. Undated; project aspirations and funding descriptions are not presented as a current completion audit.

sources.title: Pueblo of Acoma Laws, Title 13: Cultural Resources
sources.annotation: Published file marked 2019 edition; internal heading says Laws 2003 (2017 Replacement), with origins and amendments noted. Read Chapter 1, especially §§13-1-1–13-1-4 on language, families, tribal and school responsibilities, and Chapter 3 on historic preservation. Primary tribal law demonstrates policy and authority; the text alone does not measure implementation or confirm the absence of later amendments.
sources.publicationDate: 2019 edition; 2017 replacement text with amendment notes

sources.title: H’aakume Dzeeni Language Program
sources.annotation: Read the complete substantive program description, “What We Do,” objectives, goals, and community work. Describes dictionary work begun in 2017, fluent-speaker editing, school/home learning, exclusion of sensitive vocabulary, and member-access goals. Undated project counts and staffing details are not treated as current. Restricted learning material was not accessed or reproduced.

sources.title: Acoma Pottery: The story of our handmade pottery and local artisans
sources.publisher: Sky City Cultural Center and Haak’u Museum / Pueblo of Acoma
sources.annotation: Read the complete public account on vessel uses, construction choices, individual expression, and continuity and change in artistic work. A community cultural center’s interpretation, rather than a sales listing or anonymous style guide. The embedded video was not independently reviewed, and no designs or material-collection locations are reproduced.

sources.title: Lucy M. Lewis
sources.annotation: Read both the museum biography and Luce Artist Biography, including observation-based learning, personal style, sales, recognition, and descendants’ work. Named Acoma artist, 1902–1992 as catalogued by the museum. A useful collection-based account rather than a complete autobiography; its references to locally held knowledge do not grant permission to disclose it.

sources.title: Our Land: Loving Our Changing Homelands
sources.annotation: 2024 broadcast with public transcript. Inspected the Acoma segments featuring Theresa Pasqual on care and stewardship and Aaron Lowden on climate changes, youth farming, seed saving, rematriation, and exchanges. This review is of the transcript, not independent listening or translation of Keres speech. Other interviewees’ experiences in the same program are not attributed to Acoma.

sources.title: Tree-Ring Studies of the Pueblo de Acoma: A Preliminary Report
sources.publisher: Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research, University of Arizona
sources.annotation: William J. Robinson, 1987. Read printed pp. 1–10 on meetings with Acoma homeowners and representatives, rehabilitation, methods, and results, plus p. 11’s dating-symbol key. Selected roof timbers support seventeenth-century construction and later repair; a beam date is not a founding date for Acoma. The study is preliminary and samples only parts of the village. Room-by-room owner and location details are not reproduced here.
sources.author: William J. Robinson

sources.title: Christine Pasqual Sims: Testimony on Maintaining and Revitalizing Native Languages for Future Generations
sources.publisher: Christine Pasqual Sims / U.S. Senate Committee on Indian Affairs
sources.annotation: August 22, 2018 hearing, S. Hrg. 115–367. Read Sims’s oral remarks on printed pp. 25–26 and prepared statement pp. 27–31. The Acoma educator discusses teacher training, tribal decision-making, school policy, and early childhood language learning. Her examples include several distinct communities, especially Cochiti and Jemez; those schools and their outcomes must not be relabeled as Acoma programs. Other witnesses’ statements were not reviewed as part of this source check.
sources.author: Christine Pasqual Sims

relationshipNote: Acoma is an individual sovereign Pueblo nation. Keres identifies a linguistic relationship, while Pueblo is a broader regional term encompassing distinct peoples and languages. Acoma and Laguna share a Rio San José water-rights settlement context while retaining separate governments and community histories.
researchGaps: Add a fully inspected critical edition of the 1598–1599 trial, translated Acoma testimony, and specialist historical work. Compare casualty, sentencing, and implementation claims without treating colonial proceedings as neutral evidence or repeating uncertain numerical totals.

Deepen Acoma-specific accounts of the 1680 revolt, Spanish return, seventeenth-century mission labor, and community rebuilding; the included IPCC resource supplies regional context rather than that full local history.

Trace the current status of the Rio San José settlement through later Pueblo statements and enacted instruments, and document water-delivery outcomes. A 2024 request for legislation is not evidence that it became law.

Compare the landholding inventory with current Pueblo records and primary grants, executive orders, statutes, and trust decisions. The inventory is historical and has not been converted into a present boundary map or current acreage claim.
Add direct public interviews and writings by more Acoma artists, scholars, teachers, farmers, women, and young people; expand community life beyond the mesa and beyond the examples represented here.

Seek dated language-program, school, and restoration evaluations while respecting member-controlled access and the Pueblo’s authority over cultural and linguistic materials. No Atlas community review has been recorded.

name: Adai
region: Southeast · northwestern Louisiana, including the Natchitoches–Robeline region
overview: Explore Adai histories and the contemporary Adai Caddo community through public community accounts, institutional records, language scholarship, historical documents and archaeology. Keep the people, the language and the colonial establishment called Los Adaes distinct.

sections.title: Names and a living community
sections.text: Adai, Adaes, Adaize and Adaizan appear in different historical, linguistic and contemporary contexts. Today the Adai Caddo Indian Nation publishes an account centered on family relationships, teaching and enduring connections with northwestern Louisiana. Its history page combines community self-description with quotations from older writers. Begin with that public voice, then compare the particular claims with the dated records below. The historical people, the language, the colonial establishment called Los Adaes and the present organization require distinct descriptions. Caddo affiliation in contemporary identity does not, by itself, settle the historical language’s classification.

sections.title: Kinship, mobility and church life
sections.text: An undated briefing prepared by historian Michael Lawson with Rufus Davis and anthropologist Maria Wade describes relatives living away who return for family occasions. Its later pages connect Depression-era and wartime work migration with continuing visits, church and homecoming. The community’s current history page also gives Catholic faith a prominent place. Together these sources offer attributed accounts of connection across distance, rather than proof that every family shares one religious experience or an identical migration history.

sections.title: Contemporary institutions and recognition records
sections.text: The bylaws effective March 2, 2024 name the corporation Caddo Adais Indians, Inc., with Adai Caddo Indian Nation among its public names. They distribute responsibilities among six council offices, prescribed elections and appointed officers. A Council of Elders advises on social and cultural activities, youth mentoring and elders’ needs. These published rules reveal how the contemporary organization assigns work and preserves records; they should not be treated as an unchanged model of historical Adai government. On October 20, 2026, Louisiana’s official directory placed Adai Caddo Indians of Louisiana under State Recognized Tribes. The January 30, 2026 BIA list, still linked by its live directory, includes Caddo Nation of Oklahoma and contains no Adai entry. These records concern distinct political names and administrative systems; absence from this list is not a documented petition denial.

sections.title: Homelands and a colonial place name
sections.text: Los Adaes names a Spanish mission, presidio, and settlement whose history intersects with Adai history. The Texas Beyond History exhibit describes Adai communities maintaining settlements around waterways while visiting and trading with the colonial establishment. Its account also distinguishes the wider region’s peoples and explains why European spellings and administrative categories require scrutiny. A place bearing the Adai name is therefore evidence of a relationship, rather than a complete map of where all Adai families lived. The exhibit’s later heritage discussion acknowledges living communities, even where other passages use older language of disappearance.

sections.title: Choices around the mission and the limits of its records
sections.text: In May 1768, Franciscan inspector Gaspar José de Solís described the Los Adays mission and presidio as separate buildings across a small plain. He reported no resident Indigenous congregation while describing numerous Indigenous people nearby who preferred visiting the presidio. The account records limits on Spanish conversion efforts; its explanations of baptism motives partly reflect settlers’ reports and the inspector’s suspicions. Lack of a mission congregation does not establish absence from the surrounding country. George Avery’s archival study supplies another caution: a 1766 Louisiana list omitted the Adaes because officials placed them under Texas jurisdiction. Avery also left the meaning of an unfilled Adaes symbol on a 1757 map unresolved. Omissions and uncertain map symbols require investigation with particular records and family histories. A Spanish surname alone does not prove an Indigenous woman’s ancestry.

sections.title: Adai communities in the early United States records
sections.text: John Sibley’s 1805 account describes an Adaize community at Lac Macdon, connected with the Bayou Pierre branch of the Red River. He places the old Spanish establishment some distance to its south and says it was named for the people. The passage distinguishes a community from the mission and presidio. His estimate concerns about twenty men, with more women; it cannot be quoted as twenty people in total. A distinct 1807 journal records parties and chiefs arriving on August 13 from several nations, including the Adaize, and discusses provisions, travel and horses. This is evidence of named Adai presence within a regional network, filtered through an administrator’s priorities. A later formal council list does not name Adai: the earlier visit cannot establish a treaty signature or participation in every subsequent meeting.

sections.title: Language use and language descent
sections.text: The same account says the Adai had a language of their own while also speaking Caddo and, in many cases, French. Those statements can coexist: using a neighboring language does not establish that one's ancestral language belongs to the same family. Mithun's 2017 discussion revisits the limited documentation and reports Chafe's rejection of identifying the recorded language as Caddo. She argues that an isolate is suggested, while explaining the broader difficulty of distinguishing an isolate from a language whose record is too limited to classify. This linguistic question should remain separate from contemporary Adai Caddo identity and the community's own reconstruction work.

sections.title: Population estimates and the persistence of names
sections.text: Swanton's 1942 sourcebook assembles estimates whose units vary between men, families, and total inhabitants. Its table even calculates some totals by multiplying warrior counts. These figures are evidence of what particular observers counted or estimated, rather than directly comparable modern censuses. Swanton also quotes land records using Adaes or Adaise and acknowledges uncertainty about the identity of a later village bearing that name. A place name alone cannot establish the inhabitants' identity or a complete genealogy. His further claim that Adai were entirely merged with other Caddo should be identified as his historical interpretation, rather than used to erase a present community's account of continuity.

sections.title: Reading archaeological interpretations
sections.text: Webb and Gregory’s state-published study gives the Adaes a distinct section within a wider Caddo account. It considers dispersed hamlets, trade, pottery and possible village identifications. Those identifications remain attributed hypotheses; broad archaeological periods do not establish when the Adai people began. A separate 2004 journal article compares documentary expectations with pottery, imported goods, buildings and food remains at Los Adaes. Indigenous-made vessels were central to this mixed settlement alongside French and Spanish objects. Its authors interpret combinations through exchange and accommodation. A vessel alone does not establish an Adai maker, and cooperation in particular activities does not establish equal power in every relationship. Both works are useful for understanding how scholars connect documents and material evidence, with their different dates, classifications and assumptions kept visible.

sections.title: Language teaching and practical community programs
sections.text: The organization describes rebuilding Adaizan teaching materials from limited documentation, comparing John Sibley’s spellings and developing a writing system. Its programs page reports translations and instructional videos, with a dictionary and children’s book underway. These are accounts of reconstruction and teaching work, rather than a current speaker census or independent linguistic classification. The same page describes member-led seminars at quarterly council meetings, field trips and a volunteer emergency-management program offering supplies, training and communications resources. These reported activities give a broader view of community priorities; the page does not independently measure participation, educational outcomes or emergency readiness.

sections.title: Public history, learning and a cultural center
sections.text: A March 31, 2026 report describes a weeklong trip through public historical and cultural institutions in the Natchitoches region. Organizer Robert Brevelle framed the visits around education and relationships with ancestors and land, while historian Dee Niette Thompson thanked participating institutions. This dated report makes the field-trip program more concrete. Its historical and genealogical assertions still need their own evidence. The community’s cultural-center page describes a museum and meeting facility near Robeline. Its public explanation of the Great Seal, attributed to Paige Holsapple and Robert Brevelle, connects particular motifs with its own historical memory and faith. That interpretation belongs to this community and this seal; it is not a universal guide to Caddo designs. A public facility location is also distinct from an ancestral territorial boundary.

sections.title: Acknowledgment priorities in a participant’s words
sections.text: In a May 2025 Native America Calling interview, council member Robert Brevelle connected federal acknowledgment with elder health care, young people’s education and cultural preservation. He also described the cost and specialized work involved in pursuing acknowledgment. The tribal-posted transcript preserves these priorities in an identified participant’s voice. His hopes and account of the process should be distinguished from an agency ruling, current petition status or grants actually awarded.

sources.title: History
sources.annotation: Read the complete substantive history page, including its contemporary self-description and church affiliations. It presents the organization’s own account of identity and continuity alongside quotations from older writers. Useful as community public history, with historical priority, land-title, genealogy and broad Caddoan-language claims requiring separate verification. The general About directory is not an additional resource.

sources.title: Programs & Services
sources.annotation: Read the complete page. Describes language reconstruction, seminars, field trips and volunteer emergency services. Dictionary and children’s-book projects are described as underway. The page’s categorical Caddoan classification is not adopted as linguistic consensus. Listed equipment is reported capacity, not an independent readiness audit; page sections and links do not count as separate works.

sources.title: Bylaws of Caddo Adais Indians, Inc.
sources.publisher: Caddo Adais Indians, Inc. / Adai Caddo Indian Nation
sources.annotation: Read PDF pages 1–10 of 12, including Articles I–II, IV, VI and VIII–IX. The document states a March 2, 2024 revision and effective date. It identifies the corporation and its Adai Caddo public name, council responsibilities, elections, elders and appointed roles. These are published institutional rules, not a federal acknowledgment decision or proof of unchanged historical government.

sources.title: Introducing the Adai Indian Nation
sources.publisher: Morgan, Angel & Associates, LLC; digital copy at the Newberry Library
sources.annotation: Read pages 1–7 and 15–19 of the 19-page briefing. Michael L. Lawson prepared it in cooperation with Chief Rufus Davis and anthropologist Maria D. Wade. Its community-collaborative account discusses dispersed relatives, work migration, church and homecoming. Undated; PDF creation metadata does not establish publication date. Recognition arguments are advocacy; inconsistent grant/cession dates are not used. This is not an agency determination.
sources.author: Michael L. Lawson, in cooperation with Rufus Davis and Maria D. Wade

sources.title: Adai Caddo Indian Nation holds 2nd Annual Field Trip visiting sites across Natchitoches and CENLA
sources.annotation: Read the complete March 31, 2026 report and visually checked all three pages of the tribal-hosted archived screenshots. Reports a March field trip and quotes organizer Robert Brevelle and historian Dee Niette Thompson. Evidence for a reported educational activity and participants’ aims; historical site identifications, genealogy and land-ownership assertions are not independently established here. Original article and archived PDF are one work.

sources.title: Native America Calling — May 28, 2025 Adai interview transcript
sources.publisher: Native America Calling / Koahnic Broadcast Corporation; transcript posted by Adai Caddo Indian Nation
sources.annotation: Read all six pages of the tribal-posted transcript of Shawn Spruce’s interview with council member Robert Brevelle; also checked the official episode page. Brevelle discusses acknowledgment, elder health, youth education and cultural preservation. These are attributed priorities and advocacy, not proof of petition status, eligibility or funding received. Recording not independently audited against this transcript; other episode interviews are not represented as reviewed.
sources.author: Shawn Spruce (host); Robert Brevelle (interviewee)

sources.title: Historical Sketches of the Several Indian Tribes in Louisiana: Adaize account
sources.publisher: John Sibley; reprinted in American State Papers, Boston: Munroe, Francis, & Parker, 1808; scan from Internet Archive via Wikimedia Commons
sources.author: John Sibley
sources.annotation: 1805 account, communicated with Jefferson's 1806 message; inspected in a dated 1808 Boston reprint, printed pp. 42–44, especially the complete Adaize entry on p. 44 (PDF p. 52). Sibley distinguishes the community at Lac Macdon from the old Spanish establishment and describes multilingualism. His estimate concerns men, not the whole population. This is an official observer's account, containing judgments and secondhand claims; it is not an independently verified census or a tribal-authored history.

sources.title: A Report from Natchitoches in 1807
sources.publisher: Museum of the American Indian, Heye Foundation, Indian Notes and Monographs 25; Smithsonian Libraries / Internet Archive
sources.author: John Sibley; edited with an introduction by Annie Heloise Abel
sources.annotation: 1922 edition of Sibley's 1807 journal. Read the introduction's printed pp. 5–8 and August entries on pp. 49–56, especially August 13 on p. 50. Adai parties and chiefs appear among visitors receiving provisions. The August 18 formal council list on p. 56 does not name Adai, so the earlier visit must not be turned into a treaty-signature claim. The publication and its introduction reflect two different periods of outsider authorship.

sources.title: Source Material on the History and Ethnology of the Caddo Indians
sources.publisher: Smithsonian Institution, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 132; full-text transcription hosted by the Louisiana Anthology
sources.author: John R. Swanton
sources.annotation: 1942 sourcebook. Inspected selected Adai passages on printed pp. 13–15, 21–23, 75, and 84–85. Swanton compares discrepant population estimates, reports Caddo recollections, and warns that a later village called Adaise cannot securely be identified as Indigenous. Its historical synthesis and quoted records require source-specific reading. His assertion that Adai were entirely merged with other Caddo is a dated author's conclusion, not a verdict on today's communities or their identities.

sources.title: Language Isolates of North America
sources.publisher: Routledge, in Language Isolates, pp. 193–228; author-posted full text on ResearchGate
sources.author: Marianne Mithun
sources.annotation: 2017 chapter, DOI 10.4324/9781315750026-8. Read printed pp.193–195 of the author-posted full text, including the Adai analysis. Mithun explains documentation limits and argues the evidence suggests an isolate, citing Wallace Chafe. Use this for linguistic reasoning, not compressed mission chronology. The underlying vocabulary manuscript and Chafe’s unpublished communication were not inspected. A later automated availability request returned403; this does not establish a reader paywall.

sources.title: Los Adaes — Cultural Worlds, archival research, and legacy
sources.publisher: Texas Beyond History · Texas Archeological Research Laboratory
sources.author: Hiram F. Gregory, George Avery, Francis X. Galán, Steve Black, and contributors including Mariah F. Wade
sources.annotation: Read Cultural Worlds, Los Adaes Archival Research, Legacy, and the contributor credits. The exhibit distinguishes Adai communities from the colonial establishment and discusses Indigenous-made pottery, trade, and later heritage. Its contributors include an Adai specialist and acknowledge Chief Rufus Davis’s assistance. Some language about disappearance and colonial cultural hierarchies is dated; do not adopt it as a verdict on living identity. The linked exhibit sections count as one resource, not four.

sources.title: The Caddo Indians of Louisiana — second edition, The Adaes section
sources.publisher: Louisiana Division of Archaeology · Anthropological Study No. 2
sources.author: Clarence H. Webb and Hiram F. Gregory
sources.annotation: Inspected the cover, reissue foreword, historical context, and The Adaes section on PDF pp. 22–24. The foreword says this edition largely reissues a 1978 text. A substantial, explicitly Adai-focused account considers dispersed settlement, mission connections, pottery, and possible village identifications. Several sites and affiliations are hypotheses. Its confident Caddoan classification and colonial mission dates require comparison with later specialists; regional archaeological periods do not date the origin of the Adai people. Sensitive locations and funerary details are not reproduced.

sources.title: Presidio Los Adaes: Spanish, French, and Caddoan Interaction on the Northern Frontier
sources.publisher: Historical Archaeology 38(3), pp. 65–77 · Society for Historical Archaeology; authorized Texas Beyond History copy
sources.author: H. F. Gregory, George Avery, Aubra L. Lee, and Jay C. Blaine
sources.annotation: Actual scanned article visually inspected at printed pp. 65, 67–71, and 74–75, including the excavation overview and conclusions. Compares documentary expectations with Indigenous pottery, French and Spanish goods, architecture, and food remains at the presidio. Material patterns concern a mixed colonial settlement; they do not identify every maker as Adai or prove equal power and universal harmony. Site-specific counts and social interpretations need their original contexts. This authored journal study is distinct from the later public exhibit.

sources.title: Archival Investigations of the People of Los Adaes
sources.annotation: Read printed pp.65–67,70,77,80–85; visually checked pp.65,77,80. A directly relevant archival study explains why jurisdiction, inconsistent names and ambiguous mapping limit conclusions about Adai presence. Its baptism total conflicts with the inspected Solís translation. The displayed Spring 1996 issue date also conflicts with later references; neither anomaly is silently corrected.

sources.title: Diary of a Visit of Inspection of the Texas Missions Made by Fray Gaspar José de Solís in the Year 1767–68
sources.publisher: Gaspar José de Solís; translated by Margaret Kenney Kress, introductory note by Mattie Austin Hatcher — Southwestern Historical Quarterly 35(1), July 1931:28–76
sources.annotation: Read printed pp.28–29 and 61–66 of the public issue scan; visually checked 65–66. The translated 1768 inspection distinguishes mission and presidio and discusses surrounding Indigenous people and selective participation. This Franciscan account, filtered through a 1931 translation, is not Indigenous testimony or a population census. Original Spanish manuscript and the complete diary were not read.

sources.title: Government — Great Seal interpretation
sources.annotation: Read the complete government page and public explanation of the seal, attributed to Paige Holsapple and Robert Brevelle. The community interprets particular motifs through its own history and faith. Short supporting interpretation, kept outside the substantive-source count. It does not establish universal Caddo symbolism, historical title or the historical accuracy of every association.

sources.title: Cultural Center
sources.annotation: Read the complete short page: public museum/exhibit and meeting-facility description, photographs and published street address. Supporting visitor and geographic information only. It supplies a present facility location, not a historical homeland boundary. The community publishes LA-485, while the state directory prints LA-486; no coordinates were inferred from the conflicting roads.

sources.title: Federally and State-Recognized Tribes
sources.publisher: Louisiana Office of the Governor / Indian Affairs
sources.annotation: Read the federal and state headings and Adai entry on the live official directory on October 20, 2026. It places “Adai Caddo Indians of Louisiana” under State Recognized Tribes. Supports that precisely attributed listing, without establishing its legal origin date, federal status or equivalence to another Caddo government. Name/contact listing kept outside the substantive-source count.

sources.title: Indian Entities Recognized by and Eligible To Receive Services From the United States Bureau of Indian Affairs
sources.publisher: Bureau of Indian Affairs; Federal Register / Government Publishing Office
sources.annotation: Read the notice introduction and relevant alphabetical entries in the official five-page PDF, 91 FR 4102–4106, and searched its complete extracted text. Caddo Nation of Oklahoma is listed; Adai/Adais is absent. BIA’s live directory still points to this notice. Supports a dated list comparison, not a finding that any particular petition was denied. Supporting status check outside the substantive count.

relationshipNote: Adai Caddo Indian Nation and Caddo Nation of Oklahoma are distinct contemporary political names. The Caddo and Natchitoches entries provide regional and historical connections, not interchangeable identities. Los Adaes names a colonial mission, presidio and settlement; not every person called Adaeseño in that regional history can be assigned Adai ancestry.
researchGaps: Compare more community-authored histories and publicly shared family accounts; this profile is an introduction and has not received community review.

Obtain and read the full Pleasant 2013 settlement-location article before adopting its proposed geography. Colonial place names and candidate archaeological sites do not establish a single precise homeland boundary.
Reconcile language classifications through surviving documentation and specialist analysis; neither an old categorical classification nor a modern political affiliation settles linguistic descent.
The Solís translation and Avery study report different baptism totals. Compare the underlying manuscript and alternative translations; baptism entries are not a census of the Adai people.
Verify land-grant and cession chronology against original instruments. The collaborative briefing contains internally inconsistent dates, so this article does not adopt a land-title conclusion.

No present acknowledgment petition disposition, complete documentary petition, current speaker census or comparable membership series was verified. Interview advocacy and dated counts have limited scopes.
The community cultural-center address and state directory disagree on the highway number. Resolve that discrepancy before any later geocoding; do not infer wider territory from a public facility.

Extend coverage of nineteenth- and twentieth-century change, community livelihoods, teaching outcomes and the range of family experiences without generalizing one representative’s account to everyone.
evidenceNotes: Fifteen substantive works were inspected on October 20, 2026. Four short supporting records are explicitly excluded from that substantive count. Identified pages or excerpts were read where annotations specify a limited scope; no unread book is counted. Sources sharing earlier records are distinct works but not independent corroboration of every claim. Historical statements about language loss or absorption are not evidence of a people’s disappearance.

name: Ahtna
region: Alaska / Copper River Basin and neighboring Interior Alaska drainages
overview: Explore Ahtna homelands and community life through named voices, village planning, language teaching, historical studies and stewardship research. Distinguish village tribal governments, Native corporations and regional organizations while following each source’s perspective and date.

sections.title: Copper River homelands and living relationships
sections.text: Ahtna people’s histories center on the Copper River region and connections extending into neighboring Interior Alaska drainages. The Alaska Native Language Center identifies Ahtna as an Athabascan language of the Copper River and upper Susitna and Nenana areas. Ahtna, Incorporated’s cultural overview places family fishing, hunting, gathering and other food work within seasonal relationships that continue amid changing lives. A cultural homeland, a language’s described distribution and the property owned by particular corporations are different kinds of geography. Neither a park boundary nor a corporate shareholder total describes the whole people.

sections.title: Connected institutions with distinct roles
sections.text: AITRC identifies eight member tribes and the landholding corporations Ahtna, Incorporated and Chitina Native Corporation. It describes coordinating resource work rather than replacing village governments. Ahtna’s short village history also explains that seven village corporations merged with the regional corporation in 1980 while Chitina’s remained separate. That corporate reorganization should not be confused with a merger of tribal governments. Gakona’s own page separately describes its government and community services.

sections.title: Land, kinship and changing settlement
sections.text: The community-coauthored 2019 study The Ahtna Homeland describes nineteenth-century land relationships through regional bands, matrilineal clans and particular leaders. Winter villages were connected with fishing camps, hunting areas and trails. Rights to use places were recognized, while kinship also carried obligations to share resources, particularly during shortages. This was an organized inhabited landscape before colonial authorities classified land through public and private property. The study follows pressures toward permanent road-connected settlements, including schooling requirements, restricted livelihoods and opportunities for paid work. Its account of movement toward Cantwell shows a gradual process with continued seasonal travel. These historical relationships should be distinguished from today’s tribal governments and Native corporations; none of those categories automatically substitutes for the others.

sections.title: Colonial pressures and forced displacement
sections.text: Simeone and Miller’s 2024 assessment combines historical records with elders’ accounts of colonial change. It distinguishes earlier Russian encounters from the expanding American presence after the 1898 gold rush, including mining, roads, schooling and pressures on livelihoods. Its wartime history describes forced removal from Dry Creek in 1942–43: homes were burned or dismantled to make way for an airfield. At Gulkana in 1943, bridge and road construction divided the village and forced resettlement across the river. These were local displacements within a homeland where Ahtna connections continued. The assessment also documents subsequent political organizing. Reading remembered experiences alongside government records matters, especially where official files omit removals. The authors’ synthesis preserves named narrators and differing perspectives; it does not speak for every family.

sections.title: Maps and the visibility of Ahtna presence
sections.text: In his 2022 chapter, Simeone treats maps as historical arguments shaped by their makers’ purposes. He contrasts the sparse Indigenous information on Colton’s 1868 map with later surveys and development maps. A 1918 map used in advocacy over the Copper River fishery instead emphasized Ahtna villages and estimated populations. His discussion also considers a map produced by Ahtna, Incorporated that places corporate landholdings within a larger traditional homeland. Together these examples show why an apparently blank map cannot establish an uninhabited country, and why settlement dots do not capture a whole land relationship. Historical homeland representations, corporate parcels and present legal boundaries answer different questions. The chapter’s interpretations are useful reading guides, rather than authority to draw a precise territorial boundary.

sections.title: Chitina’s own public history
sections.text: Chitina Native Corporation dates its incorporation to 1973 and describes shareholders as primarily residents or descendants of the Native Village of Chitina, which it identifies as a separate tribe. Its public history recalls named leaders including Nicolai, Hanagita and Goodlataw, and Doc Billum’s river transport and knowledge of copper deposits. These attributed biographies place particular people and family relationships within exploration, transport and mining histories; their approximate dates should remain qualified.

sections.title: Landholding and traditional-use geography
sections.text: Ahtna, Incorporated’s land FAQ distinguishes the property it owns from a much larger traditional-use landscape. It also identifies Chitina Native Corporation as a separate landholder. The FAQ describes different arrangements for recreation, research, filming and reserved public routes. These distinctions matter when reading a map: cultural relationships, corporate ownership and particular access rights describe different things. The corporation’s general account does not determine every parcel or route’s legal status.

sections.title: Stewardship and corporate responsibilities
sections.text: Chitina’s distinct land statement connects cultural history and food resources with responsibilities to future generations. It gives shareholders and descendants priority in cultural, subsistence and recreational use while describing conditions for public access. This is the corporation’s account of managing its property. It should be read alongside current permissions and the status of particular land, rather than treating a broad Ahtna regional label as either public access or one uniform ownership.

sections.title: Learning through relationships and observation
sections.text: In her 2007 interview, Kathryn Martin describes time spent traveling with her grandmother Katie John as a central part of her education. Watching relatives and listening over time connected knowledge with responsibilities to land and people. Martin also discusses the choices facing younger generations and her hopes for schooling that makes room for Ahtna language and culture alongside other educational opportunities. Her account resists reducing education to a textbook or a short list of cultural facts. She explicitly considers the consequences of sharing knowledge outside the community. This is one person’s public reflection at a particular moment, and its examples should retain her attribution and date.

sections.title: A dictionary built through collaboration
sections.text: Kari’s 1990 dictionary makes its Ahtna contributors visible, including Katie and Fred John Sr., Chief Jim McKinley, Mildred Buck, Ruth Johns, and speakers from several regions. Its historical introduction credits Buck, Jeff Leer, Michael Krauss, and Kari with establishing the writing system in 1973, and describes Buck’s work training other Ahtna writers. The dictionary combines roots, affixes, and examples with an English index. Its regional labels help readers recognize variation; they should be read within that work’s framework. Kari also acknowledges missing words and possible errors. The book is therefore a substantial learning and research tool whose own introduction invites correction and continuing community knowledge.

sections.title: A teaching resource with a named voice and place
sections.text: The Mentasta lessons feature Katie John’s recorded Upper Ahtna speech, with transcription by John T. Ritter and James Kari and editing by Cynthea L. Ainsworth. Their monthly sequence connects conversation with seasonal activities, then develops vocabulary and grammatical patterns through questions and answers. The inspected units cover weather, food, family, everyday activities, and learning to understand the language. The introduction also credits intergenerational teaching work in Mentasta. Readers should approach this as a resource grounded in a particular speaker and variety, rather than assume that every pronunciation or expression represents every Ahtna community. The 2018 web version preserves a teaching work published in 2009.

sections.title: Archives as places for community learning
sections.text: Berez’s 2013 study shows how the Ahtna Heritage Foundation’s C’ek’aedi Hwnax connected preservation with active learning. Its account of an August 2013 workshop brings learners, elders, and linguists together to work with archived recordings, transcription, grammar, and dictionary use. The study also documents local control over access: staff consulted families about legacy recordings whose original permissions could be unclear. These are historical descriptions of the archive’s decisions, rather than confirmation of today’s procedures. The wider lesson is practical: a recording’s survival and a researcher’s ability to describe it do not by themselves settle who may hear it, copy it, or publish it.

sections.title: A Gulkana planning conversation
sections.text: Gulkana’s January 2024 public review draft master plan connects cultural life with housing, training, community facilities and environmental resilience. A small 2023 survey, open to Tribal and non-Tribal respondents, records local concerns and aspirations; it is not a census of Ahtna opinion. Proposed actions include protecting cultural places, improving housing and providing additional subsistence-skills learning. The draft shows a particular community considering its future, without establishing final adoption or completed construction.

sections.title: Tazlina’s practical environmental work
sections.text: A Fall 2018 Kanas article describes Tazlina’s effort to address contamination around the former Copper Valley School, including work on land the Village did not then own. It connects environmental programs with community access, recycling and energy needs, reporting a heating project completed that September. A pedestrian route remained in planning. The account shows village initiative across institutional and property constraints at that date; it is not a current ownership record or contamination clearance.

sections.title: Cooperative wildlife management
sections.text: A 2016 agreement between the Interior Department and AITRC identifies a shared purpose: sustaining wildlife and opportunities to continue customary subsistence practices. It provides a framework for rulemaking, cooperative research and an advisory process, with Ahtna knowledge contributing to management decisions. The document also retains federal responsibilities, makes proposed actions conditional on applicable procedures, and states that it creates no enforceable obligations or rights. Reading those provisions together shows a negotiated process whose implementation must be traced through later decisions, rather than assuming that signing the agreement transferred land or complete wildlife authority.

sections.title: What a community harvest program records
sections.text: Kosbruk and Simon’s January 2026 report follows the Community Harvest System through administration, registration, hunting effort and participants’ feedback. It describes pooled harvest opportunities under a federal framework and explains the inclusion of federally qualified rural residents of the named communities. For 2023–2025, its moose-program summaries report no successful harvests, alongside continuing outreach and coordination. This is a bounded account of one program, not a measure of all Ahtna hunting or food sharing. The authors connect access, competition and environmental conditions with participants’ difficulties and advocate regulatory changes; that advocacy does not establish what later regulators decided.

sections.title: Community questions and salmon research
sections.text: AITRC’s salmon-health account connects fishers’ observations with a research program involving tissue samples, measurements and laboratory work. Sampling across locations and portions of the run helps examine variation that a single collection could miss. Working with people already harvesting salmon links monitoring to community food priorities and practical knowledge of the river. The project is described as preliminary surveillance with partner laboratories and federal support. Its sampled observations provide a starting point for continued investigation; they cannot establish every fish’s condition or explain salmon trends across other watersheds.

sections.title: Winter travel, knowledge and changing conditions
sections.text: Miller’s collaborative study brings regional residents’ experiences into an account of changing winter access. Interviewees describe later or less reliable river ice, variable snow and effects on trapping, firewood gathering and travel. Their observations differ, and the nine interviews were selected for experience rather than as a population survey. Ahtna elders’ accounts appear alongside Upper Tanana and other residents’ testimony. The article also examines wage employment, settlement and changing transport technology. Those connections show why environmental change belongs within a wider history of work and access, while historical descriptions cannot establish safe crossing places today.

sources.contentReviewScope: Read printed pp.102–103 and 107–116 (PDF 1–2,6–15), including methodological notes; visually checked p.108. Historical rights and settlement accounts were reviewed, not original interviews or current legal status.

Proposed regulatory changes are recommendations, not demonstrated later decisions.

sources.title: Copper River Salmon Health Surveillance
sources.annotation: Read the substantive project text, sampling design, community participation and laboratory-method sections. This undated page describes work illustrated by 2023–2025 activity. It supplies a substantial account of community-led monitoring and partnerships. Preliminary sampled-fish observations do not establish watershed-wide prevalence, a causal explanation for salmon declines, or food-safety advice. Images and linked pages are not extra counted works.

Nine purposively selected interviews include Ahtna, Upper Tanana and other regional residents. Their accounts connect environmental and socioeconomic changes, with differing experiences. Historical travel descriptions and crossing maps are not current safety guidance or public-access routes.

sources.title: About the Ahtna Intertribal Resource Commission
sources.annotation: Read the complete substantive About text, membership, territory description and simplified timeline. sources.title: Ahtna Villages
sources.annotation: Read the complete short prose statement naming eight regional villages and describing the 1980 merger of seven village corporations, with Chitina remaining separate. Short supporting institutional reference only; the interactive map was not audited for boundaries or access rights.

sources.title: Ahtna History & Culture
sources.annotation: Read the complete substantive prose and captions surrounding resource links. Describes the Copper River name, seasonal family food work and continuing practices; shareholder totals are not a people’s census. Short overview/resource gateway kept outside the substantive inspected-source count. Linked videos, books, lesson pages and Smithsonian items are not represented as read or watched. Undated language/dialect claims require specialist context.

sources.title: About Us — Native Village of Gakona
sources.annotation: Read the complete short page describing sovereign government, services, council and justices. Short service/staff directory kept outside the substantive count; no current staffing or service availability inferred beyond the posted account.

sources.title: Ahtna — language overview
sources.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks
sources.annotation: Read the complete short overview, geography, publication-history statement and credited examples. Supporting orientation outside the substantive inspected-source count. Its undated speaker and population estimates are not adopted as current counts; linked publications are not represented as separately read. A separate automated request failed certificate verification; the page was read through the web research tool.

relationshipNote: Ahtna is a Northern Dene people and language name. Ahtna, Incorporated and Chitina Native Corporation are Native landholding corporations; village tribal governments and AITRC have different roles. The eight regional member tribes form an institutional partnership, not a statement that every resident has one language or identical affiliation. The Dene entry supplies wider context and is not a single government encompassing these institutions.
researchGaps: Add more village-authored histories and contemporary perspectives from Cantwell, Mentasta, Cheesh’na, Kluti-Kaah and other communities; this introduction has not received community review.

name: Akateko
region: Guatemala / Huehuetenango; Mexico / Chiapas, Campeche and Quintana Roo; diaspora
overview: Follow Akateko histories through community language scholarship, place names, teaching resources, refuge and settlement studies, local planning and a named diaspora voice. This introduction keeps different communities, dates and kinds of evidence in view, with annotations that show what was actually read and what remains to investigate.

sections.title: A people, a language and several local settings
sections.text: Akateko is a Maya people and language name. INPI records Kuti’ as a self-designation. A Guatemalan school history places communities around San Miguel Acatán, San Rafael La Independencia and Jo’om. These descriptions neither draw fixed boundaries nor establish a single government.

sections.title: Language names and relationships
sections.text: Akateko and Awakateko are different Maya languages: the Akateko grammar groups Akateko with Q’anjob’al, Chuj and Popti’, while the Awakateko community’s atlas places Awakateko in the Mamean group and identifies its original core in Aguacatán.

sections.title: Place names as community knowledge
sections.text: The 2019 toponymy study treats names as part of Akateko cultural heritage and language continuity. It revises earlier work through local knowledge, combining place descriptions, historical accounts and analysis of meaningful word parts. The conclusion credits older community members as important sources. Reading such entries shows how language and local history meet, while particular explanations remain attributed to the study. Published names and dated settlement descriptions should not be mistaken for current demographic records or an authorization to enter private or culturally sensitive places.

sections.title: Reading a history alongside community memory
sections.text: The Landívar school volume combines regional history with narrated community memories. It connects San Miguel Acatán and San Rafael La Independencia and describes their separation into municipalities in 1924. Its historical account follows changing labor demands and later wartime displacement. Read it as a dated teaching synthesis: memories and regional summaries invite comparison with original records. The PDF carries a 1997 copyright even though another catalogue lists 2016. Neither date makes its population figures current.

sections.title: Building a community after refuge
sections.text: A study coauthored by José Luis Francisco Mateo, identified by the publisher as of Akateko and K’anjob’al origin and a child of refugees, follows families who chose to remain in Chiapas. It recounts repeated moves, work and collective efforts to obtain land before establishing San Marcos in La Trinitaria. Education promoters and continuing visits to relatives across the border also appear in the account. This is a particular mixed community’s history, rather than evidence that every Akateko family followed the same route or made the same choice.

sections.title: Local institutions in Chiapas
sections.text: INPI’s ethnography distinguishes municipal agency roles from ejido land administration in La Gloria. It also describes religious diversity and public San Miguel celebrations connecting settlements with Guatemala. These are accounts of particular Mexican communities, not a universal institutional or religious pattern. The source’s discussion of clothing links changing use to security, cost and migration; dress should be understood through those histories rather than as an unchanging test of identity.

sections.title: Young people, education and belonging
sections.text: Ruiz Lagier’s 2011 study compares young people in La Gloria, San Francisco and Nueva Libertad. Her interviews connect schooling, work, migration and family expectations with changing ideas about adulthood and gender. Young returnees can seek different choices while still asserting a Migueleño connection with San Miguel Acatán. The author compares public expectations with everyday practices, rather than treating them as identical. These dated accounts show negotiation within and across communities; they are neither a current survey nor instructions for how all Akateko people should live.

sections.title: Shared writing conventions
sections.text: The Akateko community’s 2024 normative grammar presents writing conventions for teachers, public servants and other readers. Its letter distinguishes standardizing written forms from changing people’s speech and recognizes that rules may be revised. Later examples compare regional pronunciations before specifying written forms. The work offers a substantial guide to community language planning, while proposed conventions remain distinct from a claim that everyone speaks identically or uses the book.

sections.title: Documenting variation through community research
sections.text: The 2013 descriptive revision draws on fieldwork and review workshops in San Miguel Acatán and San Rafael La Independencia. It describes differences between their speech while leaving open precisely how to classify that variation. Its discussions of classifiers and regional vocabulary demonstrate that learning the language involves grammatical relationships and situated usage. The introduction explicitly presents a description of speech at a particular moment. It should not be converted into a timeless catalogue of how every Akateko person speaks.

sections.title: Teaching listening, speaking, reading and writing
sections.text: Kukuy Ti’e Akateko offers teachers a sequence linking listening and speaking with literacy. Its introduction places Akateko culture at the center of learning and connects teachers, students and families. Actual lessons pair written forms with Spanish glosses, pronunciation practice and classroom prompts; later exercises provide space for learners’ written responses. The work documents a developed educational approach. Its aims and preparation credit do not by themselves establish where it is taught today or how learners have experienced it.

sections.title: Literature as a teaching resource
sections.text: The Akateka language community’s 2020 literary publication sets out separate approaches for first-language revitalization and second-language learners. Its guides connect oral storytelling, proficient speakers, reading and writing. The introduction describes adapted and translated narratives rather than claiming an exclusively Akateko origin for every story. This is evidence of community educational work and stated teaching methods; publication alone does not demonstrate how many classrooms used the material or what learners achieved.

sections.title: A dated municipal view of priorities
sections.text: San Miguel Acatán’s 2019–2032 development plan offers a local-government perspective. Its diagnosis discusses school access, water and health services, alongside agriculture and markets. It identifies infrastructure and economic opportunities while proposing future improvements. The 2032 vision is a planning goal, not an achieved condition. Municipal statistics mix years and some schooling estimates are attributed to local officials; they should not be treated as current community-wide rates. This document concerns one jurisdiction rather than every Akateko settlement.

sections.title: Photographs, memory and who represents the community
sections.text: Returning to La Gloria in 2021, Ruiz-Lagier considered how earlier refugee photographs became part of remembering the community’s origins. Her 2024 article describes a local cultural promoter seeking photographs for community use and reflects on the different perspectives of residents, photographers and researchers. She also notes that religious participation had changed. This makes memory a continuing social process, rather than a single unchanging story. The article does not establish a completed museum or authorize copying its images; its account remains an attributed interpretation.

sections.title: One family’s route to Los Angeles
sections.text: In Getty’s 2022 interview, Aurora Pedro, identified as Maya Akateko and Q’anjob’al, recounts her family fleeing Guatemala to Chiapas in 1982 and later moving to Los Angeles, where she was born. She connects experiences of racism across borders with the work of building community. Speaking about CIELO’s advocacy, she calls for schools, hospitals and other public institutions to provide meaningful language access. Her family’s account makes one diaspora history visible without turning a dual identity, an organization’s work or an individual route into a description of all Akateko migrants.

sections.title: Using a locality catalogue carefully
sections.text: INALI lists Kuti’ under Akateko and supplies localities in Chiapas, Campeche and Quintana Roo, including La Gloria, Maya Tecún I and Maya Balam. The table helps a reader follow names into more detailed research. A short language catalogue cannot establish a complete population count, the extent of historical homelands, or political equivalence among the listed communities.

The Comunidad Lingüística Akateka is an ALMG language institution, not a single political government for every Akateko community. researchGaps: Extend Guatemalan colonial, labor and archaeological history with original records and specialist comparisons. A dated school synthesis is not an independently corroborated chronology, and the present introduction does not offer a comprehensive early history.
Add more directly focused community accounts from Campeche and Quintana Roo and a wider range of Guatemalan local perspectives; a Mexican language-locality table does not fill those gaps.

Establish present community-approved teaching use, learner experiences and outcomes. Publications record educational work and intended methods, rather than current adoption, success rates or speaker totals.
Expand women’s, young people’s, artists’ and land users’ accounts without treating one person or one settlement as representative of everyone. The introduction has not received community review.

Follow municipal plans and dated local accounts through later implementation and current evidence. No present health or education rates, exact diaspora counts, land-title conclusions or officeholders are established here.

Compare earlier naming and population categories with their own dates and geographic scope. Distinct grammars and different studies can share earlier research; repeated background is not automatically independent confirmation.

Inspect the retained Prospera scholarship when ordinary lawful full-text access permits. Current repository download failures do not prove that every reader faces a paywall, and abstracts remain separate from article-body checks.

Check community context, image permissions and cartographic rights before later visual design or mapping. Public place-name publications do not grant entry to cultural sites or permission to reproduce photographs or boundary geometry.
