name: Arapaho
overview: Arapaho histories include distinct Northern and Southern community experiences. This reading path connects historical change with particular governments, language education, community-authored research and collaborative public history, keeping regional perspectives separate.

sections.title: Northern and southern historical trajectories
sections.text: The Arapaho Project’s Northern Arapaho history distinguishes northern communities centered on the North Platte from southern communities associated with the Arkansas valley. It places the Northern Arapaho move to Wind River in 1878. Its account also connects boarding schools, allotment and pressures on language with later community-controlled education and cultural renewal. This is a Northern-focused historical synthesis; its undated descriptions of contemporary conditions require fresh corroboration.

sections.title: Finding the Northern Arapaho government's own resources
sections.text: The Northern Arapaho Tribe's website identifies Wind River as its location and links governmental and departmental resources. It offers a starting point for a particular tribal government's public information. Its brief homepage is a navigation source; the linked publications require their own reading and dates before supporting detailed historical or policy claims.

sections.title: A shared government's constitutional framework
sections.text: The Tribes' amended constitution identifies ratification on April 4, 2006. Its preamble links self-government with languages, education and protection of the natural environment. Article II establishes four branches, including the Tribal Council; Articles V–VI distinguish that adult membership body from a legislature representing four Cheyenne and four Arapaho districts. This describes the shared Oklahoma government's framework rather than a constitution for all Arapaho people.

sections.title: Education as an expression of self-determination
sections.text: The Tribe's 2006 Education Code presents education as part of Northern Arapaho self-determination. It prioritizes Arapaho language, history and culture alongside academic learning and parent and community participation. It expressly disclaims authority over Eastern Shoshone education policy. This dated publication documents the Northern Arapaho government's stated priorities; its presence online does not verify implementation, educational outcomes or unchanged current law.

sections.title: Southern language teaching and public cultural work
sections.text: The Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes describe teaching both distinct languages through community classes, youth outreach, Elder partnerships and an adult apprenticeship program. These are the institution's stated approaches, without a measured fluency outcome. Its Culture Program also describes representatives working on repatriation and with the National Park Service on public interpretation of Sand Creek. These responsibilities concern the shared Oklahoma institution, rather than every Arapaho community's programs or cultural authority.

sections.title: Apprentices describe language learning
sections.text: In Latoya Lonelodge's 2023 Tribal Tribune interviews, Arapaho apprentice Arianna Long describes progressing from isolated words toward conversation and learning with coworkers while attending college. Rachelle RomanNose discusses pronunciation, expressing herself and the continuing work of learning. Her interest in teaching is an aspiration, not evidence that certification was completed. Their accounts bring individual Southern Arapaho women's voices into a discussion that also includes separately identified Cheyenne learners.

sections.title: Approaching Arapaho grammar
sections.text: The Arapaho Project explains that words can combine many meaningful elements. Verbs can express information that English distributes across several words, including participants, tense and aspect. Its animate/inanimate distinctions are grammatical, rather than a simple division between living and nonliving things. These introductory explanations offer a starting point for exploring language structure; the linked collection should be used with community teaching and does not certify proficiency.

sections.title: A grammar grounded in documented usage
sections.text: Cowell and Arapaho coauthor Alonzo Moss, Sr. present their grammar through communicative use as well as forms and rules. Its introduction explains a corpus combining historical records, educational materials and more recent speech, with sources from Wyoming and Oklahoma. The authors identify revisions and corrections to earlier transcriptions. This makes the book useful for understanding how linguistic knowledge is documented, while its evidence remains distinct from a current speaker census.

sections.title: Community collaboration in language documentation
sections.text: Kelly and Cowell describe virtual-reality language documentation developed through iterative work with the Northern Arapaho Language and Culture Commission. Elders helped select contexts, and applications were checked for usability and cultural appropriateness. Sessions in 2019–2020 informed the study. The authors compare elicited language with other documentation methods; their findings concern recorded speech and research design, rather than proof that an application produces fluent learners.

sections.title: Food sovereignty and telling community histories
sections.text: In a 2019 study, Northern Arapaho researcher Melvin L. Arthur, with Christine M. Porter, relates food sovereignty to community control over historical storytelling. Interviews, talking circles, personal experience and historical research inform his account of disrupted food access and reclamation. He places these changes within colonial dispossession. This is a situated Northern Arapaho interpretation, without demonstrating current clinical outcomes or unanimity among community members.

sections.title: Descendant knowledge and documentary investigation
sections.text: The NPS overview describes descendant knowledge alongside archival research in locating and interpreting Sand Creek. Its short orientation provides a starting point for public history, rather than a complete account of the 1864 attack or its aftermath. The linked individual testimony and media were not inspected for this collection.

sections.title: Who controls an oral-history project?
sections.text: Alexa Roberts describes the Northern Arapaho Tribe choosing to conduct its part of the 1999 oral-history project internally. Her account explains why participation and control of research materials mattered, while describing different arrangements with Cheyenne communities. This is evidence about a particular collaborative process. The underlying recordings, interviews and photographs were not accessed or reproduced, and their permissions are not Atlas reuse rights.

sections.title: A dated framework for collaborative public history
sections.text: The December 2017 foundation document identifies tribal histories and consultation as important to interpreting the site. Its planning entries call for further community involvement and review of research. These are dated institutional priorities and identified needs, not proof that proposed projects were completed. They do not establish a single position shared by every Arapaho government or person.

sections.title: Directories as access points
sections.text: The departmental directory lists an Ethete immersion entry alongside other public services. Such listings help readers find Northern Arapaho institutions. A directory alone does not establish current staffing, availability, teaching methods or results. Detailed claims about educational work need a dated publication that explains its purposes, practices and evidence.

This provides an institutional starting point for the shared Oklahoma government; its organization should be kept distinct from Northern Arapaho institutions at Wind River.

name: Arikara
overview: Arikara, or Sahnish, is a distinct people within the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation. This reviewed starting guide covers village histories, river-community displacement and educational priorities. Deeper Arikara-specific research remains unfinished.

sections.title: A shared government and distinct peoples
sections.text: MHA Nation’s official site identifies the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation at Fort Berthold in North Dakota. It describes a Tribal Business Council with a chairman and representatives from six segments. This provides institutional orientation to a shared government; it does not make Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara interchangeable names or turn the reservation into their entire historical homeland.

sections.title: Village movements and river-community displacement
sections.text: MHA Nation’s history distinguishes Sahnish village movements from Mandan and Hidatsa histories. Its narrative and timeline differ between 1862 and 1863, so the move into Like-a-Fishhook is described here as the early 1860 s. The page also recounts Garrison Dam relocation as a loss of fertile bottomlands and connected communities, with relocation completed by fall 1954.

sections.title: Language priorities and community educational work
sections.text: MHA Nation presents Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara as separate languages and acknowledges Elders, teachers, Nueta Hidatsa Sahnish College and the MHA Language Project. Its portal identifies learning materials and past Arikara class recordings. This is an institutional account of educational priorities and collaboration; listing resources does not establish their contents, effectiveness or present class schedules as independently checked.

sections.title: Gardening and village economies
sections.text: North Dakota Studies identifies Sahnish as the people’s own name and places Arikara village history along the Missouri River. Its educational account describes earthlodge homes, gardening of corn, beans and squash, food preservation and hunting. It also discusses epidemics and movement toward Like-a-Fishhook. These selected historical explanations do not describe every family or establish present practices.

sections.title: Reading expedition accounts critically
sections.text: The NPS introduction identifies Arikara as a Caddoan language and describes farming villages and regional trade. It explicitly warns that expedition observers’ accounts were not necessarily correct from Indigenous perspectives and that the displayed excerpts have been adapted. These limits matter: similar-looking homes do not establish common origins, and an edited excerpt is distinct from an original journal.

sections.title: A reconstruction used for public interpretation

Its interpretation concerns Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara peoples together. The listing offers an introduction to public historical interpretation, rather than an unchanged ancestral settlement or an exclusively Arikara village; present visitor arrangements require separate checking.

name: Assiniboine
overview: Assiniboine is an outside name for northern Plains peoples who use names including Nakoda, Nakota and Nakona in community contexts. Their histories and kinship cross the Canada–United States border, while contemporary governments remain distinct. Fort Belknap, Fort Peck and Saskatchewan First Nations offer different perspectives on land, language and continuing political life.

sections.title: Names, language and origin accounts
sections.text: Fort Belknap’s history identifies Assiniboine people as Nakoda or Nakota. Assiniboine derives from an Ojibwe name associated with cooking with heated stones. These names should be read in their local contexts. Linguistically, Nakoda belongs to the Siouan family. Linda Cumberland’s grammar also cautions against an old classification that treated Nakoda simply as a minor variant of Dakota and Lakota. Linguistic relationships do not settle every question of historical origin: Fort Belknap preserves oral accounts that differ from familiar outsider migration narratives.

sections.title: Bison, mobility and trade networks
sections.text: Bison supplied food, hides and materials for mobile Plains communities. Assiniboine people also traded meat and pelts with Missouri River agricultural communities for crops and other goods. Their relations with European trading companies built on Indigenous knowledge, diplomacy and exchange. At Fort Union, founded in 1828, Assiniboine permission enabled the post’s establishment, and Assiniboine traders became its principal partners. Women’s marriages and kinship relationships helped sustain those connections. This history places Indigenous communities at the center of the trading economy rather than at its margins.

sections.title: Epidemics and the coercion of reservation life
sections.text: Smallpox repeatedly devastated northern Plains communities, including Assiniboine people connected with the Upper Missouri trade. The University of Saskatchewan’s synthesis places these epidemics alongside changing commercial networks and the destruction of bison herds. It describes later reserve life as shaped by restricted mobility, hunger, residential schooling and prohibitions on cultural and political activities. These pressures differed across the international boundary and among local communities. Reservation settlement consequently cannot be explained as a simple voluntary abandonment of older lifeways or as the end of Indigenous collective identity.

sections.title: Carry the Kettle and Cypress Hills homelands
sections.text: FHQ Developments’ community account dates the Treaty 4 adhesion by ancestors of Carry the Kettle to September 25, 1877 at Fort Walsh. It identifies the western Cypress Hills, including the Head of the Mountain, as a homeland of enduring significance. The community-authored history Owóknage follows forced removal from those lands to the area south of Sintaluta, Saskatchewan. Its published contents bring together land use, treaty-era farming, language, sacred places, harvesting and environmental concerns, drawing on Elder interviews as well as documentary research.

sections.title: Distinct peoples within contemporary governments
sections.text: Fort Belknap Indian Community in Montana unites Nakoda and Aaniiih, also called Gros Ventre, in a shared government. The reservation was established in 1888 and represents only part of the peoples’ wider ancestral territories. Fort Peck institutions separately serve Assiniboine and Sioux communities; their language department distinguishes Nakona/Nakoda from Dakota. Carry the Kettle is another particular First Nation rather than a name for all Assiniboine people in Canada. Shared institutions, broad peoplehood and individual governments therefore need to be kept distinct when tracing contemporary sovereignty.

sections.title: Language renewal and community knowledge
sections.text: Fort Peck’s language department describes revitalization through community curriculum, Elder stories, history, songs and daily cultural learning. Its stated vision includes developing immersion education, which should be distinguished from evidence that a particular new school has already opened. Cumberland’s 2025 grammar provides a complementary reference on Nakoda sounds, grammar, kinship and writing systems, with attention to different practical orthographies. Community teaching and scholarly documentation serve related purposes, but the authority of particular speakers, families and institutions remains essential to how knowledge is learned and shared.

sources.title: Fort Belknap History

Stoney Nakoda has close historical and linguistic relationships, but a Nakoda spelling alone does not identify the same community, language variety or government.

name: Atakapa
overview: Atakapa/Atakapan is a historical label used in Gulf Coast records for multiple groups in present-day Louisiana and Texas. The Atakapa-Ishak Nation of Southwest Louisiana and Southeast Texas, Grand Bayou Indian Village’s Atakapa-Ishak/Chawasha community, and the Attakapas Opelousas Prairie Tribe are identified as distinct present organized groups in the sources cited here; The Louisiana Attakapas Eagle Band also appears in a short page as a self-described present organization; the relationship between its Four Winds affiliation wording and the Governor’s roster entry “Four Winds Cherokee” remains unresolved here. These accounts are not collapsed into one government. This profile attributes historical syntheses and community perspectives to their authors, and does not infer disappearance from language loss or older population claims.

sections.title: Names and community scope
sections.text: The Nation’s own pages use Ishak and Atakapa-Ishak and describe its Southwest Louisiana and Southeast Texas scope. Jeffery U. Darensbourg’s public-history essay and the Handbook of Texas show how older outside records used forms such as Atakapa/Atakapan for several groups and adjacent bands. Darensbourg also describes other organized Ishak groups, including the Attakapas Opelousas Prairie Tribe and Grand Bayou Indian Village. These sources do not establish a single present government for everyone associated with the historical label; the cultural and political accounts remain community-specific. A separate Louisiana Attakapas Eagle Band webpage describes the group as part of the Four Winds Tribe Louisiana Cherokee Confederation and claims the Calcasieu/Eagle band is state recognized. On the roster checked October 23, 2026, the Louisiana Governor’s Office lists “Four Winds Cherokee” under State Recognized Tribes but does not separately list an Attakapas Eagle Band entry. Since the names are not identical, these two short records do not establish whether the roster entry covers that Band. They document the group’s self-description and the public roster wording, not independent historical evidence or a verified recognition determination. A 2021 Texas Observer interview with Mary LeBlanc, identified by the reporter as Akokisa and a retired Nation council member, offers her account of clan names and local geography. The newspaper says its Unceded project worked with tribal representatives on mapping homelands on their own terms. These are LeBlanc’s reported perspectives; the article’s map is not treated here as boundary evidence, and sensitive ceremonial locations are not reproduced.

sections.title: Gulf Coast history and colonial records
sections.text: The Handbook of Texas and the 1932 Bureau of American Ethnology volume summarize communities and language documentation along the southwest Louisiana–southeast Texas coast. Their accounts depend substantially on European colonial records and early ethnography, with inconsistent group names and dated framing. Claims about cannibalism and rapid demographic loss are reported as historical-source claims, not repeated as settled descriptions of living people. Original colonial records and the archival field cards described by the Smithsonian have not been inspected for this profile. LeBlanc also gives a first-person account of mound use, continuity and change in the region. Those statements are attributed to her and are not independently verified archaeological findings in this guide.

sections.title: Ishakkoy documentation and learning
sections.text: The community account uses Ishakkoy and Yukhíti Kóy for the language and identifies contemporary writing and song activity. In a 2021 essay, Nation member Jeffery U. Darensbourg describes composing poems and song lyrics from examples in the Ishakkoy dictionary and collaborating on the film Hoktiwe; this is his account of a specific creative process, not a measure of language proficiency or community-wide program outcomes. The Living Dictionary says its 2022 edition was produced in close collaboration with Ishāk community members; selected entries and the project overview were inspected, but its permission terms preclude copying its content here. The 1932 dictionary preserves historical materials collected by Gatschet and Swanton, and Geoffrey Kimball’s later grammar reanalyzes those notes. Only selected grammar excerpts were available.

sections.title: Identity, art and cultural memory
sections.text: The Atakapa-Ishak Nation’s cultural page describes elder-led work, artists, basketry, shellwork and beadwork, and connects zydeco to its own community interpretation and named scholarship. Darensbourg’s interview and essay give his personal perspective as a Nation member on Ishakkoy poetry, place and historical food memory. His essay explicitly distinguishes inherited memory from his own experience and builds on an older written account; that reflection is valuable as a contemporary community voice but is not independent proof of every historical detail or of a universal Ishak cultural practice.

sections.title: Contemporary communities and coastal life
sections.text: The Atakapa-Ishak Nation of Southwest Louisiana and Southeast Texas and the Atakapa-Ishak/Chawasha community of Grand Bayou Indian Village appear in distinct first-party and reported accounts. An Associated Press report quotes named Grand Bayou members about their own fishing, community life and coastal stewardship. The First People’s Conservation Council page is a brief corroborating community-context link. These sources describe particular organizations and people; they do not speak for every descendant or community linked to historical Atakapa names. The Observer interview adds one named Akokisa elder’s perspective on community continuity, visibility and safety in southeast Texas. It should be read alongside the Nation’s own pages and Grand Bayou’s separately scoped accounts, not generalized to all present groups.

sections.title: Trade and conditional participation around a mission
sections.text: Margaret Swett Henson places El Orcoquisac within competing French and Spanish efforts to control trade in southeastern Texas. Her account distinguishes colonial plans for a mission and presidio from local people’s participation: offers of supplies, disagreements and conditions on settlement shaped their encounters. Read its names, including Orcoquisa and Attakapa, in that eighteenth-century setting. The article is a historian’s reconstruction through earlier documentary scholarship, not a first-person Indigenous account or proof of present affiliations. Its underlying colonial manuscripts still need direct review.

LeBlanc discusses distinctions among clan names, local geography, community life and her recollections of place and change. These are a named community member’s reported perspectives, not independently verified archaeological conclusions or a statement for every Atakapa/Ishak community. The article includes sensitive cultural-site discussion and an accompanying map; the Atlas does not reproduce the map or disclose nonpublic ceremonial locations.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the complete visible article, including author/interviewee identification, project context and interview through the final learning-resources question. The interviewee’s statements about ancient continuity, mound dimensions and functions, and historical movement are retained only as her attributed account, not independently checked. sources.title: "El Orcoquisac" 1756–1771: The Mission Nuestra Señora de la Luz del Orcoquisac, the Presidio San Agustín de Ahumada, and the Rivalry between the Spanish and the French for the Indian Trade in Southeastern Texas

sources.annotation: A historian’s account of a Spanish mission and presidio amid French–Spanish trading rivalry. It helps contextualize named Orcoquisa, Bedais and Attakapa actors, but relies heavily on older documentary scholarship. Its historical labels and interpretations do not establish present community identity, descent or consent to colonial rule.
sources.contentReviewScope: Complete article body and footnotes, printed pp. 115–126, read visually in all seven PDF scan frames. The preceding map page 114 was encountered but not evaluated for evidence, rights or reuse. Original colonial manuscripts and works cited in the footnotes were not independently inspected.
sources.countReason: One new substantive regional historical study actually read, addressing the mission-history gap; not another count for its bibliography or source documents.
sources.accessNotes: Public English PDF, no account/paywall encountered. Image-only scan: pypdf returned no extractable article text, so all narrative pages were rendered and read visually. This limits screen-reader/text-search access; use the Atlas’s cited plain-language synthesis and existing readable Handbook route as orientation. No reuse license established; link-only. No map, site coordinates, cemetery detail or archaeological material reproduced.
sources.accessStatus: Public image-only PDF; not searchable text

relationshipNote: Atakapa is a historical outside label; Ishak is a self-designation. The people and their associated historical groups are broader than any single present-day Ishak organization. A Louisiana Attakapas Eagle Band page is included as its own contemporary self-description, alongside an official state roster. The Band’s webpage states an affiliation using the name “Four Winds Tribe Louisiana Cherokee Confederation” and asserts state recognition for its Calcasieu/Eagle band; the Governor’s roster uses “Four Winds Cherokee” and does not list “Louisiana Attakapas Eagle Band” separately. These records do not resolve whether the names refer to the same listed body, so no equivalence or separate recognition determination is inferred.
researchGaps: The colonial and early ethnographic record needs closer review in French, Spanish and original archival materials; broad labels such as Atakapa, Akokisa and Deadose are not always used consistently.

The language guide relies on historical documentation alongside a collaborative online resource. The full Kimball grammar was not accessed, and present learning activity or outcomes should not be inferred from resource availability.
Archaeological, regional oral-history and mission histories need deeper comparison. No historical map was added because a sourced map/community connection was not reviewed in this batch.

A Louisiana Attakapas Eagle Band webpage now supplies that group’s self-description, but the relation between the Band’s longer Four Winds affiliation name and the Governor’s roster label “Four Winds Cherokee,” and the Band’s state-recognition claim, remain unresolved from these short records. Additional relevant community and government documentation would be needed.

Perspectives from other organized groups and descendant communities remain uneven; the Louisiana Attakapas Eagle Band is represented only by its short self-description and a public state roster whose wording does not settle the organization’s relationship to the listed Four Winds Cherokee entry.

The 2021 Texas Observer interview supplies an important but individually scoped Akokisa perspective. Independent archaeological and archival corroboration is still needed for historical-site and deep-time statements; sensitive places should not be republished.

initialAdequacy.rationale: One newly read regional mission-history study adds useful Texas context to the twelve-work guide, bringing the substantive count to thirteen. It does not resolve inconsistent historical names or replace direct colonial-record, archaeological and broader community review. The additional archival dossier located in this pass remains unread and uncounted.
remainingLimits: Original Spanish/French records, mission files, specialist archaeology and the Smithsonian’s Swanton/Morse manuscript cards remain unread.
Current community perspectives are meaningful but not comprehensive across all groups connected to the historical label.
The complete Kimball grammar and Darensbourg–Kaufman language-renewal chapter were not accessed.
No community review is recorded; historical identity and group relationships remain unresolved in the sources examined.

The 2021 Texas Observer interview is one elder’s reported perspective; its accompanying map and underlying archaeological evidence were not independently reviewed, and sensitive cultural-site details are deliberately omitted.

gaps: French, Spanish and Mexican colonial manuscripts and mission records need direct inspection; the current historical synthesis inherits older naming schemes and does not resolve all relationships among Atakapa, Akokisa, Deadose, Bidai, Opelousas and Chawasha.

Current community material represents the Atakapa-Ishak Nation of Southwest Louisiana and Southeast Texas, one Nation member’s authored work, and Grand Bayou’s specific community context. Other organized-group and descendant perspectives require their own sources; no community review or endorsement is recorded.

The Smithsonian MS 2424 field cards are described by a finding aid but remain unread. The 1932 dictionary is represented by selected pages, and Kimball’s full grammar and Darensbourg and Kaufman’s 2019 language-renewal chapter were not accessed.

A 2013 Louisiana Folklife overview and an Inter-Tribal Council booklet were examined as leads but not adopted as substantive evidence: they are brief and/or repeat older group and disappearance narratives without enough transparent support for current educational synthesis. A legacy Atakapa-Ishak site result contained unrelated pharmacy spam and is excluded as compromised.
No historical map is added in this batch: no map-to-community connection and reuse terms were independently reviewed.

The Texas Observer interview adds one Akokisa elder’s account, but claims about ancient continuity and mound form/function were not independently checked against archaeological publications; the accompanying map was not reviewed for reuse or connection evidence.

Image-only reader-access limit recorded. Historical names do not establish modern identity. No additional maps or archival leads counted.

name: Atikamekw
overview: The Atikamekw Nehirowisiw are a distinct nation whose homeland, Nitaskinan, lies in the interior of Québec. Manawan, Opitciwan and Wemotaci have their own councils and cooperate through Atikamekw Sipi. Language, family responsibilities for territory and the assertion of continuing sovereignty connect community life with wider political and environmental concerns.

sections.title: Nitaskinan and territorial responsibility
sections.text: Manawan's account locates identity in a territory inhabited by ancestors and entrusted to future generations. It describes a family system in which responsibility for managing a territory passes between generations; collective belonging differs from individual land ownership. Rivers, travel routes and place names connect Manawan with the Saint-Maurice, Outaouais and neighboring watersheds. This understanding of homeland reaches beyond the boundaries of any one reserve and beyond Québec's more recent administrative regions.

sections.title: Language and knowledge
sections.text: Nehirowimowin is the Atikamekw language. Manawan's language page presents speech, territory and identity as inseparable, emphasizing vocabulary shaped by local environments and the self-designation Nehirowisiw. It also describes relationships with other Algonquian-speaking peoples, without making those nations interchangeable. Québec's profile identifies Atikamekw-language educational materials among Atikamekw Sipi's services. The combination matters: language is both an everyday medium of community life and a means through which institutions transmit knowledge and support younger generations.

sections.title: Industrial development and displacement
sections.text: Québec's historical summary places a major turning point in early twentieth-century industrial forestry. A sawmill at La Tuque and the railway's expansion toward Wemotaci and Abitibi brought workers and other resource users into Atikamekw territories. Dam building caused further moves between 1950 and 1972. These developments changed access to land and patterns of settlement. They should be understood as interventions in an existing homeland, rather than as the beginning of Atikamekw history or presence in the region.

sections.title: Local councils and nation-wide cooperation
sections.text: Atikamekw Sipi, founded in 1982, works across Manawan, Opitciwan and Wemotaci. Its published governance structure distinguishes ordinary members, elected representatives with voting responsibilities and the board made up of the Grand Chief/President and the three community chiefs. The assembly uses consensus, while the board uses majority decisions. Social, educational, linguistic and technical services operate alongside political representation and negotiations. These overlapping institutions show why the nation, its coordinating council and its three local governments should be identified separately.

sections.title: The 2014 sovereignty declaration
sections.text: On September 8, 2014, the nation's leaders publicly affirmed continuing sovereignty over Nitaskinan. Their declaration states that the territory had not been ceded or sold and links governance to occupation, language, inherited responsibilities and relationships with neighboring nations. It demands Atikamekw consent for resource development and use. This is the nation's political position and statement of rights; it should not be confused with a completed territorial settlement or a declaration that Canadian and Québec authorities have accepted every claimed jurisdiction.

sources.title: Territoire
sources.annotation: Manawan's explanation of collective territorial belonging, intergenerational management responsibilities, travel routes and local place names. Its perspective is specifically grounded in Manawan.

sources.title: Langue
sources.annotation: Community explanation connecting Nehirowisiw identity, language and environmental knowledge. Provides a first-person complement to external linguistic classifications.

sources.title: Atikamekw

name: Atsugewi
overview: Atsugewi homelands lie south of the Pit River in northeastern California, including Hat Creek and Dixie Valley. Atsugewi identity has both local historical dimensions and a place within the present Pit River Tribe. Language archives, seasonal land-use histories and the work of Atsugewi cultural interpreters provide complementary routes into that continuing history.

sections.title: Homelands and seasonal movement
sections.text: Hat Creek connected fishing grounds, winter settlements and routes into the Lassen highlands. In warmer months, Atsugewi people traveled along Hat Creek and Lost Creek into areas now within Lassen Volcanic National Park. Snow and elevation shaped seasonal use rather than making the high country uninhabited or without owners. National Park Service interpretation distinguishes the Atsuge of the pine-covered Hat Creek area from the Apwaruge of the drier country farther east; Berkeley also identifies Dixie Valley within the language's traditional area.

sections.title: Atsugewi within the Pit River Tribe
sections.text: The Pit River Tribe's own introduction identifies eleven autonomous bands, including Atsugewi, whose homeland encompasses parts of Shasta, Siskiyou, Modoc and Lassen counties. Atsugewi is consequently neither a synonym for every Pit River person nor simply an obsolete label. The modern tribal framework brings distinct bands together while acknowledging their autonomy. Readers should also distinguish Ajumawi, a band name in the Tribe's list, from the spellings Achumawi or Achomawi used in linguistic and historical publications.

sections.title: Language relationships and the documentary record
sections.text: Berkeley's California Language Archive identifies Atsugewi and Achumawi together as Palaihnihan, while describing the larger Hokan grouping as a hypothesis. Linguistic relatedness does not make the languages identical. The archive's guide points to D. L. Olmsted's 1984 lexicon and Leonard Talmy's 1972 dissertation, Semantic Structures in English and Atsugewi, alongside archival collections. These resources preserve vocabulary and analysis, but each reflects particular speakers, collection circumstances and scholarly questions rather than an exhaustive account of Atsugewi knowledge.

sections.title: Women as public cultural educators
sections.text: Selena LaMarr began interpreting Atsugewi cultural practices at Lassen in June 1952 and became the park's first woman naturalist. She demonstrated basket weaving and acorn processing outside the Loomis Museum, wearing Atsugewi dress as her park uniform. Dessie Snooks joined the work in 1954; Laverna Jenkins and Lillian Snooks later continued demonstrations. Their teaching documents named Atsugewi people's active roles in deciding what visitors learned, rather than treating baskets and food-processing tools as anonymous remains of the past.

sections.title: Continuity and the limits of archival categories
sections.text: Park accounts describe tribal participation in identifying museum collections and reviewing exhibits and publications. The Tribe's own website also advertises Pit River language sessions, although that announcement alone does not establish their Atsugewi-specific content. Berkeley's statement about the absence of first-language Atsugewi speakers draws on a 2011 linguistic reference. It describes language transmission at that source's date, not the disappearance of a people, the end of learning, or the authority of outsiders to define present Atsugewi belonging.

sources.title: American Indian Heritage
sources.publisher: Lassen Volcanic National Park, National Park Service
sources.annotation: Park overview describes Hat Creek seasonal travel, Atsuge and Apwaruge regional distinctions, and tribal collaboration on collections and interpretation. Relevant Atsugewi passages are separated from the page's other peoples.

sources.annotation: Specialist guide to the language area, proposed relationships, archival collections, Olmsted's lexicon and Talmy's dissertation. Speaker-status wording cites Golla 2011 and should retain that temporal context.

relationshipNote: Atsugewi is distinct from Achumawi, although the languages are related and the peoples share Pit River connections. Atsugewi is also one of the Pit River Tribe's eleven autonomous bands.

name: Awakateko
overview: Awakateko people have their principal homeland around Aguacatán in Huehuetenango, Guatemala, with communities also established in Mexico. Their Maya language is called Qa'yool or Qyool in Mexican sources. Community-led language research, school materials and migration histories reveal an identity rooted in a particular highland region while extending across national borders.

sections.title: Names and a highland homeland
sections.text: Mexico's Indigenous-peoples atlas records qatanum, meaning our people, as a self-designation and explains Awakateko through the place name Aguacatán. The community's own linguistic atlas locates its homeland at the foot of the Sierra de los Cuchumatanes. Awakateko is one of several distinct Maya languages, rather than another word for Maya as a whole. Its close linguistic relationship with Ixil should also be distinguished from the similarly spelled Akateko, a different language and people in this directory.

sections.title: Displacement and communities in Mexico
sections.text: INALI connects the Awakateko presence in Mexico with flight from Guatemala's civil war and military repression. Its migration account describes the relocation of Guatemalan Indigenous communities to different Mexican states in 1984–1985, followed by further movement for work, including to the United States. A newer INALI profile specifically identifies Maya Tecún I, Maya Tecún II and Santo Domingo Kesté in Champotón, Campeche. These settlements belong to a transnational history; migration does not make Aguacatán the only legitimate location of Awakateko life.

sections.title: Work, clothing and adaptation
sections.text: The INPI ethnography describes garlic and onion cultivation, seasonal crops, sheep raising, weaving, professional employment and agricultural migration. Its discussion of women's clothing identifies embroidered huipiles, woven skirts and sashes as forms of cultural expression. These are examples within a changing community, not a dress requirement or a complete occupational portrait. The same account notes adaptation of plant knowledge after settlement in Chiapas and Campeche, where different climates and vegetation created new conditions for everyday life.

sections.title: Hearing local variation directly
sections.text: The Atlas Lingüístico Sonoro del Awakateko is led by the Comunidad Lingüística Awakateka within Guatemala's Maya-language academy, with advice from CIESAS and CIMSUR-UNAM. Its first version compares 400 entries from nine Aguacatán communities through maps, recordings and practical and phonetic transcriptions. Two speakers represent each location. Differences occur in sounds, word forms and vocabulary, sometimes within one community. This direct evidence shows why INALI's single catalogued Mexican variety should not be read as proof that everyone speaks identically.

sections.title: Teaching and community authorship
sections.text: In June 2025, Guatemala's government news agency reported the distribution of approximately 2,050 copies of Literatura Maya: Principios y Valores Culturales Awakateko to schools in Aguacatán. The Comunidad Lingüística Awakateka coordinated with educational authorities, reaching institutions at several school levels. Alongside its sound atlas and earlier grammars, this work places community knowledge into learning materials. It also changes the research perspective: Awakateko speakers are authors, investigators and teachers, rather than merely subjects counted in endangered-language statistics.

sources.annotation: Ethnographic overview provides qatanum self-designation, work, dress and adaptation in Mexican settlements. Treat its generalized cultural descriptions as examples, rather than universal practices; full indexed text was inspected.

sources.annotation: Community-led interactive atlas with 400 entries, nine research locations, speaker recordings and transparent sampling methods. Explains local variation and provides a bibliography of community grammars and dictionaries.

sources.annotation: Binational overview identifies Aguacatán and named Campeche settlements and describes the Awakateko–Ixil relationship. Its Mexican catalog classification is administrative in scope; demographic totals are not used here.

name: Awaswas
overview: Awaswas names an Ohlone language associated with the north shore of Monterey Bay and the Santa Cruz region. Its speakers belonged to distinct local communities, including the Uypi. Descendant histories continue through the Amah Mutsun Tribal Band, whose cultural and land-stewardship work connects this regional history with living people and present responsibilities.

sections.title: A language region with distinct local peoples
sections.text: Awaswas is useful as a linguistic and regional label, but it should not turn every historical community into a single centralized tribe. The Santa Cruz Museum identifies its own site as Uypi homeland and describes the Uypi as Awaswas-speaking. The Amah Mutsun Tribal Band explains that its ancestors belonged to numerous communities with distinct territories and leadership, linked through trade and marriage. Ohlone supplies a broader connection, while Awaswas, Uypi and Amah Mutsun identify different aspects of that history.

sections.title: Missionization and descendant continuity
sections.text: Spanish missions brought people from different villages under coercive institutions that disrupted family life, land access, ceremonies and language use. The Amah Mutsun Tribal Band traces its lineages to communities affected by Mission Santa Cruz and Mission San Juan Bautista. Its history describes forced relocation, restrictions on leaving the missions and the continuation of practices under repression. The present Band is therefore a descendant community shaped by this history, rather than a convenient substitute for supposedly vanished people.

sections.title: What survives in the linguistic record
sections.text: The California Language Archive locates Awaswas on Monterey Bay's north shore and identifies it as one of the Ohlone languages, distinct from Mutsun, Rumsen and others. Its documentation survives in wordlists rather than a large recorded speech corpus. The guide links published Pinart and Henshaw vocabularies and William Shipley's study of Awaswas. Such limited material supports research into vocabulary and relationships, but cannot be treated as a complete dictionary of community knowledge or as evidence that descendants ceased to exist.

sections.title: Returning to stewardship
sections.text: The Amah Mutsun Land Trust states that its purpose includes conserving cultural and natural resources in the territories of both Mutsun- and Awaswas-speaking peoples. It describes a 2005 Tribal Council decision to renew stewardship, the creation of the Trust in 2013 and incorporation in 2015. Partnerships with landowners restore access for ceremony, learning and land care. Its stated area extends from Año Nuevo through the Santa Cruz Mountains and Monterey Bay to the Pajaro, San Benito and Salinas watersheds.

sections.title: Environmental pressures are cultural concerns
sections.text: California's climate-impact account describes drought, wildfire, changing rainfall and rising seas as threats to Amah Mutsun physical, spiritual and cultural health. Culturally important plants become harder to restore, while erosion exposes and destroys coastal archaeological places. The account highlights the cumulative effects of fire suppression, land management and climate change in the 2020 CZU fires. These concerns connect historical Awaswas territories to contemporary stewardship; they should not be reduced to museum preservation or separated from the people responsible for those places.

sources.title: First Peoples of California
sources.publisher: Santa Cruz Museum of Natural History
sources.annotation: Local exhibit identifies Uypi homeland and Awaswas language, explains food processing and material practices, and states that displayed local materials involve Amah Mutsun consultation. Useful for geographically specific learning.

sources.title: Land Trust: Our Mutsun Identity
sources.annotation: Tribal account explains the distinct territories and leadership of ancestral communities and the contemporary Band's shared identity. The page links onward to the Land Trust's newer website.

sources.title: History
sources.annotation: The Band's extended account of mission coercion, suppressed practices and continuing family lineages. Contains some inconsistent dates and older recognition-process statements; those details are not adopted in this profile.

sources.title: Awaswas
sources.publisher: California Language Archive, University of California, Berkeley
sources.annotation: Specialist overview identifies the language's area, Ohlone relationships and wordlist-based documentation. Provides specific Pinart, Henshaw and Shipley references rather than a generic language search.

sources.title: Our History and Vision
sources.annotation: The Trust's own account dates its stewardship initiative and organizational development and explicitly includes Awaswas-speaking territories. Distinguishes conservation activity from claims about historical political boundaries.

sources.title: Impacts of climate change on the Amah Mutsun Tribal Band
sources.publisher: California Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment
sources.annotation: August 2023 summary links climate hazards, culturally important species, coastal sites and tribal stewardship. Its environmental discussion connects descendant community priorities with the broader Awaswas–Mutsun region.

relationshipNote: Awaswas is a historical Ohlone language and regional label; Uypi names a local Awaswas-speaking people. The Amah Mutsun Tribal Band includes descendants of Awaswas- and Mutsun-speaking communities. These terms are related but not interchangeable.

name: Ayapaneco
overview: Ayapaneco refers to a language and community associated with Ayapa in Jalpa de Méndez, Tabasco. Also called Ayapa Zoque or numde 'oode, the language belongs to the Mixe-Zoque family. Community authors, teachers and media projects provide a fuller introduction than sensational stories about a disappearing language and its supposedly last speakers.

sections.title: Ayapa and the language's names
sections.text: Ayapa lies on Tabasco's Gulf coastal plain, near the Cuxcuxapa River, in a region shaped by cacao cultivation and contact among Zoque, Nahua, Chontal and other populations. Ayapaneco is also called zoque-ayapaneco or Ayapa Zoque; numde 'oode, numdi oode and numte oote appear in different publications. These spellings refer to the language, not separate peoples. Linguist Jhonnatan Rangel places it in the Mixe-Zoque family and treats interrupted transmission as a specific linguistic challenge.

sections.title: Community life beyond speaker counts
sections.text: INPI's account describes a community with agricultural work, trades, shops, professional employment and migration to regional cities. Cacao remains part of foodways through drinks such as pozol and chorote. Patron-saint celebrations create occasions for local and neighboring communities to gather, with San Miguel especially significant. These practices connect livelihood, food and collective identity. They also show why the number of fluent speakers cannot stand in for the number of community members or the extent of their cultural life.

sections.title: Reading work by named community authors
sections.text: Las partes del cuerpo humano en ayapaneco was published in 2013 under the authorship of Manuel Segovia and José Manuel Segovia, with other Ayapaneco speakers credited as collaborators. It combines an introduction, discussion of sounds and writing, illustrated vocabulary and a glossary in Ayapaneco, Spanish and English. The introduction explicitly notes that spelling was not standardized at publication. This makes the book both a practical learning resource and evidence of community authorship, while warning against treating its orthography as timeless or universally fixed.

sections.title: Public teaching and language celebration
sections.text: INALI's report of the first Ayapaneco language festival in May 2013 describes workshops with schoolchildren, poetry, theater, music and traditional games in Ayapa. Materials about the body and a collection of legends were prepared with speakers and distributed during the event. The report recognizes several named contributors, including Manuel Segovia, Isidro Velásquez and Cirilo Velásquez. This dated account documents collaborative teaching and public recognition; it does not establish the size or results of any program in 2026.

sections.title: Ayapanet and access to recorded knowledge
sections.text: A contribution by Rangel with the independent community collective Retoño de mis Raíces describes documentation and revitalization work since 2012. Their Ayapanet project responds to a practical problem: audiovisual materials existed, but local infrastructure made them difficult to use. They proposed a low-cost media library accessible through a local wireless network without internet. The contribution describes a testing phase, not a completed universal service. Its emphasis is community control over content and access, alongside education and language learning.

sections.title: Understanding endangerment without the media shortcut
sections.text: Daniel Suslak's 2011 article examines the circulation and consequences of the story that Ayapaneco was dying because two speakers refused to talk to one another. Its abstract traces publicity through institutions and international media. That anecdote cannot replace the documented work of multiple contributors. Rangel's research identifies limited documentation, costly annotation, scarce equipment and unreliable connectivity as obstacles, and links language work with inequality and discrimination. These structural conditions give a more useful context for understanding revitalization needs.

sources.title: Ayapanecos – Etnografía
sources.publisher: Instituto Nacional de los Pueblos Indígenas
sources.annotation: Detailed account of Ayapa's coastal setting, work, cacao drinks and patron-saint celebrations. Full indexed text was inspected; its speculative language-origin claim is excluded from this profile.

sources.title: Challenges for Language Technologies in Ayapaneco
sources.publisher: Jhonnatan Rangel / Language Technologies for All
sources.annotation: Research poster identifies Mixe-Zoque affiliation and practical barriers involving annotation, equipment, connectivity and training. Its speaker estimates describe the research context and are not repeated as present-day totals.

sources.title: Las partes del cuerpo humano en ayapaneco

sources.annotation: 2013 illustrated book by named community authors, crediting additional speakers. Includes sound and spelling guidance, body vocabulary and a trilingual glossary; explicitly states that its spelling was not standardized.

sources.title: Primer festival de la lengua ayapaneca: Shem yeh chotz numdi oode
sources.annotation: May 13, 2013 release records children's workshops, locally compiled publications and named speakers honored at the festival. The site's migrated title contains 2025, but the actual event and release are from 2013.

sources.title: Ayapanet: creando una mediateca virtual comunitaria soberana, in Experiencias en educación popular y tecnologías libres
sources.publisher: Jhonnatan Rangel with Retoño de mis Raíces / Universidad Popular
sources.annotation: Pages 49–50 describe a community collective's local media-library project and its testing stage. Offers a collaborative first-hand account of documentation access and control, rather than an outsider rescue narrative.

sources.annotation: 2011 study analyzes the circulation and consequences of the two-speakers story. The freely readable abstract and bibliography were inspected; full article access may require a subscription.

name: Babine
region: British Columbia / Babine Lake and Babine River
overview: Babine histories connect lake and river communities, salmon fisheries, hereditary leadership, and relationships across north-central British Columbia. This introduction centers Lake Babine Nation’s own publications, alongside collaborative scholarship and public records. Its reading collection follows historical trade and colonial interference through language learning, community planning, stewardship, and work toward self-government.

sections.title: A nation of connected communities
sections.text: Lake Babine Nation’s community plan organizes its discussion around Tachet, Fort Babine or Wit’at, Old Fort, Pinkut Lake/Donald’s Landing, and Woyenne, alongside members living away from home. This is a network of communities with shared and distinct priorities, rather than one village whose location captures the entire homeland. The treaty office’s public account places the traditional territory around Babine Lake and describes four clans and hereditary leaders with responsibilities toward land. Its institutional and treaty-stage descriptions are older material, however, and should not be taken as a current administrative directory.

sections.title: Balhats and the study of law
sections.text: The balhats, or feast system, belongs within an account of law, leadership, and responsibilities. In Cis dideen kat—When the Plumes Rise, Jo-Anne Fiske and Betty Patrick frame their study as a descriptive account of Lake Babine customary law and changing relations with the Canadian state. Their publicly available introductory chapter explains that research began in 1993 and that historical documents were examined alongside the knowledge of hereditary chiefs and elders. They explicitly acknowledge limits concerning narratives, territorial detail, and language. Their work offers an important sustained reading path without making one study a complete or timeless statement of Lake Babine law.

sections.title: Trade, salmon, and historical records
sections.text: The treaty office reproduces Daniel Williams Harmon’s account of his January 1812 journey among Babine villages. It describes hospitality, salmon-based livelihoods, and trade connections reaching toward the coast through neighboring peoples. The office also warns that Harmon’s knowledge was limited by observation and interpretation. His writing is a record of a colonial visitor encountering an already connected society. It does not mark the beginning of Babine history, establish an exact population, or supply an objective description of every community. Reading the excerpt with the office’s commentary makes the source’s position visible.

sections.title: The barricade dispute and community resistance
sections.text: In its account of 1906, the treaty office describes women defending a rebuilt fishing weir when fisheries officers attempted to dismantle it. It recounts arrests and negotiations in which chiefs sought provisions and services in exchange for removal of the weirs. The account calls the resulting agreement the Barricade Treaty. This history connects colonial control of fishing to food security, resistance, and political negotiation. A later UNBC report describes archaeological work conducted with Lake Babine Nation at a Babine River fishing village, where earlier work had established occupation extending back at least 1,300 years. The collaborative study concerns a particular site, not a date for the origins of the people.

sections.title: Language learning and public resources
sections.text: Nedut’en is the name used by Lake Babine Nation’s FirstVoices collection. Its public pages offer an alphabet, recordings, words, phrases, and stories; individual records identify contributors. These are community-created learning resources, with their own access and reuse conditions. FPCC’s March 2025 account adds a specific example of intergenerational learning: Brian Lacerte learning from his mother, Rosalie MacDonald, through a mentor-apprentice program. It also describes MacDonald’s own learning and teaching work. Together, the collection and dated account show different forms of language transmission. Neither provides grounds for a current speaker census or a claim that one teaching method represents every family.

sections.title: Planning, governance, and the Foundation Agreement
sections.text: The 2017–2022 community plan records priorities in language, education, housing, access, health, and stewardship, developed through engagement with members. It is evidence of community priorities during a stated planning period; it is not a report that all goals were achieved. The Nation’s November 2020 update explains the Foundation Agreement as a twenty-year framework for implementing rights and developing self-government, rather than a finalized treaty settlement. Its governance page describes a proposed Nation-level and community-level model and steps toward ratification and implementation. A February 2024 federal announcement records a further funding agreement supporting governance capacity and infrastructure priorities for Wit’at and Tachet. That announcement documents commitments, not the completion of all funded facilities or a transition to the proposed government.

sections.title: Stewardship and decisions about development
sections.text: Lake Babine Nation’s environmental-assessment explanation identifies sustainability, benefits, socioeconomic effects, and respectful relationships as criteria for evaluating proposed development. It distinguishes an assessment collaboration agreement from work toward a further consent agreement. A different publication, issued in July 2023, announced closure of the recreational salmon fishery along part of the Babine River corridor in response to warm water and pressure on salmon. Read as a dated action, it shows how stewardship is expressed through decisions concerning food, water, and future generations. The notice should not be used as current fishing guidance. More recent regulations and Nation communications would need checking before a visit.

name: Bannock
overview: Bannock histories connect the Snake River Plain with Northern Paiute communities and wider Great Basin and Rocky Mountain travel networks. At Fort Hall, Bannock and Shoshone people share the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes government while maintaining distinct languages. Community publications connect treaty history, language teaching, food sovereignty, and environmental stewardship.

sections.title: People, language relationships, and homelands
sections.text: Bannock is both a people’s name and the name of a Northern Paiute language variety. Linguist Tim Thornes locates historical Bannock territory around the Snake River Plain of southwestern Idaho and the Boise River Valley, and describes sustained contact with Shoshoni. The Tribes’ own overview places Bannock bands within a shared history with Northern Shoshone bands, across ancestral lands extending well beyond present reservation boundaries. Their related Numic languages belong to the Uto-Aztecan family. A shared government and close cultural relationships coexist with linguistic distinctions; neither Bannock nor Northern Paiute should be treated as simply another name for Shoshone.

sections.title: Routes, place names, and responsibilities to land
sections.text: The Language and Cultural Preservation Department’s 2024 essay describes Tennambo’i, the lava-flow country now within Craters of the Moon, through ancestral memory and living place names. It connects routes across the Snake River Plain with salmon fishing, buffalo hunting, and camas and wild-carrot gathering farther afield. These paths linked important food areas and relationships across a large region. The department also explains its work with the National Park Service to bring tribal interpretations into public signage. Its account connects historical travel with present responsibilities, including collaborative efforts against invasive grass threatening camas habitat at Centennial Marsh.

sections.title: The treaty, an unfulfilled reservation promise, and Fort Hall
sections.text: The treaty signed at Fort Bridger on July 3, 1868, contains different provisions for Eastern Shoshone and Bannock people. Article 2 promises a future Bannock reservation; the published text names Portneuf and “Kansas Prairie,” while the Tribes’ public interpretation identifies Camas Prairie. Article 4 addresses reservation residence and hunting on specified unoccupied lands. In its Treaty Day account, the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes explains that the separate Bannock reservation was never created and that Bannock people were instead relocated to Fort Hall in 1869. The Tribes’ historical overview describes subsequent losses through surveying, legislation, and allotment. Reading the treaty beside tribal interpretation helps distinguish the agreement’s text from what the United States actually implemented.

sections.title: Camas, colonial deprivation, and food sovereignty
sections.text: A 2023 study coauthored by tribal citizens and university researchers connects the Bannock War of 1878 with restricted access to food, damage to camas grounds, and unmet federal obligations. Its historical discussion places hunger and displacement at the center of the conflict rather than describing war as an isolated outbreak. The study also documents a contemporary project to make camas more accessible at Fort Hall through cultivation experiments and community activities. Seeds and transplanted bulbs offered possible ways to strengthen access, although the authors identify questions about genetic differences and longer-term effects. This work connects experimental science, tribal oversight, and relationships maintained through food.

sections.title: Language teaching and a narrator’s history
sections.text: The Tribes’ Language and Cultural Preservation Department describes instruction in both Bannock and Shoshone, taught by tribal members and connected to history, identity, and treaty knowledge. Its archival and digital preservation programs retain documents, recordings, interviews, and family histories. Thornes’s 2020 publication provides a different kind of evidence: Bannock-language narratives with transcription, grammatical analysis, and translation. The autobiographical narrative of Lizzie Edmo was recorded by Sven Liljeblad at Fort Hall in 1959. Her recollections describe travel, gathering, fishing, and exchanges among families. The article preserves an individual speaker’s experience and linguistic knowledge; it should not be generalized into a single life story for every Bannock family.

sections.title: Shared government and the care of public history
sections.text: The published constitution and bylaws identify the Fort Hall Business Council as the governing body of the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes and provide for seven elected members. The document records a constitution approved in 1936 and later amendments. This is a primary source for the shared government’s formal structure, rather than a description of every earlier Bannock political arrangement. Cultural work is also institutional: the preservation department maintains archives, supports historical research, and addresses misleading representations and exploitation of tribal intellectual property. Its museum presents community history, art, and the Benedicte Wrensted photographic collection. Publicly shared information sits alongside material the department explicitly treats as confidential or sensitive.

sections.title: Horses and knowledge passed within families
sections.text: The Tribes describe Indian relay racing as a continuing horse tradition passed to younger generations by tribal families. Its public explanation outlines a team of four people and three horses, with the rider changing horses between laps while teammates manage the exchanges. This gives readers a concrete view of coordination and skill. The page’s broader claims about the sport’s origin represent the Tribes’ own account; this profile does not turn its undated historical claims into a precise chronology.

sections.title: Fish, water, energy, and contemporary priorities
sections.text: The shared government’s Fish and Wildlife Department links habitat restoration and fisheries work to the exercise of treaty rights. The Tribes’ salmon advocacy also calls for removal of the four lower Snake River dams, framing recovery as a cultural responsibility as well as an ecological issue. Its Water Resources Department describes protection of water quality, administration of reservation water use, and implementation of the 1990 Fort Hall water agreement. A separate 2022 Community Action Plan brings air monitoring, community survey findings, renewable energy, and efficiency measures into environmental planning. Together these sources show distinct forms of contemporary tribal action. They document governmental priorities and proposals, rather than proving that every proposed project or policy has been completed.

Includes named community perspectives and discussion of a 2021 congressional proposal. Read as a policy position, not proof of a completed dam-removal decision.

sources.annotation: Tribal account of the 1990 Fort Hall water agreement, department formation, water-use administration, and quality monitoring. Read “History and Direction” and “Water Quality Program.” Explains governmental responsibilities; it is not a substitute for the agreement’s full legal text.

sources.publisher: Shoshone-Bannock Tribes, Tribal Department of Energy
sources.annotation: Dated November 15, 2022. Read printed pp. 1–4 for purpose, pp. 10–14 for community survey, pp. 15–21 for monitoring, and pp. 29–31 for implementation. A planning document with community input; recommended actions and dated measurements are not current outcome evaluations.

relationshipNote: Bannock is closely connected to Northern Paiute and shares government with Shoshone people at Fort Hall. Bannock and Shoshoni are linguistically distinct. Sources about the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes describe shared institutions and should not be presented as evidence of a separate contemporary Bannock-only government.
