name: Beothuk
overview: Beothuk histories belong to Newfoundland’s coasts, islands, rivers, and interior. Archaeology, the testimony and drawings of named Beothuk women, and Mi’kmaw perspectives reveal skilled communities responding to colonial pressures. Their histories also require separating the destruction of communities from claims about ancestry, language, and the authority to tell their story.

sections.title: Names, homelands, and the archaeological record
sections.text: The name Beothuk appears in vocabularies recorded from Demasduit and Shanawdithit, although European writers used several spellings. Archaeologists commonly connect historically documented Beothuk with the island’s earlier Little Passage complex. These are analytical labels: they do not make every ancient Newfoundland site Beothuk. Donald Holly shows how older scholars mixed materials from different periods and peoples, then used the resulting collections to portray Beothuk as an isolated survival from a remote past. A more careful history distinguishes particular sites, dates, and communities while recognizing connections across the surrounding region.

sections.title: Seasonal places and food knowledge
sections.text: Beothuk communities combined coastal and inland resources, with movements shaped by local opportunities rather than one island-wide timetable. Seals, salmon, seabirds, shellfish, caribou, and plant foods contributed to their livelihoods. At Boyd’s Cove in Notre Dame Bay, shell deposits helped preserve animal bones that Newfoundland’s acidic soils often destroy. These remains document a varied diet alongside house pits and other occupation evidence. Coastal and river access therefore mattered together: describing Beothuk simply as interior caribou hunters would mistake a later situation of displacement for the full range of their land use.

sections.title: Making, travel, and adaptation
sections.text: Birchbark canoes supported travel on inland waterways and at sea. Surviving models, drawings, and written descriptions preserve evidence about their distinctive construction, although no full-sized Beothuk canoe survives. At Boyd’s Cove, nails and other European metal were reshaped into projectile points, scrapers, awls, and ornaments. Acquiring material from fishing stations could provide useful iron without sustained participation in a European fur trade. Laurie McLean’s comparison of house pits further argues that settlement and architecture changed differently across places and periods. These findings show selective innovation and changing decisions, not an unchanging culture.

sections.title: Contact, dispossession, and responsibility
sections.text: Colonial violence, competition for shorelines and food, and disease transformed Beothuk lives. Yet early contact should not be reconstructed by projecting later violence backward without evidence. William Gilbert’s reassessment finds that fragmentary sixteenth-century documents do not support a simple history of permanent hostility from first contact. Qalipu First Nation’s community plan also challenges the mercenary myth that blamed Mi’kmaq for Beothuk destruction and portrayed Mi’kmaq as outsiders brought to Newfoundland by the French. This matters because historical storytelling has affected living Indigenous peoples’ identities and claims to their homeland.

sections.title: Beothuk women as historical authorities
sections.text: Oubee, Demasduit, and Shanawdithit supplied much of the surviving recorded vocabulary, under circumstances shaped by capture and coercion. Shanawdithit’s drawings document homes, foods, family relationships, travel, killings, and encounters with settlers. Her work offers a Beothuk account within an archive largely assembled and annotated by outsiders. Sarah Roberts’s 2024 study follows her capture in 1823, years in the Peyton household, transfer to St. John’s, and death in 1829. The Rooms reported revising the colonial descriptions attached to her drawings in 2023–24, showing that even catalogue labels carry interpretations requiring scrutiny.

sections.title: Language and the limits of documentation
sections.text: The principal written word lists came from Oubee, Demasduit, and Shanawdithit through different recorders. Linguist John Hewson brought these materials together into a master list of 325 glosses, with numerals and month names. Their survival is significant, but the evidence is limited and filtered through inconsistent transcription. Scholars have disagreed about whether, and how closely, Beothuk belongs with Algonquian languages. The language guide summarizes both Hewson’s argument for a relationship and Ives Goddard’s skepticism. It is therefore preferable to present the affiliation as debated rather than confidently equating Beothuk with Innu-aimun or Mi’kmawi’simk.

sections.title: Survival narratives, ancestry, and DNA
sections.text: Shanawdithit is often called the last Beothuk, but Mi’kmaw oral histories challenge the conclusion that nobody survived beyond her death. Historical community destruction, genealogical descent, genetic relationships, and present political identity are different questions. Duggan and colleagues’ 2017 ancient-DNA study distinguishes sampled Maritime Archaic and Beothuk maternal populations. Carr’s 2020 comparison finds some ancient maternal lineages identical or close to modern ones, while emphasizing sampling limits and warning against simplistic genetic identity assignments. Mitochondrial DNA follows one maternal line; it cannot by itself confirm or exclude all Beothuk ancestry, establish an unbroken genealogy, or decide community membership.

sections.title: Repatriation and continuing responsibilities
sections.text: In March 2020, the remains of Demasduit and Nonosabasut returned from Scotland to Newfoundland and Labrador after advocacy led by Miawpukek Saqamaw Mi’sel Joe and cooperation among Indigenous leaders, museums, and governments. The provincial announcement records Indigenous leaders’ own statements about ancestors, responsibility, and the harm of colonial collecting. The Rooms’ 2024–25 report documents the Final Resting Place Circle’s continuing deliberations and a request for support to return associated spiritual belongings held in Britain. Those are dated reports of work in progress, not evidence that every repatriation or burial question has since been settled.

sources.title: Comprehensive Community Plan — Early History of Mi’kmaq in Ktaqmkuk
sources.annotation: Read the historical discussion around printed pages 17–18. This community-owned plan traces the unsupported mercenary story through colonial writers and explains its continuing consequences for Newfoundland Mi’kmaq. It supplies a living First Nation’s perspective, not a claim to speak for all Beothuk descendants.

sources.title: Shanawdithit — Provincial Historic Commemorations research paper
sources.author: Sarah Roberts
sources.annotation: Five-page study with reproduced drawings and source references. Pages 1–4 describe Shanawdithit’s knowledge, family, capture, testimony, death, and commemoration; the opening explicitly acknowledges Mi’kmaw challenges to the last-Beothuk narrative. Historical descriptions are retained with a language advisory.

sources.title: Beothuk Language
sources.author: Ingeborg Marshall
sources.publisher: Newfoundland and Labrador Heritage Website, Memorial University
sources.annotation: Explains the three surviving vocabularies, their archival transmission, and disagreement about Algonquian affiliation. Identifies recorders and circumstances of collection; its classification should not be treated as settled consensus.

sources.title: Precontact Beothuk Land Use
sources.publisher: Newfoundland and Labrador Heritage Website, Memorial University
sources.annotation: Detailed account of coastal and inland food resources, preservation, seasonal movement, and local variation. Sections on evidence explicitly distinguish archaeological findings from possibilities. The page now flags its 2009 scholarship as requiring updating; this profile uses it for documented resource relationships rather than speculative population totals.

sources.title: The Boyd’s Cove Beothuk Site
sources.author: Ralph T. Pastore
sources.publisher: Newfoundland and Labrador Heritage Website, Memorial University
sources.annotation: The excavator explains site discovery, preservation of food remains, house pits, and iron refashioning; see Beothuk Diet and Reasons for Avoiding the Fur Trade. Its broader conclusions about extinction and other peoples reflect an older interpretive framework, explicitly flagged by the website, and require comparison with newer Indigenous perspectives.

sources.title: Transportation
sources.author: Ingeborg Marshall
sources.publisher: Newfoundland and Labrador Heritage Website / Beothuk Institute
sources.annotation: Specialist account of canoe forms, bark construction, surviving models, snowshoes, and winter transport, based on Marshall’s historical research. It distinguishes observed objects and descriptions from reconstruction and inference. No surviving full-sized canoe is available to resolve every construction detail.

sources.title: Beothuk Housepits: Barometers of Historic Transition
sources.author: Laurie McLean
sources.annotation: Archaeological synthesis comparing 22 coastal and 64 Exploits Valley house pits; see pp. 1–9 and 42–44. Differences in architecture and artifacts support varied responses to colonial pressures. Interpretations of household organization and motives remain archaeological arguments, not direct testimony from every community.

sources.title: Beothuk-European Contact in the 16th Century: A Re-evaluation of the Documentary Evidence
sources.author: William Gilbert
sources.annotation: Peer-reviewed reassessment, pp. 24–44, of early captives, voyages, geographical names, and possible trade. Paragraphs 40–44 distinguish what fragmentary documents establish from assumptions repeated by later writers. Its challenge to perpetual early hostility does not deny well-documented later colonial violence.

sources.title: A Historiography of an Ahistoricity: On the Beothuk Indians
sources.author: Donald H. Holly Jr.
sources.annotation: Author-uploaded full text of the peer-reviewed article, DOI 10.1080/0275720032000107383. Pages 129–136 examine mixed artifact collections and assumptions about isolation, language, and inevitable disappearance. Valuable for reading older scholarship critically; its own discussion predates subsequent ancient-DNA work and current Indigenous-led debates.

sources.title: Genetic Discontinuity between the Maritime Archaic and Beothuk Populations in Newfoundland, Canada
sources.author: Ana T. Duggan and colleagues
sources.annotation: Full open-access research article, DOI 10.1016/j.cub.2017.08.053. Results and Figure 3 analyze ancient maternal genomes alongside archaeological and isotope evidence. The study concerns sampled maternal populations and explicitly allows possible ancestry in living people; it is not a test of present community identity or every line of descent.

sources.title: Evidence for the persistence of ancient Beothuk and Maritime Archaic mitochondrial DNA genome lineages among modern Native American peoples
sources.author: Steven M. Carr
sources.publisher: Genome 63, pp. 349–355; author copy at Memorial University
sources.annotation: Read Discussion and Assignment of individuals, pp. 352–354. Compares ancient maternal lineages with modern database sequences, explains limited sampling and the Santu Toney inheritance example, and cautions against simplistic commercial ancestry claims. Miawpukek cooperation and approval are acknowledged. The afterword supersedes an earlier withdrawn manuscript.

sources.title: Nonosabasut and Demasduit Returned to Newfoundland and Labrador
sources.publisher: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, with statements by Indigenous leaders
sources.annotation: Primary announcement of the transfer into The Rooms’ care, with attributed statements from Mi’sel Joe and other Indigenous leaders. Its backgrounder uses a categorical extinction account and describes the administrative recognition position in 2020; those passages should not settle contested historical or contemporary identity questions.

sources.title: The Rooms Annual Report 2023–2024 — revising Beothuk collection descriptions
sources.publisher: The Rooms Corporation, Newfoundland and Labrador
sources.annotation: Printed pp. 76–77 (PDF pages 38–39) document the Final Resting Place Circle’s initial meeting and revision of colonial labels for Shanawdithit’s drawings and Demasduit portraits. This institutional self-report explains present cataloguing responsibilities and the influence of Cormack and Howley’s assumptions on collections.

sources.title: The Rooms Annual Report 2024–2025 — Final Resting Place Circle
sources.publisher: The Rooms Corporation, Newfoundland and Labrador
sources.annotation: Printed p. 66 (PDF page 69) describes the Circle’s June 2024 visits, deliberations about a resting place, and request for support to repatriate spiritual belongings held in Britain. This is a dated progress account; it does not establish a final burial decision or the outcome of later requests.

relationshipNote: Beothuk, Innu, and Mi’kmaq remain distinct directory entries. Regional connections, oral histories, and shared or related maternal lineages do not make these names interchangeable. This profile does not adjudicate living people’s membership or ancestry claims.

name: Biloxi
overview: Biloxi histories connect the Mississippi Gulf Coast with communities in Louisiana, Texas, and beyond. Biloxi is a Siouan language, distinct from Tunica. Biloxi descendants participate in the contemporary Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana, whose shared government and cultural work preserve several ancestral identities rather than a single interchangeable tribal past.

sections.title: Names, identity, and a shared nation
sections.text: A public family heritage website established in 2003 by Donna Pierite, Elisabeth-Michele Pierite, and relatives records the self-designation Taneks Hanyadi and several European spellings of Biloxi. Variant names are useful when searching archives, but those records must be interpreted in context. The Tunica-Biloxi Tribe describes its citizens as carrying Tunica, Biloxi, Ofo, Avoyel, and Choctaw heritages, with people identifying as Tunica, Biloxi, or Biloxi-Choctaw. These continuing identifications sit within a shared political community. They should not be flattened into a claim that Tunica and Biloxi originally spoke the same language or had identical histories.

sections.title: The Gulf Coast and movements into Louisiana
sections.text: The tribe’s historical account places Biloxi people in the Pascagoula River region when French expeditions encountered them in 1699. Earlier routes are less securely documented. Linguist David Kaufman has proposed southern Appalachian connections using language and place-name evidence, while acknowledging unresolved identifications. His linguistic argument is a hypothesis about an earlier past, not a dated map of an established homeland. The federal acknowledgment dossier likewise cautions that later movements involved several locations and extended periods. It discusses Biloxi communities near the Mississippi, Coulee des Grues, and Bayou Boeuf, rather than describing everyone as making one simultaneous migration west.

sections.title: Texas: alliance, expulsion, and diplomacy
sections.text: Megan Biesele’s historical overview traces Biloxi families along the Neches River in East Texas by 1828. It situates their subsequent movements within European settlement pressures and the Republic of Texas’s campaigns against Cherokee and allied communities in 1839. The same account follows other Biloxi groups through later Texas settlements and relationships with neighboring peoples. The 1843 Bird’s Fort treaty provides a complementary primary record: its proclamation names the Biloxi among the participating nations, and its signature page identifies a Biloxi chief as Hoyo Tubby. Together, these sources document negotiation as well as displacement; they do not establish the later affiliation of every Biloxi family.

sections.title: Community connections and federal acknowledgment
sections.text: The 1980 acknowledgment dossier distinguishes the Marksville community from a closely connected Biloxi-Choctaw community at Indian Creek in Rapides Parish. It describes kinship and continuing association, while recognizing uncertainty about earlier settlements. The tribe’s own history records Biloxi authorization in October 1924 for Eli Barbry to pursue union with the Tunica. Federal recognition followed in 1981, after generations of community efforts. The dossier is valuable evidence of that administrative process, not an authority that created the people’s existence. Contemporary self-government also includes a tribal court; its own program description discusses civil cases, housing, estates, and interpretation of tribal governing documents.

sections.title: Reading the Biloxi language record critically
sections.text: Biloxi belongs to the Southeastern, also called Ohio Valley, branch of Siouan and is closely related to Ofo and Tutelo. Dorsey and Swanton’s 1912 dictionary preserves Biloxi vocabulary, phrases, and thirty-one texts. Swanton’s introduction explains that he reorganized Dorsey’s unfinished materials and changed transcription conventions. The published record therefore contains both speakers’ contributions and editorial decisions. Kaufman’s later reanalysis argues that an incomplete exchange of two vowel symbols during editing makes mechanical conversion into a modern spelling unreliable. His study compares cognates and other records to reassess individual words. These works preserve substantial linguistic knowledge, while leaving uncertainties that readers should retain rather than silently resolve.

sections.title: Language relationships and the art of speaking
sections.text: Language scholarship also reveals Biloxi participation in a multilingual region. Kaufman’s 2016 comparison examines shared vocabulary and grammatical patterns involving Biloxi, Ofo, and other Lower Mississippi Valley languages. He distinguishes similarities inherited from Siouan ancestry from those potentially arising through contact; the direction of particular borrowings often remains uncertain. A separate study of Biloxi narrative particles considers how speakers expressed differing degrees of certainty about possible events. Such analyses go beyond lists of translated words to questions of storytelling and interpretation. They are scholarly readings of a limited historical corpus, and should not be mistaken for a description of every Biloxi speaker’s practice.

sections.title: Living cultural work, plants, and public institutions
sections.text: The Tunica-Biloxi Language and Culture Revitalization Program connects language classes with crafts, stories, songs, and youth activities. Its published language curriculum concerns Tunica. A 2026 article coauthored by tribal members and collaborators makes that distinction explicit while describing a wider community effort to reconnect ethnobotanical knowledge, basketry materials, and land stewardship. Elisabeth Pierite recounts learning basket traditions through family visits and regional gatherings; the authors discuss restoration and access to plant resources alongside an evolving guidebook. These are accounts of adaptation and continuity in the present. The tribe’s Cultural and Educational Resources Center brings an exhibit hall, preservation laboratory, and research library together on the reservation, providing a community-based route for further study.

sources.title: General Profile: The Tunica-Biloxi Indians of Louisiana
sources.annotation: The tribe’s substantial historical account covers Biloxi Gulf Coast connections, the 1924 union, recognition, and contemporary institutions. Much of the earlier narrative concerns Tunica history. Its proposed identification of a sixteenth-century Biloxi ruler is interpretive rather than settled evidence; no undated population figures are used.

sources.title: Taneks Hanyadi: What about the Biloxi language?
sources.publisher: Pierite family heritage website, preserved by Indigifab
sources.annotation: A short, attributed community-family account established in 2003 records a Biloxi self-designation, archival name variants, and the distinction between Biloxi and Tunica. Its dated language-status statements should not be treated as a current speaker survey.

sources.title: A Dictionary of the Biloxi and Ofo Languages, Accompanied with Thirty-one Biloxi Texts and Numerous Biloxi Phrases
sources.publisher: Smithsonian Institution, Bureau of American Ethnology, Bulletin 47
sources.annotation: The foundational 1912 collection preserves Biloxi texts and vocabulary alongside a distinct Ofo dictionary. Reviewed the contents and Biloxi introduction, pp. 1–4, through the public-domain Wikisource transcription because the institutional PDF could not be fetched. The introduction explains editorial rearrangement and notation; this is not a full review of all texts.

sources.title: A Reanalysis of the Dorsey-Swanton U-Circumflex and U-Brève in Biloxi
sources.publisher: Kansas Working Papers in Linguistics, University of Kansas
sources.annotation: Kaufman reassesses historical vowel notation using twenty-one words, related Siouan forms, and other transcriptions. Read especially the background, data, and conclusion, PDF pp. 2–9. This is a specific philological argument, not a current account of Biloxi community size or language use.

sources.title: Biloxi Realis and Irrealis Particles
sources.publisher: Kansas Working Papers in Linguistics 32, pp. 1–7
sources.annotation: Examines two Biloxi narrative particles and how speakers may mark certainty and potential events. The discussion and conclusion distinguish analysis from unresolved questions, including proposed connections with gendered speech. It interprets archival examples rather than reporting new community fieldwork.

sources.title: Two Siouan Languages Walk into a Sprachbund
sources.publisher: Language Science Press, in Advances in the Study of Siouan Languages and Linguistics
sources.annotation: A 24-page chapter on Biloxi and Ofo participation in Lower Mississippi Valley language contact. Reviewed the introduction, distinctions between inheritance and contact, lexical comparisons, and conclusion, especially printed pp. 39–42 and 54–59. Proposed earlier Biloxi locations and borrowing directions retain explicit uncertainties.

sources.title: Recommendation and Summary of Evidence for Proposed Finding for Federal Acknowledgment of the Tunica-Biloxi Indian Tribe of Louisiana
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of the Interior, Bureau of Indian Affairs; GovInfo
sources.annotation: The 1980 proposed-finding dossier includes historical and anthropological reports. Reviewed the recommendation and Biloxi sections, particularly PDF pp. 1–3, 27–28, 33, and 36–37. It distinguishes communities and states evidentiary limits. Its administrative criteria and period terminology reflect a federal recognition process, not community self-definition.

sources.title: Biloxi Indians
sources.publisher: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas
sources.annotation: Biesele’s entry follows Biloxi families, alliances, coercive movements, and diplomacy in nineteenth-century Texas. Published in 1976 and updated in 2020. Its older terminology and conjectures about earlier migration require care; it is a regional historical overview, not a present-day community description.

sources.title: Bird’s Fort Treaty Ratification Proclamation, 1843
sources.publisher: Texas State Library and Archives Commission
sources.annotation: Digitized proclamation and transcription name the Biloxi among parties to the September 29, 1843 treaty. Reviewed pp. 1–2 and the signature transcription on p. 10, identifying Hoyo Tubby. Read the complete linked document for treaty terms; the Republic’s language and diplomatic frame are historical evidence, not neutral ethnography.
authors: Republic of Texas and participating Indigenous representatives

sources.title: Language & Culture Revitalization Program
sources.annotation: The tribe explains language materials, classes, cultural workshops, youth camps, and its research library. The language teaching described is Tunica; this page does not establish a separate Biloxi language curriculum. Undated class schedules and counts are excluded from the synthesis.

sources.title: Cultural & Educational Resource Center
sources.annotation: The tribe’s own guide locates its public museum and identifies the exhibit hall, preservation laboratory, and library/research center. Useful for pursuing community-based research and understanding preservation infrastructure; the center serves the contemporary tribe and is not exclusively a Biloxi collection.

sources.title: Hɔhka Moluni: Creativity and Continuity in the Linguistic and Cultural Reclamation of Tunica-Biloxi Ethnobotany
sources.annotation: Coauthored by tribal members and academic collaborators. Reviewed the project methodology, Elisabeth Pierite’s account, restoration discussion, and footnote 1. It connects basketry and plant relationships with a developing ethnobotany guidebook; the authors explicitly identify its Indigenous-language content as Tunica. The article describes work in progress, not a finished guidebook.

sources.title: Tunica-Biloxi Tribal Court: Program Description
sources.annotation: The tribal court explains its institutional responsibilities and relationship to tribal governing documents. Used for a limited description of contemporary self-government. The undated page is a program overview, not a complete statement of current jurisdiction or legal advice.

relationshipNote: Biloxi and Tunica are distinct peoples and languages. The Tunica-Biloxi Tribe is a contemporary government with multiple ancestral communities; its Tunica language initiatives must not be relabeled Biloxi language programs. Ofo is a linguistic relative of Biloxi, while shared political history does not make these identities synonyms.
researchGaps: Add more publicly shared Biloxi family oral histories and community-authored accounts beyond the Marksville-centered collection; this profile does not map all descendants or adjudicate other communities’ identities.
Compare proposed pre-1699 Appalachian connections with additional specialist historical and archaeological scholarship. Similar names alone cannot establish a migration route or a people’s identity.

Locate and inspect the more recent Biloxi dictionaries and additional original field materials. The 2011 KU dictionary and some journal downloads were inaccessible during this review and are not counted as inspected sources.
Seek a community-authorized account of present Biloxi language learning priorities. The accessible Tunica-Biloxi language and ethnobotany materials principally document Tunica reclamation.

Thirteen inspected reading sources provide a substantial starting collection, including sources scoped to the shared Tunica-Biloxi government. This is an expanded introduction, not a completed or community-reviewed history.

name: Caddo
overview: Caddo is a living Indigenous people with historical communities across the Red, Ouachita, Sabine, and Neches river regions. The Caddo Nation of Oklahoma is a contemporary tribal government formed from historically related communities; Caddoan language relationships do not make neighboring nations the same people. This Texas-focused guide distinguishes archaeological interpretation, written colonial records, Caddo oral histories, and current community work.

sections.title: Names, related communities, and the Caddo Nation today
sections.text: Historical sources use Caddo both for a particular northern community often called Kadohadacho and, more broadly, for several related Caddo-speaking communities. Caddo Nation language materials describe the historical Kadohadacho, Natchitoches, and Hasinai confederacies and emphasize that Pawnee, Wichita, Arikara, and Kitsai are linguistically related but remain culturally and historically separate Nations. The present Caddo Nation of Oklahoma is a contemporary government formed through 1930s reorganization; its 1938 constitution records one dated stage in that history, not today’s governing rules. The narrower Kadohadacho entry by Howard Meredith should be read for that community rather than generalized to every Caddo group.

sections.title: Homeland and place through time
sections.text: Caddo historical communities are associated with river valleys across what are now northeast Texas, northwest Louisiana, southwest Arkansas, and southeast Oklahoma. The Caddo Homeland exhibit describes a large central homeland and a northern Arkansas Basin whose relationship to Caddo identity remains debated. It also explains that territories changed over time and that archaeological sites do not create fixed political borders. A separate Caddo oral-history synthesis describes three broad historical groupings and named villages using both community memory and colonial records. These regional descriptions document historical relationships; they do not define a present-day boundary or suggest that all Caddo people live in one place.

sections.title: Ancestors, archaeology, and what the evidence can show
sections.text: Archaeological sequences trace distinctive Caddo pottery, villages, mound centers, agriculture, and long-distance exchange over many centuries. Researchers infer parts of that history from durable remains, but the timeline exhibit cautions that most ordinary lives and events leave little archaeological trace. The Texas Historical Commission’s Caddo Mounds account describes one important ceremonial and settlement center, not the whole Caddo world. A useful starting method is to compare archaeology with Caddo oral histories, language, written records, and later scholarship, while keeping uncertainty visible where those sources do not align.

sections.title: Contact, diplomacy, and records written by outsiders
sections.text: Spanish, French, Mexican, and United States records describe encounters with Caddo communities, but they reflect the observers’ aims and assumptions. The Texas Beyond History research guide explains how missionary, travel, and government records can be useful while remaining selective and biased. Its Caddo Voices material, researched and written by enrolled Caddo historian Cecile Elkins Carter, combines oral histories with archival evidence and gives specific speakers and dates. Those accounts offer situated perspectives rather than one interchangeable story for every Caddo family or community.

sections.title: Treaties, displacement, and movement west
sections.text: The 1835 treaty printed in the United States Statutes at Large records the cession agreement and related terms negotiated with named Caddo leaders. The instrument is evidence of the legal document and its signatories; it cannot by itself describe the different experiences of all Caddo communities or prove how every provision was carried out. Caddo Voices recounts movement from Louisiana into Texas, violence and loss of homes, and later movement to the Brazos area and west. Fallis Elkins’s 1973 family account and Sadie Bedoka Weller’s 1968 recollection are explicitly attributed testimony, not anonymous folklore. State and federal site histories add an institutional chronology of the 1855 reservation and 1859 removal, which should be read alongside those Caddo accounts.

sections.title: Language, cultural continuity, and renewed practice
sections.text: The Caddo Nation’s language program describes Caddo language as Hasinai in some contexts and situates language work within community history, gatherings, and cultural life. The program states that other Caddoan-language Nations are separate peoples. It also documents contemporary language-archive and learning work; language change or the loss of fluent speakers does not mean that Caddo people or culture have disappeared. The Texas Beyond History pottery exhibit connects ancient material evidence with Jeri Redcorn’s first-person account of learning and renewing Caddo pottery. A Texas Historical Commission exhibit developed with Caddo citizens and featuring artist Chase Kahwinhut Earles presents selected community knowledge about Caddo Mounds. These works are specific examples and do not stand for every citizen’s practice.

sources.title: Early Caddo History
sources.annotation: A concise NPS exhibit locates historic Caddo communities in the Piney Woods and distinguishes Hasinai, Kadohadacho, and Natchitoches areas. Its chronology and population statements are institutional summaries, not current community counts; consult the cited oral-history and archaeological works for nuance.
sources.contentReviewScope: The complete visible article, including its 1687 map caption, related-page links, and 2020 update date, was read. The linked map itself was not added to the historical-map room or assessed for reuse in this batch.

sources.title: Language Preservation

sources.annotation: The Caddo Nation language program describes Hasinai/Caddo language work, the historical confederacies, community archiving, and the distinction between linguistic relationship and separate Nations. This is the Nation program’s own account of its work and language history.
sources.contentReviewScope: The full visible page was inspected, including the program lead, goals, language-history section, linked dated news items, and statement of continuing community work. No current speaker count was inferred from older media links.

sources.title: Caddo Mounds History
sources.annotation: A site history summarizes the settlement and ceremonial center at Caddo Mounds and later Hasinai and Caddo movement. Its account is useful for this particular site and institutional chronology, not a complete history of the Caddo people.
sources.contentReviewScope: The full visible history article and its listed chronology were read. Interpretations of why the center was vacated remain attributed to the site’s archaeological account.

sources.contentReviewScope: The visible exhibit text and chapters for High Temple Mound, prairie/garden, grass house, Low Platform Mound, and burial mound were inspected. Embedded external material and any cultural knowledge outside the public exhibit were not accessed.

sources.title: Caddo Ancestors: Uncovering Early Caddo History

sources.title: Caddo Homeland
sources.publisher: Texas Beyond History; researched and written by Cecile Elkins Carter
sources.annotation: Cecile Elkins Carter, an enrolled Caddo historian, presents a Caddo-centered synthesis using oral history, archival records, and historical group names. The page distinguishes broad Caddo use from the narrower historical Cadohadacho label; these are attributed historical interpretations rather than a universal current naming rule.
sources.contentReviewScope: The full visible page and the separate credits page were read. Its account is Carter’s researched and written synthesis; underlying cited archives and all referenced books were not independently reviewed.

sources.title: Twenty Years Without a Home, 1836–1859
sources.publisher: Texas Beyond History; researched and written by Cecile Elkins Carter
sources.annotation: This page follows displacement and movement among Louisiana, Texas, the Brazos area, and Indian Territory using archival records and named Caddo testimony. Testimony from Fallis Elkins (1973) and Sadie Bedoka Weller (1968) is identified by speaker and date; it is situated family memory, not a generic or interchangeable Caddo story.
sources.contentReviewScope: The full visible page, narrative, map caption, archival references, and attributed oral-history excerpts were read. The complete recordings and all referenced primary records were not inspected.

sources.title: Created in Clay: the Caddo Pottery Tradition
sources.publisher: Texas Beyond History; Texas Archeological Research Laboratory and partners
sources.annotation: This exhibit explains the archaeological importance of Caddo pottery and directs readers to a separate account of contemporary Caddo potter Jeri Redcorn’s practice. The archaeological framing and present-day artistic work are connected but should not be collapsed into a claim that cultural practices are unchanged.
sources.contentReviewScope: The full visible exhibit introduction and its described pottery galleries and linked sections were read. Gallery images and the separate pages are not counted as independently inspected here.

sources.title: Reviving a Lost Tradition
sources.publisher: Texas Beyond History; interview within the Created in Clay exhibit
sources.annotation: Caddo potter Jeri Redcorn describes her own process of learning and reviving pottery practice and reflects on removals and boarding schools. This is a named person’s first-person account, not a claim that one maker speaks for all Caddo people.
sources.contentReviewScope: The complete visible interview page and credited contextual material were read. The profile attributes its reflections to Redcorn and does not reproduce restricted or unpublished material.

sources.title: Learning About the Caddo Past
sources.publisher: Texas Beyond History; Texas Archeological Research Laboratory and partners
sources.annotation: This methods essay describes the strengths and limitations of oral history, archaeology, linguistics, ethnography, and European accounts. It directly cautions that missionary and explorer records can reflect the authors’ motives and prejudices, a useful guide for interpreting older documentary sources.
sources.contentReviewScope: The complete visible essay, named source traditions, image captions, and bibliography leads were inspected. The books and archival documents it describes remain separate leads unless listed as inspected.

sources.title: Treaty with the Caddoes, 1835 (7 Stat. 470)
sources.publisher: United States Statutes at Large, hosted by GovInfo
sources.annotation: The printed federal treaty text records the 1835 agreement, parties, cession, and supplementary articles. It is evidence of the document and federal legal framing; it cannot establish the views or experiences of every Caddo community, or by itself verify implementation.
sources.contentReviewScope: Both pages of the treaty text and supplementary articles were inspected. This is the published statutory transcription, not an examination of the signed manuscript or separate ratification and implementation files.

sources.annotation: Howard Meredith’s entry concerns Kadohadacho in particular and describes its Red River villages and later participation in the 1938 Caddo government. Its narrower subject is valuable for distinguishing a historical community from the broader Caddo people, but it must not be generalized to all Caddo communities.

sources.contentReviewScope: The page sections on reopening, site management, public interpretation, and visits were read. Admission and schedule details are not reproduced because they can change.

initialAdequacy.rationale: Seventeen distinct substantive works were inspected across Caddo Nation program material, Caddo-authored oral-history synthesis and testimony, archaeology and public history, a treaty text, and a historical governance document. This supports an accessible initial account of identity, homeland, archaeology, displacement, language work, and continuity. The collection remains unfinished because the post-removal era and current community/government perspectives are still thin, the region and named communities require more comparative review, and further primary and specialist works need direct inspection. The source count is a quantity measure, not completeness, endorsement, or community review.
remainingLimits: The Caddo Nation official language page is a strong contemporary community source, but additional Nation-authored histories, cultural publications, and current government materials should be inspected.
The post-removal history, including the Civil War, allotment, federal policy, and the 1860–1902 period, needs deeper work with Caddo-centered and archival sources.
The three historical confederacies and named local communities are not fully surveyed here; terms vary across oral history, colonial records, and later scholarship.
The 1835 treaty is read as a printed statutory text only; signed manuscript, ratification files, later agreements, and implementation records were not separately inspected.
The Caddo Archeology Journal PDF was inaccessible to the text-review tool and remains an unread lead; this does not establish a paywall.
Archaeological interpretations of ancestral continuity and the northern Arkansas Basin remain debated; no fixed homeland boundary is asserted.
No present population figure, current fluent-speaker count, exhaustive community list, or claim of community endorsement is made.

evidenceNotes: Reviewed October 22, 2026 (America/Denver): 17 substantive works have actual-content inspection records; two supporting or out-of-scope references are excluded from the count. Links from a source bibliography and external embedded media are not treated as reviewed.

The source set combines Caddo Nation program material, Caddo historian Cecile Elkins Carter’s attributed oral-history/archival synthesis, identified first-person testimony, government interpretation, archaeology education, a primary treaty printing, and a dated constitution. Their scopes and perspectives are labeled at the source cards.

The language family is not a peoplehood shortcut: Caddo Nation materials state that Pawnee, Wichita, Arikara, and Kitsai are linguistically related yet distinct Nations. The Adai Caddo Indian Nation source is retained only as an explicit distinction and contributes no Caddo evidence or source count.

The 1835 treaty and 1938 constitution are primary records for their own text and dates. They are not treated as complete accounts of community experience or current law/governance. The 2010-era OSDE figures are excluded from current claims.

No new historical-map association was added. The NPS early-history page and Texas Beyond History exhibits contain map imagery, but map inspection, rights review, and a profile-specific association were outside this research batch.
researchGaps: The Caddo Nation official language page is a strong contemporary community source, but additional Nation-authored histories, cultural publications, and current government materials should be inspected.
The post-removal history, including the Civil War, allotment, federal policy, and the 1860–1902 period, needs deeper work with Caddo-centered and archival sources.

name: Coahuiltecan
overview: “Coahuiltecan” is a later umbrella label used for many distinct Indigenous groups of South Texas and northeastern Mexico. It does not identify one uniform historical nation, language, government, or present-day community. The surviving colonial record is uneven, and scholars disagree about terminology and relationships. This page distinguishes group-specific evidence from the separate public accounts of Tāp Pīlam Coahuiltecan Nation and the Miakan/Garza Band.

sections.title: A broad label, not one uniform people
sections.text: Historical records name many autonomous communities, while later scholarship grouped some South Texas and northeastern Mexico peoples under “Coahuiltecan.” Authors disagree about whether the word began as a colonial regional label or a later scholarly classification. A 2014 CHAPS chapter describes a scholarly category; a current National Park Service page attributes the name to Spanish geography. The evidence reviewed here does not resolve that conflict, and neither account makes the label a universal self-name. The safest use is as a broad, contested umbrella—not a single polity or shared culture.

sections.title: Named groups and varied regional lives
sections.text: Educational and archival syntheses identify Payaya, Pacuache, Mariames, Aranama, Tamiques, Manos de Prieta and many other names, often from particular places or mission records. The sources describe varied languages, seasonal movements, resource use and relationships; some groups’ territories overlapped while others were distant or hostile. These reconstructions are uneven and often depend on Spanish accounts. A name appearing near a place or in a mission list is not by itself proof of a single people’s complete homeland or identity.

sections.title: Language evidence and classification remain limited
sections.text: The surviving language material is fragmentary. Researchers have debated which documented languages were related to Coahuilteco and whether a wider “Coahuiltecan” language family is supported. Mission lingua-franca use further complicates identifying who spoke which language. The Institute’s language-reclamation page documents its program history, but its statement that the language is extinct because fewer than 1,000 people speak it is internally contradictory and uncorroborated; this profile does not use that number or claim a current speaker count.

sections.title: Mission records describe specific, changing communities
sections.text: Spanish mission records are valuable but incomplete sources created for colonial administration and religious purposes. A 1985 San Antonio mission study documents conflicting registers and warns that names, languages and earlier locations are difficult to match consistently. A separate Espíritu Santo case study discusses Aranama, Tamiques and Manos de Prieta, and records disagreement over whether Aranama and Mariames were distinct. These findings apply to a specific mission setting, not to every community grouped under the umbrella.

sections.title: Contemporary community histories are distinct
sections.text: Tāp Pīlam Coahuiltecan Nation publishes its own history and timeline; that account should be read as the Nation’s perspective on its community, not as a substitute for all South Texas peoples. Separately, the Indigenous Cultures Institute says it was founded by members of the Miakan/Garza Band and describes that Band’s history, public programs and repatriation priorities. A peer-reviewed 2023 article documents one Miakan-Band Elders’ educational program. These sources present distinct community and program scopes; they do not establish that either organization represents every community connected to the broad label.

sections.title: What this evidence does not establish
sections.text: Older sources sometimes describe groups as extinct or cultures as lost. Such statements reflect authors’ interpretations of a limited archive and their historical categories; they do not prove that descendants disappeared. A 2001 National Park Service report describes differing views about continuity and calls for further consultation in one mission context. The present sources do not establish an exhaustive list of descendant communities, current legal status, population figures, or one shared cultural account. Community review remains open. No individual historical map was examined in this batch, so no map association was added.

sources.publisher: Texas Beyond History, University of Texas at Austin and Texas Archeological Research Laboratory
sources.annotation: An educational synthesis presenting Coahuiltecan as a geographic catch-all for diverse South Texas and northeastern Mexico peoples. It names Payaya, Pacuache and Mariames and describes seasonal movement, language diversity and overlapping relationships. Its deep-time continuity inference and other reconstructions are the exhibit authors’ interpretations, not demonstrated genealogies for every named people.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the complete substantive exhibit page, its historical and foodways passages, the ending and credits/source links. Embedded primary quotations were read as presented; cited works and archival records were not opened independently.

sources.title: Coahuiltecans of the Rio Grande Region
sources.author: Russell K. Skowronek and Bobbie L. Lovett
sources.publisher: In Native American Peoples of South Texas, Community Historical Archaeology Project with Schools (CHAPS), University of Texas–Pan American
sources.annotation: A chapter in a regional scholarly volume. The authors characterize “Coahuiltecan” as a later scholarly category and discuss its thin linguistic basis and internal diversity. They also make cultural-loss claims; these are dated author conclusions that should be weighed against community accounts and later work. The chapter is not a comprehensive account of all contemporary peoples.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read chapter 2, printed pages 13–17 (PDF pages 20–24), including its terminology and summary passages. Other chapters, full references, original archaeological collections and the book’s map were not independently reviewed. The volume states all rights reserved; linked for reading, not reproduced.

sources.title: Indian Groups Associated with Spanish Missions of the San Antonio Missions National Historical Park
sources.author: T. N. Campbell and T. J. Campbell
sources.annotation: A dated group-by-group study of communities recorded at the San Antonio missions. Its authors emphasize conflicting and incomplete mission registers and the uncertainty of identifying groups, languages and premission locations. The report is a regional historical analysis, not a present-day community or legal-status determination.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the report’s methods/limitations, conclusions and selected mission-by-mission discussions in the HTML edition. Other entries and underlying Spanish registers were not exhaustively checked; cited archival records were not independently opened.

sources.title: History & Culture — San Antonio Missions
sources.author: National Park Service
sources.annotation: A park-specific overview of San Antonio’s mission communities, archaeology, archives and descendant stories. It attributes a Spanish origin for the term Coahuiltecan; this conflicts with the 2014 CHAPS chapter’s account of a later scholarly label and with other treatments of the word. The page is useful for the park’s own public interpretation, not a definitive regional ethnography.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the complete substantive History & Culture page, including its mission-descendant section and archaeological interpretation. Linked family stories, archives and collections were not independently opened.

sources.title: Native Peoples in a Spanish World — Mission Espíritu Santo
sources.author: Texas Beyond History exhibit contributors
sources.publisher: Texas Beyond History, University of Texas at Austin and Texas Archeological Research Laboratory
sources.annotation: A focused case study of people associated with three locations of Mission Espíritu Santo, especially Aranama, Tamiques and Manos de Prieta. The exhibit records disagreement over possible Aranama/Mariame equivalence and notes sparse, ambiguous Spanish documentation. Its statements concern this mission setting, not every group placed under the broader label.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the complete visible Native Peoples page and its mission-specific discussion. Linked mission records and the exhibit’s archaeological sources were not independently opened.

sources.title: About — Indigenous Cultures Institute
sources.author: Indigenous Cultures Institute
sources.annotation: The Institute’s own account says it was founded by Miakan/Garza Band members and describes the Band’s family continuity and 2013 Texas legislative recognition. This is a first-party institutional description of the Miakan-Garza Band, distinct from Tāp Pīlam; the Institute is not presented here as a tribal government or as representing every Coahuiltecan-descended community.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the full substantive About page and its founder/organization sections. Linked profiles, presentations and legislative documents were not independently reviewed.

sources.title: Coahuiltecan Language Reclamation Program
sources.author: Indigenous Cultures Institute
sources.annotation: A first-party description of the Institute’s language-reclamation program, including its 2022 launch and later course-development activity. The same page contradicts itself by calling the language extinct while claiming fewer than 1,000 speakers; that speaker figure and status statement are not repeated as facts. This page documents the organization’s program, not a linguists’ consensus or every community’s language.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the full visible program page, including its internally inconsistent language-status sentence and the stated 2022–2025 program chronology. Linked dictionary, course materials and future class application were not inspected.

sources.title: Reassessing Cultural Extinction: Change and Survival at Mission San Juan Capistrano, Texas
sources.author: Alston V. Thoms, editor
sources.publisher: National Park Service and Texas A&M University
sources.annotation: A NPS baseline report that discusses differing interpretations of cultural extinction and survival in one San Antonio mission context and recommends further consultation. It records a 2001 research/consultation setting; its recommendations and legal discussion do not establish current NAGPRA status or speak for present communities.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the full 26-page PDF, including the summary, discussion of local descendant connections, contrasting interpretations and recommendations. Family-level details are not reproduced here; present legal status and underlying case files were not checked.

sources.title: Encountering creative climate change pedagogies: Cartographic interruptions
sources.author: Fikile Nxumalo and Pablo Montes
sources.annotation: A peer-reviewed study of one Indigenous Summer Encounter for Latinx and Indigenous children led by Miakan-Band Elders. It offers a specific collaborative education example and the authors’ interpretation of climate pedagogy; it is not a general history or a survey of all South Texas peoples. Culturally specific content is not reproduced here.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the open-access full article, including abstract, author/context statements, research discussion and conclusions. No program materials, recordings or culturally restricted details were independently accessed or repeated.

sources.title: Three Ancestors Held by UT-Austin — Miakan-Garza Band statement
sources.author: Indigenous Cultures Institute / Miakan-Garza Band
sources.annotation: A first-party Miakan-Garza account of a specific request to rebury three ancestors and the Band’s stated position. It documents that community’s own account of the dispute, not an independent legal determination, current case status, or shared position of all Coahuiltecan-descended peoples.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the full visible statement, including its dated chronology and quoted community position. The linked video, open letter, university correspondence and later developments were not inspected; no private family or sacred-site details are reproduced.

sources.title: Land and Water Acknowledgement — San Antonio Missions
sources.author: National Park Service
sources.annotation: A present-day park acknowledgment that names multiple communities associated with San Antonio missions. It is contextual evidence of the park’s stated relationships, not an exhaustive list, a sovereignty determination, or proof that the named peoples share one identity.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the complete acknowledgment. It is retained as supporting context only and does not count as a substantive historical work.

sources.title: Voces de otros tiempos. Lenguas originarias del noreste de México — selected methodological discussion
sources.author: Moises Valadez Moreno (as printed on the article)
sources.publisher: Noroeste de México / Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia
sources.publicationDate: Date unresolved: article received/accepted in 2024; PDF running header identifies January–June 2022
sources.annotation: Selected methodological pages explain the author’s reorganization of earlier vocabulary lists and discuss disputed language classifications. This is a secondary reconstruction, not a new speaker survey. The article also makes sweeping disappearance claims; those are the author’s assertions and are not adopted as evidence that descendants ceased to exist. The vocabulary tables were not systematically evaluated.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual public 54-page publisher PDF: printed pp. 164–169 (PDF1–6); the ‘Lenguas y voces’ methodological passage on p.172 (PDF9); and final comments on p.206 (PDF43). References on pp.207 and215–217 inspected as locators only. Title page visually inspected. Full vocabulary tables and intervening sections were not content-reviewed; cited original works were not independently inspected.
sources.countReason: Retained as inspected supporting criticism of a secondary reconstruction. Partial scope and unresolved broad claims do not warrant promoting the earlier lead into an excellent substantive work merely to increase the count.

inspectedSubresources.title: Actual publisher PDF
inspectedSubresources.scope: Selected printed pp.164–169,172(methodological passage),206;54-page PDF not read in full.

sources.accessNotes: Public Spanish PDF with English abstract downloaded normally through PowerShell; no reader account or paywall encountered. The article-record route returned a server error and web-tool PDF retrieval timed out, but actual PDF text was accessible and selected content read. Printed first page states received January13,2024 and accepted April15,2024; running headers say Noroeste de México, nueva época,no.5,January–June2022. Publication chronology is unresolved. No vocabulary, maps, ceremonial detail, archaeological locations or images reproduced; link-only use.

initialAdequacy.rationale: Twelve substantive resources have actual-content inspection records, including first-party Tāp Pīlam and Miakan/Garza materials, a peer-reviewed study of one Miakan-Band program, scholarly and educational syntheses, and targeted mission research. They support a careful introductory profile and document major disagreements. The source target is a quantity measure, not a finding that the broad umbrella entry is complete or that these communities endorse the synthesis. The previously unread INAH lead now has an explicit selected-content inspection record, but remains excluded from substantive quantity. No new excellent work or independent identity/continuity claim is established by this bounded pass.
remainingLimits: The entry covers a broad historical umbrella; the evidence cannot stand in for separate research on the many named peoples and contemporary communities placed under it.

name: Coeur d'Alene
overview: The Coeur d’Alene Tribe identifies itself as Schitsu’umsh, “Those who were found here.” This guide follows the Tribe’s own public accounts of homeland, governance and language alongside historical agreements, a Supreme Court decision, a tribal-authored history and environmental records. The sources describe different periods and kinds of evidence; none of the regional or legal summaries is a complete map of community history.

sections.title: Names, community and living government
sections.text: The Tribe’s public “Our Tribe” page uses Schitsu’umsh and explains the English name “Coeur d’Alene” as a French label applied by outsiders. The Tribe describes a continuing people with its own government and language. These are the community’s own public descriptions. A 1947 constitution scan records an earlier formal government structure; its text is a historical document, and current government or membership rules should be checked against current tribal publications rather than inferred from this edition.

sections.title: Homeland, waterways and historical change
sections.text: The Tribe describes a homeland organized around waterways, villages, trade and seasonal relationships. Its ancestral-lands page and 2012 Integrated Resource Management Plan emphasize continuing relationships with land and water while recounting later cessions and the loss of land access. The Tribe’s acreage descriptions vary by document and method; they should be read as attributed community or planning statements, not fixed boundaries. Public historical agreements also record proposed or conditional arrangements. Read together, these records show colonial-era legal changes without implying that a document alone captures consent, lived experience or the full extent of homeland.

sections.title: Language, writing and teaching
sections.text: The Tribe’s language materials distinguish the Coeur d’Alene language from the larger Salish language family and from neighboring languages. A tribal account describes documentation and orthography work by Lawrence G. Nicodemus and Joseph N. Bitar, and the Tribe’s elementary curriculum page describes a four-year STEP grant and a Tribe-created social-studies curriculum. These sources document published approaches and a dated program; they do not measure present language fluency or establish current program availability. The brief language overview is retained as a starting point but is not counted as a substantive work.

sections.title: Agreements, reservation history and a defined legal holding
sections.text: The July 1873 agreement proposed a reservation and included terms subject to further federal action; the archive records it as not ratified. The September 1889 agreement described a northern land cession and made its operation conditional on ratification of an earlier agreement. These are primary texts, useful for studying what their signatories and drafters wrote, not self-explanatory accounts of consent. In Idaho v. United States (2001), the Supreme Court held that the United States holds specified submerged lands within the current reservation in trust for the Tribe. That decision concerns submerged-land title within reservation boundaries; it does not decide ownership of the entire lake or every water and land interest in the basin.

sections.title: Stewardship, mining and environmental history
sections.text: The Tribe’s resource plan and its public lake-management account describe relationships among land, water, health and cultural resources, as well as the effects of mining and dam operations. A 1995 federal environmental review preserves a tribal position statement and a history attributed to Bingo Sijohn; these are important, specifically attributed tribal perspectives inside a government compilation. The EPA’s Bunker Hill record independently documents mining-related contamination, cleanup actions and continuing risks across the basin. EPA figures and work status change over time, so its live site and its July 2024 bulletin are dated snapshots. The compiled exhibits contain sensitive cultural-resource details; this guide does not reproduce those locations.

sections.title: How to read this collection
sections.text: Begin with the Tribe’s own identity, land and language pages, then compare its planning documents with the agreements and court opinion. Use the EPA records for environmental cleanup history and the 1995 exhibits for the Tribe’s position as it was submitted in that review. The constitution, agreements and court decision each answer different legal or historical questions. Dates, authorship and selected-page limits matter throughout; none of these works alone represents every family, period or current community perspective.

sources.title: Our Tribe
sources.annotation: Read the Tribe’s public self-description and naming account. It identifies the people as Schitsu’umsh, explains the French-derived English label, and describes continuing government, community and language. This is a concise community-authored introduction, not a legal history or full account of internal diversity.

sources.title: History
sources.annotation: Community historical overview covering place, naming, government and changes in land ownership. Its acreage and timeline statements are attributed to the Tribe’s page and should be compared with dated treaties, court records and planning documents; no old population estimate is reused as current.

sources.title: Ancestral Lands
sources.annotation: Community account of homeland connections to waterways and villages, stewardship, land loss and later legal developments. Read as the Tribe’s public perspective, not a survey boundary. Specific sensitive sites are not reproduced.

sources.title: Language — Coeur d’Alene Tribe
sources.annotation: Brief community language orientation, reviewed in full. Useful as a direct entry point to the Tribe’s language materials, but too short to count as a substantive inspected work.

sources.title: Reading and Writing in the Coeur d’Alene Language
sources.annotation: Read the complete public article and its alphabet/lesson material. The Tribe recounts a 1973 documentation effort and credits Lawrence G. Nicodemus and Joseph N. Bitar with language documentation and orthography work. This community narrative and teaching resource describes a particular language project, not a fluency survey.

sources.title: Questions about our Schitsu’umsh Language
sources.annotation: Read the full Q&A, including the Tribe’s distinction between its language and the broader Salish language family and its account of writing conventions. This is an attributed community explanation; linguistic classifications should be read at the language level, not as a single shared language across the family.

sources.publisher: Coeur d’Alene Tribe, Department of Education
sources.annotation: Read the page’s curriculum and STEP-grant sections. The Tribe describes a four-year project and its own elementary social-studies curriculum, linking education with sovereignty and cultural continuity. Program details are a dated account, not an evaluation of current course availability or outcomes.

sources.title: Integrated Resource Management Plan
sources.publisher: Coeur d’Alene Tribe, Natural Resources Department
sources.annotation: Tribal planning document, 319 pages. Inspected printed pp. 15–16, 66 and 188–190 for sovereignty, the Tribe’s resource philosophy and land-history discussion, including 1867/1873 reservation records and later cessions. Only these selected pages were read; acreage descriptions are plan-specific estimates and not mapped boundaries.

sources.title: Constitution and Bylaws of the Coeur d’Alene Tribe
sources.publisher: Coeur d’Alene Tribe; Library of Congress digital copy
sources.annotation: Inspected the complete six-page scan, printed constitution approved August 8, 1947, with later reproduction/imprint details. This is a historical constitution text, including period-specific membership language; it must not be presented as the current constitution or used to state present membership rules.

sources.title: Agreement with the Coeur d’Alene, 1873
sources.publisher: Oklahoma State University, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties; underlying record cited to NARA RG 75
sources.annotation: Read the complete digitized agreement record and text. Dated July 28, 1873, it proposed a reservation and contains terms conditioned on additional federal action; the database identifies it as not ratified. Classify as an agreement, not a ratified treaty. The text documents proposed terms, not a complete account of consent or lived effects.

sources.title: Agreement with the Coeur d’Alene, 1889
sources.publisher: Oklahoma State University, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties; underlying record cited to NARA RG 75
sources.annotation: Read the complete digitized agreement record and text dated September 9, 1889. It records a proposed cession and payment terms, and states that it would bind only if an earlier agreement were ratified. Read its conditions alongside the ratification record and later court history; do not treat the document alone as proof of consent.

sources.title: Idaho v. United States, 533 U.S. 262
sources.publisher: Supreme Court of the United States
sources.annotation: Read the opinion in volume 533, pp. 262–280 (bound PDF pp. 265–280 in an 868-page volume). The Court held that the United States holds in trust for the Tribe the specified submerged lands within the reservation, including portions of the lake and river. The holding is limited to title in the disputed submerged lands; it is not a ruling that the Tribe owns the whole lake or every basin interest.

sources.title: Coeur d’Alene Tribal History, Cultural Resources & Position Statement (1995 EIS exhibits)
sources.publisher: Bureau of Reclamation, Bonneville Power Administration and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, System Operation Review Final EIS exhibits; includes Tribe-submitted material
sources.annotation: Inspected selected exhibit pages 143–165 in the 175-page PDF: Ernest L. Stensgar’s November 1994 comments, a 1995 Coeur d’Alene position statement, and a history attributed to Bingo Sijohn. These are tribal-submitted perspectives preserved in a federal review, not neutral editorial findings; OCR and framing are uneven. Sensitive site details are intentionally omitted.

sources.title: Lake Management: Challenges
sources.annotation: Read the complete public page, including its discussion of the lake’s spiritual and material importance, mining pollution, the 1991–95 management plan and hydropower licensing. The page explicitly dates several conditions and procedural details to 2005; use it as historical context, not a current status report.

sources.title: Bunker Hill Mining & Metallurgical Complex: Cleanup Activities
sources.annotation: Inspected the live EPA site profile’s background, cleanup and status sections. It describes the Superfund area across northern Idaho and eastern Washington, mining-related heavy-metal contamination, cleanup actions and remaining risks. EPA’s current figures and status are date-sensitive and do not substitute for the Tribe’s account of cultural effects or priorities.

sources.title: Basin Bulletin: Updates on the Coeur d’Alene River Basin Cleanup
sources.annotation: Inspected the complete eight-page July 2024 bulletin. It records the 50th-anniversary event with Coeur d’Alene Tribe representatives, cleanup and lead-exposure information, and then-planned community-involvement work. Its property totals, schedules and risk notices are explicitly a July 2024 snapshot, not current measurements.

sources.title: Language — Culture Department overview
sources.annotation: Short program page describing dated internal language-lesson plans and teaching tools. Read as a historical project snapshot, not evidence of current enrollment or present-day fluency; kept as support rather than counted as a substantive work.

sources.title: Natural Resources Department
sources.annotation: Brief departmental mission and program overview, including a 1992 program-consolidation note. Useful orientation only; detailed historical and environmental evidence is cited to the Tribe’s plan and EPA records, so this brief page is excluded from the substantive count.

initialAdequacy.rationale: Fifteen substantive works were inspected, including multiple Coeur d’Alene Tribe publications, two agreement texts, a Supreme Court opinion, a tribal-authored position preserved in a federal EIS, and EPA cleanup records. The collection now supports a useful, cited introduction to identity, language, land, governance and environmental history, but the evidence is uneven across periods and subjects. Source quantity alone does not make the research complete or community-reviewed.

name: Comanche
overview: Comanche people’s histories connect the Southern Plains, Texas and the present Comanche Nation in Oklahoma. This foundation brings the Nation’s own account together with community-directed language history, a consulted Texas report, an edited treaty and attributed educational accounts. Historical bands, the broader people and the present government retain their own contexts.

sections.title: Names, a wider people and a present Nation
sections.text: The Comanche Nation uses Nʉmʉnʉʉ for its people. Its own historical account connects movement onto the Plains with horse-based life and kinship-based bands. This people-level directory route and the present government are related levels of description, rather than one unchanged organization across all periods. Current membership numbers and governing rules require separate dated verification.

sections.title: Bands need their own context
sections.text: The consulted TxDOT report describes changing local bands and wider divisions, with relationships that could form and change. Penateka, Nokoni and Quahadi are among its historical labels. These names should remain individually searchable when their identities and aliases are checked; a list of bands does not prove that each is a separate present government.

sections.title: Plains movement and Texas history
sections.text: The Nation’s account follows movement southward and emphasizes horses and bison. TxDOT’s selected historical chapters connect Texas history to military pressure and removal to reservation life. These broad accounts provide a starting chronology, not precise homeland boundaries. The report contains internal date problems that remain disclosed in its source card.

sections.title: Reading the 1867 treaty critically
sections.text: The Medicine Lodge treaty transcription contains a reservation provision, a reserved hunting clause and a consent requirement for later cession of reservation land. It also sets out federal services and compulsory English-school attendance. The text places promises of protection and services alongside compulsory schooling and requirements to make the reservation a permanent home. The wording alone does not establish implementation, universal agreement or present-day legal rights.

sections.title: Community-directed language institutions
sections.text: The Language Department’s account traces its planning to community organizing in 2017 and funding for fiscal 2019. It recognizes the earlier preservation committee and describes teacher certification, curriculum and digital resources among its goals. These are the department’s reported history and aims; this review did not test an app, inspect a curriculum or measure fluency.

sections.title: A dated record of teaching across communities
sections.text: Fuentes’s 1999 source book records preservation work and a Toya Band language class in Albuquerque and Santa Fe. It describes volunteer teaching, intergenerational participation and materials in that historical setting. The two program entries form one reviewed educational work. They do not establish today’s schedule, participation or separate-government status.

sections.title: Language, family memory and individual experience
sections.text: The Boulder report presents Ruth Toathy’s and Rosemary Chibity’s differing memories of language use at home and pressure toward English, alongside Leonard Chibity’s comments on place names. These are named personal accounts within an edited public report. They help readers see lived experiences without turning one recollection into a statement about every Comanche family.

sections.title: A Texas primary document before Medicine Lodge
sections.text: The 1844 Tehuacana Creek text joins peace provisions with regulated trade, government agents and proposed English-language, Christian and agricultural instruction. Its 22 articles make those different aims visible together. The document lists several Indigenous parties separately; a shared instrument does not merge their identities. References to a line do not themselves establish a precise agreed territorial boundary.

sections.title: Penateka diplomacy and German settlement
sections.text: Babcock’s study of the 1847 Meusebach agreement gives Comanche leaders and intermediaries a role alongside the German negotiator. He challenges accounts that credit one man alone and places negotiations within settlement pressures. His interpretation is useful to compare with the primary record; it should not become a claim that every Comanche band accepted the same agreement or that later pressures disappeared.

sections.title: Remembering code talkers through families and language
sections.text: In the Nation’s report, Lloyd Heminokeky explains the importance of honoring code talkers through family participation and language-department work. LaNora Parker describes her father Simmons Parker as a teacher of Comanche history and pride. These named accounts connect public remembrance with family learning, without defining every family’s experience or reproducing songs and ceremonial material.

sections.title: What this foundation still needs
sections.text: Nine inspected works now offer a wider reading foundation. Texas diplomacy can be studied through an edited 1844 document and a focused 1847 scholarly reassessment, alongside community voices about later remembrance. More Comanche-authored historical scholarship, original negotiation and implementation records, and careful band-level comparisons remain needed. No comprehensive history, current legal assessment or community endorsement is claimed.
