name: Coushatta
overview: Coushatta histories connect distinct communities in Texas, Louisiana and Oklahoma. This reading path distinguishes the peoples and their governments while introducing community history, archives and public language work.

sections.title: The shared Texas government has a particular history
sections.text: The Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas describes Alabama and Coushatta as separate peoples with a long association. Its history connects migration into East Texas with relationships under successive colonial and state governments. The Tribe’s timeline dates federal restoration to 1987. This public account concerns the joint Texas institution, rather than making Louisiana and Oklahoma Coushatta communities branches of that government.

sections.title: Village leaders and a changing institutional name
sections.text: The Tribe’s Chief History distinguishes leaders of Alabama villages, leaders of Coushatta villages and later Alabama-Coushatta chiefs. It names Coushatta leaders associated with different Texas communities and describes movement onto the Alabama reservation beginning in 1859. The publication’s structure makes village-level histories visible; it should not be read as proof that every earlier Coushatta community belonged to one unchanged modern government.

sections.title: The treaty text records a proposal, not a settled outcome
sections.text: An edited transcript of the February 23, 1836 treaty names Alabama and Coushatta among groups styled “associate Bands” of the Cherokee, then proposes that those groups form one community within a described area. The document records a Republic of Texas negotiating position in that moment. Later historical accounts report that the agreement was not ratified; its text alone does not establish implementation, Indigenous acceptance of the proposed terms, or a continuing boundary.

sections.title: Federal law changed the Texas government’s legal relationship
sections.text: The 1954 federal statute provided for transfer of trust lands to Texas and termination of federal supervision and services following a proclamation. In 1987, Congress restored federal recognition, the trust relationship and services for the Alabama and Coushatta Tribes of Texas, treating them as one tribal unit for federal-law purposes. The Tribe’s constitution, amended through 2023, says the Alabama and Coushatta were formerly distinct tribes and describes their shared legal government, territory and governing institutions. These legal texts concern the Texas government; they do not erase separate peoplehood or describe other Coushatta governments.

sections.title: A 1932 history is useful only with its period and viewpoint visible
sections.text: Harriet Smither’s long article follows Alabama history in Texas through colonial records, nineteenth-century land negotiations and federal reports. It provides a route into dated records, including petitions and land actions, but its terminology and descriptions reflect an early twentieth-century outside historian. This page uses it selectively as a historical source and does not carry its old population statements or character judgments forward as current fact.

sections.title: A state history article revisits the Texas Revolution story
sections.text: The Texas Historical Commission’s 2026 article summarizes the Alabama-Coushatta role in events around the Texas Revolution, quoting historical sources and an attributed statement by Chief Colita. It also reports that the Texas Senate declined to ratify the 1836 treaty. Because this is a modern state-agency retrospective, its quotations and historical interpretations remain attributed to that article and its named sources.

sections.title: An archive route still awaiting inspection
sections.text: The original Coushatta tribal-archive link remains available as a reading route, but its body could not be retrieved in this pass. No underlying collection item, narrative, image, recording or access permission was reviewed through it.

sections.title: Louisiana’s account of movement and institutional renewal
sections.text: The Louisiana Tribe’s history describes successive settlements across a changing colonial borderland and an enduring community near Elton. It attributes renewed federal recognition in 1973 to years of community organizing and advocacy after services were withdrawn. These are the Tribe’s institutional historical statements. Its trajectory differs from the Texas restoration chronology and does not establish current eligibility, services or every family’s migration.

sections.title: Community decisions in language documentation
sections.text: Bertney and Linda Langley describe a Koasati Language Committee whose members made spelling decisions and shaped practical teaching materials. Their account connects workshops, documentation training and collaborative review with community control of the resulting work. It records activities beginning in 2006–2007, rather than current program delivery. The chapter explains a process; its reported successes are not an independently measured learner-fluency outcome.

sections.title: Texas connections extend beyond present government locations
sections.text: TxDOT’s April 2021 report explicitly acknowledges collaboration with the Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana’s heritage staff. It describes several Coushatta communities in Texas and related travel networks connecting Texas and Louisiana. The account treats village decisions and movements separately. This history helps explain why a Louisiana-based government can have Texas interests; it is not a new territorial boundary or a claim that everyone followed one route.

sections.title: The Oklahoma town’s own historical perspective
sections.text: Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town describes Alabama and Quassarte as earlier distinct towns within the Muscogee Confederacy. Its history differentiates people who moved southwest into Louisiana and Texas from those removed with the Creeks to Indian Territory. The Oklahoma community’s continuing institutional story is therefore a separate reading path, rather than another name for the Texas or Louisiana government.

sections.title: Community language work and a public Koasati dictionary
sections.text: A community-coauthored AILDI chapter describes Koasati documentation workshops and the Language Committee’s decisions about writing and teaching materials. The Louisiana Coushatta Tribe’s public digital dictionary names its committee, guides and editor and provides word forms, definitions and selected examples. A separate short language page identifies Alabama as related to Koasati, not another name for it. Together these sources document Louisiana-centered language work; they do not establish identical practice across Texas and Oklahoma Coushatta institutions, a current speaker count, or measured learning outcomes.

Citation follows the official index and page range. The law is not evidence that the people or Tribe ceased to exist.

The 1836 treaty is an edited Republic of Texas diplomatic text and a proposal; it is not used as proof of ratification, implementation, Indigenous acceptance or present homeland boundary.

Reviewed 2026-10-23: added the Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana’s digital Koasati dictionary as one substantive work after inspecting its landing page and four actual entries. Community attribution is explicit; full dictionary coverage, audio and outcomes remain unreviewed. It strengthens the Louisiana-language path without merging the Texas or Oklahoma governments.
relationshipNote: Some sources use “Koasati” for the language associated with Coushatta communities; here, “Coushatta” names the people/community collection and “Koasati” primarily names the language. Neither label is a synonym for Alabama. The Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana, Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas and Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town in Oklahoma are distinct governments and communities. Their connections do not make every family’s route, language use or political history identical. A joint Texas government is not evidence that Alabama and Coushatta were originally one people. The 1987 federal act and the Texas Tribe’s constitution describe one joint legal/governmental status for the Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas while also recognizing that Alabama and Coushatta were formerly distinct peoples; this legal arrangement does not make the three present governments interchangeable.

name: Dakota
overview: Dakota peoples include distinct communities and governments across a wide region. This Minnesota-focused reading path centers community accounts, Dakota public testimony and education, historical displacement, and a dated treaty record. It distinguishes Minnesota governments and specific historical evidence from broader Dakota identities and histories elsewhere.

sections.title: Cansa'yapi: community continuity and public history
sections.text: The Lower Sioux Indian Community identifies its members as Mdewakanton Dakota and calls its Minnesota River homeland Caŋṡayapi. Its account describes families returning despite exile. A companion historic-site page dates tribal management of the Lower Sioux Agency site to 2007. The Community’s public history booklet adds its own account of Caŋṡayapi, stewardship, sovereignty, the 1851–1858 treaty period, community continuity after 1862, Wacipi and Dakota-language renewal. These are community-specific historical and educational statements, not independent verification of broader Dakota history or a homeland boundary. Together the sources connect continuity with the Community’s authority to interpret a place shaped by federal reservation policy.

sections.title: A particular Mdewakanton government's institutions
sections.text: The SMSC identifies itself as a Dakota government within the Oceti Ṡakowiŋ, alongside related Dakota, Lakota and Nakota peoples. Its public timeline follows forced removal, later land purchases and its own 1969 governmental organization. The community dates Hoċokata Ṫi's opening to 2019. These are a particular Mdewakanton government's institutions, not a model shared by every Dakota community.

sections.title: Prairie Island's account of land and persistence
sections.text: Prairie Island identifies its members as Bdewakantunwan, or Mdewakanton, Eastern Dakota. Its history follows families who remained or returned, purchased land and maintained a community despite displacement. The Tribe also describes pressures from dam construction, a nuclear generating plant and rail transport. These concerns are its situated account of Prairie Island, rather than a general description of every Dakota homeland.

sections.title: Language activism across community boundaries
sections.text: Dakota Wicohan traces its origins to a 2001 language team involving Upper Sioux, Lower Sioux and Twin Cities Dakota, followed by nonprofit incorporation in 2002. Its account connects intergenerational language learning, teacher preparation and outreach with community relationships. This educational organization works across political boundaries; it is not another tribal government. Its undated speaker and program totals are not current measurements. A separate Dakota Wicohan curriculum was developed by Dakota scholars and educators led by Iyekiyapiwiƞ Darlene St. Clair. Its ten-lesson outline treats Minnesota as Dakota homeland and covers place, language, sovereignty, treaties, colonization, cultural continuity and living together. The public overview says teachers need training to access the lessons and that outcome research was still forthcoming; the materials have not been presented here as an evaluated program.

sections.title: Imprisonment and forced removal
sections.text: MNHS describes noncombatant Dakota imprisonment at Fort Snelling during 1862–1863 and forced transport to Crow Creek in May 1863. It distinguishes congressional actions of February 16 and March 3, 1863, concerning treaty annulment and removal. Its account also discusses a separate Ho-Chunk expulsion. These histories should not be conflated or taken to mean every Dakota person participated in the war.

sections.title: Reading the 1851 Mendota treaty carefully
sections.text: The Mendota treaty text names Mdewakanton and Wahpekute parties, rather than every Dakota community. Its published version records a land cession, differentiated payments and funding for education and farms. It also marks Article 3 as deleted and prints supplemental terms. This specific written federal record does not establish fully informed consent, oral understandings, promise fulfillment or present individual entitlements.

sections.title: Four Minnesota governments within wider Dakota peoples
sections.text: MnDOT's public inventory names Lower Sioux, Prairie Island, Shakopee Mdewakanton and Upper Sioux as Minnesota Dakota communities. Each government needs its own institutional reading. This four-government inventory is a Minnesota access point, not an exhaustive list of Dakota peoples or their communities elsewhere in the United States and Canada.

sections.title: Earlier reading links and their limits
sections.text: The retained South Dakota teaching-kit versions offer a broad comparative educational starting point; only their contents and goals were inspected here. The retained Black Hills page identifies a hosted student legal position paper. These resources do not supply Minnesota Dakota community authority, a universal cultural description or verified current law, and remain outside this collection's substantive count.

sections.title: Homeland through named Dakota voices
sections.text: In the Minnesota Historical Society’s Our Home exhibition transcript, five named Dakota speakers describe Minnesota as Dakota homeland, discuss the Seven Council Fires, and speak about relationships to land and relatives. The speakers use different formulations: Dallas Ross distinguishes Dakota as a way of life from a nation of people, while Grace Goldtooth-Campos refers to Dakota Oyate as a nation and describes its council-fire groups. Keeping each statement attributed makes the variation visible without treating one exhibition transcript as a universal definition for all Dakota people or governments. In a separate MNHS oral-history excerpt, Upper Sioux narrator Dean Blue reflects on Fort Snelling from his own experience as a veteran-service officer and expresses a personal view about the building. The interviewer notes that Dakota people held differing views; the excerpt should be read as one individual's public memory, not as consensus.

sections.title: Upper Sioux Community: Pezihutazizi Oyate and returned agency lands
sections.text: The 2025 Minnesota Tribal Government guide presents Upper Sioux Community’s account of Pejuhutazizi Kapi as Dakota homeland, the community’s formation in 1938 on 746 returned acres, and its 1995 constitution. The guide reports that the state returned the former Upper Sioux Agency State Park in 2024 and gives a resulting total land base of 3,725 acres; its membership count is a dated 2025 report figure, not a current 2026 measure. The Minnesota DNR describes the Community’s long-standing request and explains the 1862 history of starvation and death at the agency, while Minnesota law records the state’s direction to transfer park land. The DNR page and statute are state records, not substitutes for the Community’s own historical account. A separate undated state-hosted version repeats the community history with older acreage and population figures; neither version defines all Dakota homelands or a present boundary.

sections.title: Language renewal within Prairie Island and Shakopee communities
sections.text: Prairie Island describes its community language department, classes, culture camps, language-bowl activities and outreach at Red Wing High School. Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux Community describes its own language team, weekly classes, family learning events, youth camps and Dakota-language education. These are two governments’ accounts of particular programs, not a single uniform Dakota-language system. Prairie Island’s page still refers to an app expected in spring 2023; its present availability was not verified.

sections.title: Prairie Island’s cultural and historic preservation work
sections.text: Prairie Island describes its Tribal Historic Preservation Office, artifact repatriation work, restoration of the public He Mni Can site, and partnership to protect the Grand Meadow Chert Quarry. These examples show the Community’s own preservation priorities and public interpretation. Its broader archaeological statements remain attributed to the Community; no burial locations or restricted details are repeated.

sources.annotation: The DNR explains that the Upper Sioux Community had long requested return of the park because of its significance and describes Dakota starvation and deaths at the agency in 1862 in connection with treaty food that the United States failed to provide. It records the park’s 2024 closure and the 2023 law directing a state-land transfer. This is the state agency’s explanation and is retained as focused corroboration, not a community-authored history.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the page’s land-return rationale, cited 2023 legislation, closure date, and transfer-related public information (lines 5–15 and 31–35). Linked recreational listings were not reviewed.

sources.title: Minnesota Laws 2023, Chapter 60, section 97 — Upper Sioux Agency State Park land transfer
sources.publisher: Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes
sources.author: Minnesota Legislature
sources.annotation: Section 97 directs the commissioner of natural resources to convey state-owned land within Upper Sioux Agency State Park to the Upper Sioux Community without consideration; it separately authorizes a possible Minnesota Historical Society conveyance subject to Executive Council approval and legal barriers. The statute records the state’s authorization and requirements, not an independent account of Dakota history or proof of every step of conveyance.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read section 97 and its effective-date clause (lines 4363–4372), plus the associated appropriation’s stated transfer purpose. The remainder of the omnibus act was not reviewed for this profile.

sources.title: Pezihutazizi / Oyate — Upper Sioux Community historical page
sources.publisher: Minnesota Indian Affairs Council; page uses first-person community language and links to the Upper Sioux Community
sources.author: Community history reproduced through the Minnesota Indian Affairs Council; individual author and publication date not displayed
sources.annotation: The page preserves a first-person historical account of homeland, forced removal, return, government formation, enterprises and services. Its undated population and acreage statements (453 people and over 900 acres) differ from the 2025 state guide’s account of a 2024 land return and 3,725-acre total land base. These figures should be read as dated versions of a community narrative rather than treated as current or as evidence of a boundary. The linked Upper Sioux government site returned HTTP 403 to the research request; no access control was bypassed.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the full historical body and its links to elected leaders and the Upper Sioux Community website (page lines 16–36). The linked community site itself was not accessible from this request; its 403 response is not classified as a reader paywall.

sources.title: Dean Blue on Fort Snelling — U.S.-Dakota War oral-history excerpt
sources.author: Dean Blue, interviewed by Deborah Locke
sources.publicationDate: Interview recorded April 27, 2011; web page dated July 24, 2026
sources.annotation: This MNHS page publishes a short excerpt from an interview recorded in Granite Falls in 2011. Blue reflects on visits to Fort Snelling through his veteran-service work and gives his own view of whether the fort should remain. The interviewer's framing explicitly notes differing Dakota views, so this is one person's perspective, not community consensus or a general Dakota position. It is evidence about a named narrator's public memory, not independent verification of historical events.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the complete visible story page, including the transcript excerpt (lines 80–100), its citation and interview metadata. The MNHS-linked full oral-history record returned HTTP 404 during inspection; this does not establish a reader access restriction. A search-discovered copy with unverified hosting provenance was not relied on. This excerpt is retained as supporting testimony and does not count toward the substantive-work target.

sources.title: Ehaŋna k’a Dehan: Past and Present — Caŋṡayapi community history booklet
sources.publisher: Lower Sioux Indian Community; hosted by the Minnesota Department of Education
sources.author: Lower Sioux Indian Community; includes a statement from Community Council president Robert Larsen; no comprehensive individual byline displayed
sources.sourceKind: Community-produced public history and education booklet
sources.publicationDate: Undated; no publication date displayed in the inspected PDF
sources.annotation: This 19-page community-produced booklet introduces Caŋṡayapi (Lower Sioux) through community history, relationships to the Minnesota River Valley, stewardship, sovereignty, the Lower Sioux Agency site, Wacipi and Dakota language. It says the Community traces its lineage primarily to Mdewakanton Dakota, and describes Wahpekute relationships and wider Oceti Ṡakowiŋ connections. Community historical and homeland statements are attributed to this publication; they are not independently verified by this review or a boundary determination. Historic acreage and membership figures elsewhere in the booklet are not treated as current measurements.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read selected substantive sections in the publicly accessible 19-page PDF: community introduction and relationship to the land (PDF pp. 2–4); land, stewardship and homeland/treaty history (pp. 6–12); Wacipi and language (pp. 14–16); and the historic-site and resource/back-cover context (pp. 17–19). Reviewed the visible resource list and map captions, but did not extract the map as a separate historical-map record. Other material and linked resources were not claimed as read.

initialAdequacy.rationale: Thirteen substantive inspected works now support a Minnesota-focused introduction, including separate accounts from three Minnesota Dakota governments, the 2025 Upper Sioux Community account carried in a state guide, a Lower Sioux Community-produced history booklet, Dakota-created education, named Dakota public testimony, a specific 1851 treaty text and focused state records. New community pages add distinct Prairie Island preservation and language-program material and Shakopee language education. Seven supporting references remain excluded. This is still weighted toward Minnesota and institutional materials, not a deep history of every Dakota community, specialist language study, current demographic account or community-reviewed collection.
remainingLimits: The Upper Sioux Community government website returned HTTP 403 to this research request. The accessible state-hosted histories and 2025 government guide provide useful community-attributed material, but the current Community constitution, official land-conveyance instrument, and a direct government publication about the 2024 return remain unreviewed; the access failure is not treated as a paywall and was not bypassed.

Dakota communities outside Minnesota, including particular governments in the Dakotas, Nebraska, and Canada, need their own community voices and scoped sources. This collection is not an exhaustive homeland or present-community map.
Specialist Dakota language scholarship is needed for precise language variation and classification; undated public speaker totals should not be used as current demographic findings.

Original treaty scans, oral understandings, 1863 statutes, community constitutions, and additional Dakota-authored historical scholarship would deepen the collection. Treaty text, state summaries, and public exhibition testimony answer different questions.

The complete Mni Sóta Maḳoce lesson materials require teacher training; the public page gives the curriculum overview but not the lessons themselves. Outcome research was described by the publisher as forthcoming, so no effectiveness claim is made.

Dated education reports and community evaluations would be needed before describing current operations, participation, or outcomes. No clinical, legal, membership, or service-eligibility conclusion is proposed.
No Dakota community review or endorsement is recorded.
The MNHS Dean Blue oral-history source is a short excerpt; its full interview was not verified through the archive link and the individual's view does not establish a Dakota-wide position.

This is a Minnesota-focused initial source guide, not a complete history of Dakota peoples or a community endorsement. Governance, historical, educational, and language claims retain their particular community, speaker, source, and period.

Three additional community-government pages reviewed on 2026-10-23 describe Prairie Island language education and cultural preservation and Shakopee Dakota-language programs. name: Jumano
overview: Spanish and later sources used “Jumano” for peoples across Texas, New Mexico, and adjacent northern Mexico. Scholars disagree whether it named one distinct people, several groups, or a broader label; contemporary Jumano community accounts describe living descendants. This profile keeps historical classifications and present-day community identity separate.

sections.title: A historical name with contested scope
sections.text: Historical materials used “Jumano” across more than one region and context. Nancy P. Hickerson’s distinct-trading-people interpretation appears in both her Handbook of Texas article and later scholarship, while older and other scholarly models proposed a broad Spanish label or linguistic connections to different peoples. Studies also disagree about whether particular Jumano groups were distinct from, related to, or interdependent with settled Patarabueye communities at La Junta. The Texas Beyond History exhibit and Bradley Folsom’s regional summary describe trade and mutual dependence while retaining cultural distinctions; these interpretations draw on inconsistent colonial names and should not be collapsed into one settled identity for every group. A National Park Service visitor page describes Gran Quivira at its peak as home to “eastern Tompiro/Jumano people” and as a Plains–Pueblo crossroads. Because this short public-history page gives no underlying citations and uses a combined label, it is useful evidence of a modern institutional summary, not proof that Tompiro and Jumano were interchangeable.

sections.title: Trade, diplomacy, and a changing borderlands
sections.text: Historical syntheses describe Jumano travel and trade linking the South Plains, lower Pecos, Rio Grande, New Mexico, and communities farther east. They report exchanges with Pueblo, La Junta, and Caddo communities and diplomacy associated with Juan Sabeata. Robert Weddle’s biography of Juan Domínguez de Mendoza describes Sabeata’s appeal and the 1683–84 expedition; route reconstructions and the proposed location of San Clemente remain disputed. The accounts were produced in colonial settings, and their place names, population figures, and ethnic labels require attribution rather than treatment as settled facts.

sections.title: La Junta was a crossroads, not a single people
sections.text: La Junta de los Ríos, near the Río Conchos–Río Grande confluence, was a region of settled villages and movement among different communities. The Texas Beyond History exhibit distinguishes villagers described by Spanish sources as Conchos, Patarabueyes, or Amotomancos from Jumano traders and visitors, and explains how translation and later illustrations have sometimes blurred those categories. Bradley Folsom’s regional article presents a later interpretation of Jumano and Patarabueye communities as mutually dependent while culturally distinct. These are interpretations of incomplete written records and archaeological evidence; the confluence should not be assigned to a single people.

sections.title: What the colonial record can—and cannot—show
sections.text: Most historical works in this collection rely on Spanish colonial documents, translated accounts, or later scholarly syntheses. Such sources describe encounters, trade, missions, and conflict, but they were written by outsiders and use names inconsistently. Two Arizona Historical Indexes records dated August and October 1683 identify correspondence involving Jumanes, Shulimes, and Sabeata and point to archival volumes and translation files. The catalogue summaries are not the letters: the original documents and translations remain unread, so no claims in those summaries are treated as independently verified here. The 1683–84 Mendoza diary is likewise represented by scholarly summaries and a catalogue record, not a direct reading of the manuscript.

sections.title: Living communities and contemporary accounts
sections.text: A 2021 local newspaper report records Jumano Nation of Texas historian Felix Bonilla Salmeron describing the nation’s effort to connect with descendants and rejecting the claim that Jumano people disappeared. This is a dated, attributed community perspective reported by a journalist, not a census or an independently verified genealogy. Separately, the Indigenous-led People of La Junta for Preservation describes its descendant communities as including Jumano, Julime, Chisos, Concho, Lipan Apache, and others, and explains its stewardship work at La Junta. That organization’s broader community scope is not interchangeable with the Jumano Nation of Texas.

sections.title: Reading claims about disappearance and recognition
sections.text: Some scholarly summaries say the colonial record stopped identifying Jumano as a distinct people or that their trade networks and political position changed by the eighteenth century. That describes an interpretation of surviving documents, not proof that descendants or living communities disappeared. Contemporary accounts from Jumano Nation of Texas and the separate Indigenous-led People of La Junta for Preservation have their own stated scope and are not interchangeable. Texas House Resolution 1565 is a state expression honoring the Jumano Indian Nation of Texas; its historical assertions and population claim are not independently verified here and it is not a federal recognition decision.

sections.title: A translated diary is not the whole record
sections.text: Brian Imhoff’s comparison of copies and translations of the 1683–84 Mendoza expedition diary argues that some familiar English narratives omit conflict within the expedition. His reading includes testimony that Jumano participants defended a threatened soldier. This is an interpretation of colonial records reproduced in a modern study, not an Atlas inspection of the originals or an unmediated Jumano account. It strengthens caution about translations without resolving the historical identity debate.

sources.title: HR 1565 — Jumano Indians of Texas
sources.annotation: The enrolled Texas House resolution documents a state legislative expression honoring the Jumano Indian Nation of Texas. Its historical narrative and population claim are not independent verification and it is not a federal recognition decision.
sources.contentReviewScope: The enrolled resolution text was read. It is counted as a supporting primary civic record, not as a substantive historical study.

sources.author: Nancy P. Hickerson
sources.publicationDate: Article date not stated on the accessed page
sources.annotation: A substantial scholarly state-history synthesis with a bibliography. It describes several different historical groupings associated with Jumano and reviews documentary geography, trade, and migration. Its conclusion that Jumano ceased to exist as an identifiable distinct people is an interpretation of the surviving colonial record; it does not establish that descendants disappeared.
sources.contentReviewScope: The full visible article and bibliography were read, including sections on La Junta, Tompiro communities, trade, and the article’s conclusion. The works in its bibliography and original Spanish records were not independently inspected.

sources.title: Who Were the Jumano? / Jumano-Spanish Relations
sources.author: Nancy A. Kenmotsu; exhibit editor Steve Black
sources.publicationDate: Undated web exhibit; credits cite adaptation from Kenmotsu’s 1994 dissertation and 2001 article
sources.annotation: An educational exhibit that synthesizes Spanish accounts of trade, diplomacy, missions, and conflict. Its author explicitly adopts the interpretation that Jumano was a distinct nation. The later statement that Jumano culture was gone and the treatment of biological ‘blood’ are dated outsider interpretations that conflict with contemporary community accounts and should not be presented as established fact.
sources.contentReviewScope: Both substantive Jumano modules and the credits page were read. The exhibit’s embedded translations and secondary figures were inspected as presented; cited books, dissertation, article, archives, and maps were not independently reviewed.

sources.author: Herbert E. Bolton
sources.annotation: A full, early scholarly article arguing that Jumano groups remained in southern Texas into the eighteenth century and that the name was also applied to Taovayas/Wichita people. Read as a dated intervention in an identity debate, not current consensus. The article contains OCR errors and relies on colonial documents; cited manuscript originals were not inspected.
sources.contentReviewScope: The complete 26-page scan was inspected across the introduction, Nueces geography, 1683–1716 records, Apache alliances, and the 1771 Taovayas discussion. Original manuscript sources and other works Bolton cites were not inspected.

sources.title: Jumano and Patarabueye: Relations at La Junta de los Rios
sources.publisher: University of Michigan Press / Museum of Anthropological Archaeology; digital edition at JSTOR
sources.author: J. Charles Kelley
sources.annotation: A specialist monograph compares Jumano and Patarabueye using documentary, linguistic, and archaeological evidence. Kelley’s distinctions and proposed correlations are scholarly interpretations, not settled ethnic identifications. Full institutional access is required; only the page metadata, chapter structure, and selected displayed excerpts were reviewed.
sources.contentReviewScope: Displayed excerpts from the introduction and selected chapters on historical data, Jumano identity, archaeology, and summary were read. JSTOR reported that the signed-in account lacked institutional access. The complete 201-page book was not inspected.

sources.annotation: A local report on a public talk by Jumano Nation of Texas members, including historian Felix Bonilla Salmeron. His statements about continuing Jumano identity and descendant-search efforts are attributed to him; the article is not an independent demographic or genealogical study.
sources.contentReviewScope: The full visible article body was read, including its direct quotations and image credit. A sign-in interface appeared below the story; the body was accessible without bypassing it. No underlying talk recording or independent genealogical evidence was inspected.

sources.publicationDate: Current site reviewed October 23, 2026; individual page date not stated

This is a first-party community self-description about its own broader community and stewardship; it does not establish that the organization is the Jumano Nation of Texas or speaks for all Jumano people.
sources.contentReviewScope: The visible homepage was read, including its self-description as Indigenous-led, named descendant communities, and discussion of current stewardship. The other named communities and individual family histories were not independently assessed.

sources.annotation: A separate educational synthesis about La Junta’s archaeology and changing interpretations. It explains why Jumano cannot simply stand for everyone who lived at or visited the confluence, and summarizes Kelley, Kenmotsu, and Morgenthaler models. Its statements about the disappearance of Native groups are attributed historical interpretations, not proof that descendant communities no longer exist.
sources.contentReviewScope: The full visible La Junta Reconsidered page was read, including its treatment of competing models and research limits. Cited books, archival material, and underlying archaeological data were not independently inspected.

The page is useful for orientation but compresses a complex debate; its claims should be read alongside the specialist work it cites.
sources.contentReviewScope: The full visible entry and bibliography were read, including discussion of Cabeza de Vaca, later Spanish expeditions, missions, and debated Jumano–Patarabueye relations. The cited dissertations, books, and Spanish records were not independently inspected.

name: Karankawa
overview: Karankawa is a historical collective name associated with several Gulf Coast peoples, and it is also used in present-day descendant-community organizing. Historical labels, modern organizations and family histories are not interchangeable; the evidence and perspectives below are dated and attributed.

sections.title: A name used for several coastal peoples
sections.text: Historical references use Karankawa as a collective label for several coastal groups, with spellings and lists that vary across sources. TSHA and Texas Beyond History name groups including Cocos, Cujanes, Coapites or Guapites, Carancahuas, Copanes or Capoques. A 2024 speech by Chiara Beaumont describes “seven or so” clans, a different category and count. The profile preserves that variation rather than claiming one settled list or equating the historical groupings with a single present-day government.

sections.title: Coastal place, seasonal movement and material life
sections.text: Scholarly and archaeological education sources place the historical communities along the central Texas coast and describe seasonal movement between mainland, bays and barrier islands as people used coastal and inland resources. Those accounts support a broad historical association, not a precise border or evidence that every community occupied each place in the same period. The 2026 Karankawa Tribe of Texas announcement also rejects the older “nomadic” label in favor of “semi-nomadic”; this is that group’s stated correction, while more detailed source comparison remains open.

sections.title: Missions and diplomacy in colonial records
sections.text: The Rosario and Refugio entries describe shifting relationships with Spanish mission institutions, including seasonal attendance, departure, negotiation, food shortages and mission movement. Balthazar’s biography follows one Copano leader’s diplomacy and should not be generalized to all coastal groups. These accounts rely on Spanish church and government records, whose labels and judgments—including descriptions of people as difficult to control—reflect colonial observers rather than neutral community testimony.

sections.title: Archaeology and the limits of outsider records
sections.text: The Texas Beyond History exhibit links coastal archaeology and material culture to early written records, while later reporting documents the destruction and rediscovery of settlement places. Many commonly repeated descriptions passed through colonial, state or scholarly sources. The 2019 honors thesis examines the history of cannibalism claims; it is a student thesis whose argument should be read with its methods and source limits visible. No allegation from hostile or sensational historical sources is repeated here as established fact.

sections.title: Living descendants and distinct dated community accounts
sections.text: Karankawa descendants are publicly organizing today. A 2023 statement from the Karankawa Kadla Five Rivers Council describes some relatives’ family histories and its own reconnection guidance; Beaumont’s 2023 speech gives her family and Karankawa Kadla experience. A 2026 announcement on the same public site uses the name Karankawa Tribe of Texas and also refers to the Five Rivers Council. These dated sources document particular voices and public names; the precise organizational relationship across the different labels and the full range of descendant perspectives remain unverified here. Older “extinction” language and missing archival records do not establish that the people disappeared.

sections.title: Historical markers, current records and next questions
sections.text: The 2022 Texas Historical Commission packet records a request to revise an older marker and competing procedural recommendations. A community announcement and 2026 reporting say a replacement marker was unveiled in July 2026. However, the official marker record checked for this review still displays the 1976 inscription; the new full text was not verified against an updated official record. The 2021 report’s recognition statements are dated, not current status findings. Further work should compare the new marker text, commission records, archival sources and additional community publications without treating recognition rules as the definition of peoplehood.

sources.title: Karankawa Indians
sources.annotation: A substantial scholarly state-history synthesis about the coastal peoples grouped under the Karankawa name. The article is useful for chronology, named historical groups, subsistence, mobility, missions and bibliography, but carries older extinction-era framing; read it beside dated descendant accounts and do not treat its cultural-group label as a present-day government.
sources.contentReviewScope: The full visible article body and bibliography were read. Its broad description, period terminology and claims are attributed to the TSHA entry; cited books and archival collections were not independently inspected.

sources.title: History Programs quarterly packet: proposed Karankawa marker text
sources.annotation: A later Texas Historical Commission quarterly packet contains a proposed Karankawa marker text, but it largely repeats one institutional narrative and predates a reported 2026 marker replacement. Kept as a dated comparison, not current marker text or an independent substantive history.
sources.contentReviewScope: Selected Karankawa marker-text pages in the November 2025 packet were inspected. The complete report was not read, and no final/current marker status is inferred from this source.

sources.title: Karankawas: Reexamining Texas Gulf Coast Cannibalism
sources.publisher: Tim Seiter; University of Houston Honors College
sources.annotation: Seiter’s honors thesis examines how claims of cannibalism entered colonial and later writing about the Gulf Coast peoples called Karankawa. It is a substantial student thesis, not a peer-reviewed monograph; its argument and source readings should be judged in that context and compared with the older accounts it discusses.
sources.contentReviewScope: The thesis abstract, introduction, contents and selected chapters/conclusion were inspected. The full 207-page work was not read cover to cover; the thesis’s interpretation is attributed to Seiter, and no sensationalized allegation is repeated as fact.

sources.title: Statement on reconnecting with Karankawa Kadla relatives
sources.annotation: A council statement describes the ways some Karankawa Kadla relatives came to know family histories and outlines the council’s own reconnection process. It is direct evidence about this council’s guidance and experience, not a universal membership rule or a complete account of all people who identify Karankawa.
sources.contentReviewScope: The full one-page statement was read. Its genealogy and DNA comments are represented as the council’s own guidance; the Atlas does not treat genetic testing as a test of Indigenous identity or citizenship.

sources.title: Nayina Wana Ayapah (We Are Still Here)
sources.publisher: Chiara Beaumont; transcript hosted by historian Tim Seiter
sources.annotation: A 2023 speech by Chiara Beaumont, a Karankawa speaker, describes her family’s reconnection and her experience with Karankawa Kadla. The page identifies the transcription and light editorial work by the host; it should be read as Beaumont’s situated account, not as a single voice for all Karankawa people.
sources.contentReviewScope: The speech transcript was read. The page explicitly withholds a portion shared for oral listening only; that material is not reproduced or summarized. The speaker’s references to clans and family geography are attributed rather than converted into universal facts or mapped boundaries.
sources.publicationDate: Speech delivered November 2023; transcript posted August 27, 2024

sources.title: Balthazar
sources.publisher: Handbook of Texas Online / Texas State Historical Association
sources.annotation: This focused biographical entry reconstructs Copano leader Balthazar through Spanish mission and military records. Its evidence concerns one documented leader and the Copano people; it cannot stand for all Karankawa groups or present-day communities.
sources.contentReviewScope: The full visible article and bibliography were read, including the entry’s treatment of a 1789 peace meeting and a 1790 census. The underlying Bexar archival documents cited by the article were not separately inspected.

sources.title: Nuestra Señora del Rosario Mission
sources.publisher: Handbook of Texas Online / Texas State Historical Association; Kathleen Kirk Gilmore
sources.annotation: A detailed mission-history entry discusses Cujanes, Copanes, Guapites and other Karankawa people in relation to Rosario. Its narrative depends heavily on colonial church and government records; period labels such as “indolence” are quoted colonial judgments, not neutral descriptions.
sources.contentReviewScope: The visible article body and bibliography were read. It is used for the mission chronology and named groups, not as a complete account of Karankawa perspectives or present community histories.

sources.title: Nuestra Señora del Refugio Mission
sources.publisher: Handbook of Texas Online / Texas State Historical Association
sources.annotation: This entry draws on mission and baptismal records to describe changing population and movement at Refugio and Rosario. Its numbers are colonial administrative categories and should not be taken as a complete count of Karankawa people or as proof that those who left ceased to exist.
sources.contentReviewScope: The full visible article body and bibliography were read, including selected 1795–1830 mission records summarized by the author. The original registers were not inspected.

sources.title: Coastal Prairies and Marshes: Native Peoples of the Texas Coast
sources.publisher: Texas Beyond History; Texas Archeological Research Laboratory, The University of Texas at Austin
sources.annotation: An archaeologist-authored public teaching exhibit places Karankawa communities within a wider Texas coastal region and links settlement, material evidence and seasonal mobility. It was published in 2009 and uses a period “gone forever” framing in its regional introduction; that framing does not establish the absence of living descendants and is balanced with later community sources.
sources.contentReviewScope: The complete Native Peoples overview, Karankawa section, credits and bibliography were read. Linked site reports and cited books were not independently inspected; the page’s regional map is an explanatory scholarly illustration, not a present-day territorial boundary.

sources.title: The Karankawa were said to be extinct. Now they’re reviving their culture — and fighting to protect their ancestors’ land.
sources.annotation: This reported feature documents Karankawa Kadla people’s public activity in 2021, including family oral-history accounts and an effort to protect a coastal archaeological place. It identifies several named participants and institutions; the article’s 2021 statements about recognition and community size are date-specific, not current legal or population data.
sources.contentReviewScope: The complete article body and its sections on family history, archaeological records, community activity and agency responses were read. Interview testimony is attributed to the named speaker; archaeological interpretations and litigation statements remain attributed to the article and its sources.

sources.title: Indigenous groups fight to save rediscovered settlement site on Texas coast
sources.publisher: Inside Climate News and The Texas Tribune
sources.annotation: A collaborative report describes the 2025 rediscovery and preservation campaign around a Corpus Christi Bay settlement site, with testimony from Love Sanchez and named archaeologists and other Indigenous leaders. It concerns a particular site and contemporary campaign; it does not establish a single Karankawa organization’s authority over all sites or people.
sources.contentReviewScope: The complete article body was read, including the rediscovery narrative, quoted community and scholarly perspectives, archaeological access limits and permitting context. Sensitive site coordinates and restricted archaeological records are not reproduced; the article’s reported statements remain attributed.

sources.title: History Programs public packet: Karankawa marker-text request
sources.annotation: Selected pages preserve a dated public review of a request to revise a Karankawa historical marker, including community-submitted material and competing procedural recommendations. A committee packet is not a complete meeting transcript or a current statement of marker wording.
sources.contentReviewScope: Only PDF pages 43–47 concerning the Karankawa Campsite marker item were inspected. The packet contains submitted assertions and proposed motions; no final vote or current marker status is inferred from these selected pages.
sources.sourceKind: Selected pages of government meeting record

sources.title: Karankawa Tribe of Texas Celebrates Historical Marker Unveiling
sources.publisher: Karankawas.com; Karankawa Tribe of Texas public account
sources.annotation: A dated community announcement reports the July 2026 unveiling of a revised Karankawa marker and lists corrections sought by women it identifies with the Hawk Clan. It is evidence of that publication’s position and account of its participation, not a substitute for the marker text or a statement by every Karankawa-descendant community.
sources.contentReviewScope: The full visible announcement was read. Its six requested corrections and reported collaboration are attributed to the publisher; the marker’s complete new text and the organization’s relationship to earlier Karankawa Kadla naming were not independently verified.

sources.title: The Karankawa-Spanish War from 1778 to 1789: Attempted Genocide and Karankawa Power
sources.annotation: A peer-reviewed journal article identified by the author and journal as a study of the 1778–1789 war. Its full text is a useful route for interpreting colonial power and diplomacy, but it remains a scholarly argument based on archival sources and should be compared with community histories.
sources.contentReviewScope: The journal record, abstract and bibliographic metadata were inspected; the full article was not accessible in this pass. It is therefore retained as a supporting unread lead and does not count toward the substantive inspected-work target.
sources.sourceKind: Peer-reviewed journal article; full text unread

sources.title: Nuestra Señora de Rosario Mission
sources.annotation: A brief NPS summary supplies a visitor-oriented overview of Rosario and its Spanish context. It overlaps the longer TSHA mission histories and is retained as a convenient supporting introduction rather than an independent substantive work.
sources.contentReviewScope: The complete visible page was read. No underlying Spanish records were inspected through it.

sources.title: Karankawa research guide
sources.publisher: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley Special Collections and Archives
sources.annotation: A library guide offers discovery paths to repositories and literature. It is a finding aid rather than a substantive history or inspected archival collection.
sources.contentReviewScope: The full visible guide was read. The guide itself notes that the underlying primary sources are not held by the library; no linked archival item was inspected through it.

sources.title: Karankawa research resources
sources.publisher: Galveston & Texas History Center, Rosenberg Library
sources.annotation: This guide lists manuscripts, scrapbooks, vertical files, books and external research portals. It is useful for future archival work but is not itself a studied historical narrative.
sources.contentReviewScope: The full visible guide was read, including its archival catalog descriptions and bibliography. No listed physical collection, catalog object or cited book was inspected through this guide.

sources.title: Spanish Missions
sources.publisher: Handbook of Texas Online / Texas State Historical Association
sources.annotation: A wider survey briefly situates Rosario among Texas missions. Its Karankawa-specific coverage is brief and overlaps dedicated Rosario and Refugio entries, so it remains a supporting orientation.
sources.contentReviewScope: The complete visible article and its Rosario passage were read. The underlying source bibliography was not checked in this pass.

initialAdequacy.rationale: Twelve substantive works have actual-content inspection records, including community statements, first-person testimony, long-form reporting, scholarly and archaeological syntheses, and a selected government meeting record. This is a substantial initial reading path, but the distinct contemporary community names, dated marker discrepancy, uneven primary-source access and incomplete descendant-perspective coverage make an adequacy judgment premature.
remainingLimits: The complete text of the replacement marker announced in July 2026 was not verified in an updated official Texas Historical Commission record.

Primary Spanish, Mexican and Republic-era records and archaeological publications require further source-by-source inspection; TSHA and Texas Beyond History bibliographies remain leads.

evidenceNotes: This dated Texas-focused review has twelve substantive inspected works and six supporting or further-reading cards excluded from the count. The count is not a claim of completeness or endorsement.

Historical sources differ in lists, spellings and grouping categories. Beaumont’s 2023 speech uses a “seven or so” clan count, while TSHA and Texas Beyond History enumerate historical named groups differently; these categories were not collapsed into one definitive total.

Community sources are dated and attributed: a 2023 Karankawa Kadla Five Rivers Council statement, a 2023 speech by Chiara Beaumont, and a July 2026 Karankawa Tribe of Texas marker announcement. The public name shifts and organizational relationships need more careful source review; no group is declared the sole representative.

The THC’s 2022 meeting packet and a November 2025 packet document earlier marker processes. A 2026 community announcement and reporting describe a replacement unveiled July 25, 2026, while the official Atlas page checked still returns the 1976 inscription. The new text and final official record remain unverified.

The 2019 thesis is an honors thesis, and only selected sections were reviewed. A journal article on the 1778–1789 war, the full thesis, linked primary documents, cited books and archival registers remain unread leads; none are described as inspected.

The reviewed sources support broad historical coastal connections and mention specific archaeological places. No precise boundary, sensitive site coordinate or new map-to-profile association was created.

name: Kickapoo
region: Great Lakes / Kansas / Oklahoma / Texas / Mexico
overview: Kickapoo people continue in distinct communities and governments across the United States and Mexico. This Texas-focused reading path concerns the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas and selected cross-border, legal, language, education, family-policy, and planning sources; it does not represent every Kickapoo community. Several historical and ethnographic studies document particular periods and sites, while key parts of present-day community history still need direct, community-authored documentation.

sections.title: Distinct communities and the Texas-focused scope
sections.text: Kickapoo people are represented by distinct communities and governments in the United States and Mexico. The 1983 Texas Band of Kickapoo Act used a specific legal relationship to the Kickapoo Tribe of Oklahoma; the later Texas-hosted constitution packet’s preamble describes the Texas Tribe as organized separately and apart. The 2020 Interior Solicitor memorandum addresses a narrower federal-jurisdiction and fee-to-trust question. These records document legal wording and chronology, not every community’s own account of identity or the packet’s present consolidated legal status.

sections.title: Cross-border history and community participation
sections.text: Two scholarly works by Elisabeth Mager Hois examine the Texas–Coahuila relationship through different publications and periods. Her 2010 chapter surveys migration and legal/economic history, drawing in part on published literature and interviews conducted in 1996–2002; the 2020 article focuses on border crossing and includes interviews from 1985–2005. Their claims are attributed to the author and periods, not counted as independent corroboration when repeated. A separate 2017 Texas intertribal public-safety report records the Texas Tribe’s participation in statewide planning; its schematic map serves the report’s planning purpose and does not define homelands. A 1867 account attributed to No-ko-aht, recorded by federal agent Franklin G. Adams and published in an edited 1932 article, offers a distinct contemporaneous perspective on a Kansas-to-Mexico journey, the Dove Creek attack, and treaty pressure. The mediation, editorial framing, and internal chronology/group-count discrepancies are explicit; this account is not treated as a verbatim or independently corroborated record. A 1875 translated diplomatic file gives the U.S. and Mexican governments’ competing positions and attached Coahuila reports during another removal effort. These are administrative perspectives, not neutral testimony; one Coahuila report states that some Kickapoo people remained at Nacimiento and other locations. The University of Texas at Austin finding aid identifies additional Latorre field notes, manuscripts, correspondence, and other collection materials relating primarily to El Nacimiento; the collection itself was not reviewed, and the archive states photography is prohibited and image publication/exhibition permission is not being granted. It is retained as a future research route, not counted as inspected primary evidence. A 2017 peer-reviewed comparison by Mager adds a Texas-focused account of land acquisition and the later economic history of the Texas Tribe, drawing on documentary research, participant observation, interviews reported from 1995–2015, and a cited 1981–1984 Land Acquisition Committee report. This is the same researcher represented by the 2010 and 2020 works; the article’s analytical thesis and interview-based claims are attributed and not treated as independent confirmation. Only the Kickapoo-focused historical passages were used; sensitive cultural descriptions were excluded.

sections.title: What the 1983 statute and 2020 legal memorandum address
sections.text: The 1983 federal act authorizes specified services, land-acquisition activity in Maverick County, and border-passage provisions. A Texas-hosted scan of the Tribe’s constitution and attached federal records documents approval of the constitution in 1989 and later amendment elections/approvals in 2017 and 2018. Its scan labels and amendment numbering are not fully consistent, and this review did not verify whether it is the current consolidated text. The 2020 Interior memorandum addresses a narrower question about federal jurisdiction in 1934 and a particular fee-to-trust application. These are dated legal records, not legal advice or proof of current implementation. The 1875 diplomatic record shows an earlier U.S.–Mexico effort to arrange removal to U.S. reservations; it records official claims and proposals, not a complete account of individual or community decisions.

sections.title: Education and language-related programs
sections.text: The Texas Tribe’s education department publicly lists a Kickapoo language program alongside other services; some initiatives on the page are explicitly labeled under development. A 2011 INALI publication provides a much deeper, dated study of the Kickapoo variety in Coahuila: phonological analysis, an ethnographic overview based on fieldwork reported for 1980–1983 and later visits, and a practical writing-system chapter that describes consultation with speakers. The book documents a specific research and orthography project; it is not a current census of language use or a description of all Kickapoo communities. The Tribe-linked Education Department publication now provides a fuller first-party account. Its Language Department says it has developed and taught curriculum since 2017, creates learning materials, and incorporates language into Head Start, tutorial and summer programs. The Head Start page lists a Kickapoo immersion-language resource book, family-engagement activities and several learning platforms. These descriptions document the department’s published approach; they do not show measured language fluency, school outcomes or current class participation. The listed immersion book and software were not inspected. The public pages also describe family, disability and other supports, without supplying the evidence needed to evaluate their delivery.

sections.title: Publicly posted policy on family, culture, and community planning
sections.text: A public copy of the Tribe’s Chapter 20 Indian Child Welfare Code frames child-welfare policy around protecting family and Tribal connections and preserving children’s opportunity to learn about culture and heritage. Only selected pages were reviewed; the code’s enactment date and current consolidated status remain unverified, so it is presented as a published primary policy text rather than current legal advice or evidence of outcomes. The Tribe’s June 2025 transportation safety plan records a planning process that brought together several Tribal departments and external safety partners, using TxDOT and Tribal Police data while noting limits in the latter. Among its proposed strategies are community and school outreach, including media messages that use or honor Tribal/local language, symbols, or culture. These are dated plans and proposals, not proof of implementation or a general description of Kickapoo culture. The plan’s crash data, precise locations, appendices, and web GIS were not reviewed or reproduced.

sections.title: A dated housing and community-development case study
sections.text: A short HUD case feature describes housing and community-development projects involving the Texas Tribe, including FEMA mobile homes during 2009–2013 and a wellness-center project. The page’s publication date is unstated, so it is useful for a limited historical case study rather than present-day program or demographic information.

sections.title: A historical synthesis and its unresolved chronology
sections.text: A 2010 UNAM chapter and the 2011 INALI study trace Kickapoo histories through Great Lakes, Midwestern, Texas, and Coahuila settings, while focusing on different communities and drawing on different evidence. The chapter describes multiple migrations and the establishment of El Nacimiento; its own notes show disagreements among cited authors about the timing and victims of the 1873 El Remolino attack and about land-area figures. The 2011 study records its author’s fieldwork and ethnographic observations for specified periods. These works add valuable historical and language context but should be read alongside the relevant treaties, statutes, and distinct community sources rather than combined into a seamless migration story. The edited 1932 publication of No-ko-aht’s 1867 account also gives his perspective on the journey south and Dove Creek conflict. Its dates and numbers differ from the editor’s prefatory narrative, so the page preserves the discrepancy and does not use the account alone to settle the event chronology. A separate 1875 U.S.–Mexico diplomatic file preserves competing government arguments over attempts to move Kickapoo people from Mexico to U.S. reservations, alongside Coahuila reports that some remained at Nacimiento and other places. Because these are translated diplomatic and administrative documents written within removal negotiations, their language, numbers, and claims are attributed to the officials rather than treated as neutral or complete community testimony. Pool’s later study of Dove Creek adds a selected-page military-history reconstruction of the 1865 attack; only pages 367, 375, 379, and 385 were inspected, and its interpretation is not a community account. Mager’s 2017 comparative study adds another dated account of Texas land acquisition and economic change, based partly on interviews and a committee report, but shares an author with the 2010 and 2020 studies and does not provide independent corroboration of their repeated claims.

The chapter itself notes contradictory dates and figures in cited works, including the 1873 El Remolino attack and land-area totals. Read those passages as attributed historical claims rather than settled facts. The repository lists open access and CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; only a link is reproduced here.

No-ko-aht describes travel between Kansas and Mexico, the 1865 Dove Creek conflict, life in Coahuila, and his objections to treaty pressure and settler encroachment. This is a historically valuable but mediated account: the recorder was a federal agent, George A. Root edited and published it in 1932, and the surrounding editorial narrative uses period terminology and makes claims that should not be adopted as neutral fact. The printed account and editorial summary also differ in chronology and group counts; the discrepancy is retained rather than reconciled here.

Those documents use coercive period language and reflect government interests; their stated counts and characterizations are not treated as neutral community testimony or a complete account of consent, movement, or later residence.

This review inspected selected pages 367, 375, 379, and 385 only; the rest of the article was not read. The excerpt documents the attackers’ uncertain identification of the camp and the author’s reliance on conflicting reports. Its mid-20th-century military-history framing is attributed to Pool, and the article is not treated as a Kickapoo community account or as independent confirmation of every casualty or movement claim.
sources.contentReviewScope: Selected OCR-extracted article pages 367, 375, 379, and 385 were read via the UNT Portal; page images and article title/issue metadata were inspected. This is a limited excerpt review, not a full-article reading. OCR errors are possible.

It helps readers locate future primary-source research but is not a substitute for examining the materials themselves. The archive states that cell-phone photography is not permitted and that it is not granting permission to publish or exhibit collection images until further notice; standard copyright restrictions also apply. No collection images or restricted records are reproduced here.

sources.annotation: This peer-reviewed comparative study includes a dedicated section on the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas and El Nacimiento. This is the same researcher represented by sources 6 and 11, so repeated claims are not independent corroboration. Cultural descriptions outside the selected historical scope were not used.

initialAdequacy.rationale: Fifteen substantive inspected works support this Texas-focused introduction. name: Kiowa
overview: Kiowa histories connect northern and southern Plains movement, Texas and Oklahoma, while the present Kiowa Tribe publishes accounts of its government and community institutions. This foundation brings a short Tribal history together with an edited treaty, dated education reporting, a Kiowa educator’s first-person reflection, a collaborative scholarly account and art history. Alliances, the wider people, present institutions and individual voices retain their own scope. Additional reading brings an earlier primary agreement, community remembrance and a partially inspected local land-history study into the foundation.

sections.title: A people, a present Tribe and related reading routes
sections.text: Kiowa is a people-level reading route, while the Kiowa Tribe’s publications describe a present government and its institutions in Oklahoma. The Tribe’s history discusses alliances with Comanche and Plains Apache people. Those relationships do not make the names interchangeable: Plains Apache has its own directory route, and shared treaties or institutions do not by themselves establish one timeless identity.

sections.title: Movement, Texas connections and uncertain early dates
sections.text: The Tribe’s historical account and Kracht’s article both describe movement from the northern toward the southern Plains and connections with present-day Texas. Their Black Hills chronologies differ. These accounts provide a broad route into the history; precise origins, dates and archaeological identifications need further research. The Atlas does not turn a migration outline into a fixed homeland boundary or treat a community history page as an inspected archaeological report.

sections.title: Horses, bison and historical livelihoods
sections.text: The Tribe’s overview describes historical mobility, bison hunting, horse use and gathering. Read that account in its period and regional setting. It helps explain the Southern Plains history being discussed, while contemporary education, work and family life require their own sources rather than a picture of every Kiowa person living in one historical way.

sections.title: Reading the 1867 Medicine Lodge treaty
sections.text: The edited October 21, 1867 Kiowa and Comanche treaty includes reservation and conditional hunting provisions, promises of federal services, a requirement concerning later land cessions and compulsory schooling in English branches. Its terms give readers a primary document to examine. They do not alone prove implementation, universal consent or present-day rights. This named instrument should also be distinguished from the separate treaty involving Kiowa, Comanche and Apache representatives.

sections.title: Reservation change and the limits of this first history
sections.text: The Tribal history and Kracht’s account describe reservation confinement, allotment and settlement pressures. Their compressed narratives are starting points for reviewing nineteenth-century Texas and Oklahoma history. The original military, removal, allotment and implementation records have not been read in this foundation, so precise legal conclusions, landownership totals and a complete chronology remain open.

sections.title: Education as a contemporary institution
sections.text: The Tribe’s FY 2025–2026 report describes its Education Agency across child care, school partnerships, higher education, career learning and community activities. It presents Kiowa language, heritage and contemporary life as part of its educational aims. These are the institution’s reported purposes and activities. The Atlas does not promise assistance, repeat financial figures or treat the report as an independent evaluation of results.

sections.title: Language teaching across classrooms and families
sections.text: The same dated report describes a teacher-credentialing process and language classes delivered in schools, community settings and online. Melody Windsong Redbird-Post’s first-person essay gives another perspective: she recounts child-care language work, family learning and collaboration with elders, educators and parents. Her experience and future project plans remain attributed to her; neither source supplies a verified current count of speakers or proof of every learner’s proficiency.

sections.title: Community listening and a shared classroom
sections.text: In their 2018 article, Rachel C. Jackson with Kiowa Elder Dorothy Whitehorse DeLaune describe the Kiowa Clemente course and a classroom shaped by community interests. Their account explains how listening, shared decisions and language work inform their teaching. This is a situated educational interpretation and relationship, not a rule for every Kiowa person or a present course schedule. Specific stories, songs and culturally governed materials in the publication are not retold here.

sections.title: Named artists and the Kiowa Six
sections.text: Lydia L. Wyckoff’s art-historical essay identifies Jack Hokeah, Monroe Tsatoke, Spencer Asah, James Auchiah, Stephen Mopope and Lois Smoky within the group known as the Kiowa Six or Kiowa Five. It follows their painting, university-era work and mural commissions. The essay describes plain backgrounds and areas of flat color as part of this history. These are named artists and an art-group label; the account does not define all Kiowa art or authorize reuse of the artworks.

sections.title: An earlier agreement at the Little Arkansas
sections.text: The 1865 agreement predates Medicine Lodge. Its reservation provisions sit alongside written-permission requirements for hunting travel and rules about where people could camp. Article 6 discusses people not present at the council. Reading those clauses together helps distinguish the written agreement from universal assent or actual implementation; they do not determine current land rights.

sections.title: Palo Duro in community memory
sections.text: The District 7 newsletter describes the 2024 commemoration of the 1874 Battle of Palo Duro Canyon as a setting for remembrance and public education involving several Southern Plains communities. This is a dated community account of how history is remembered and shared. Its battle narrative still needs comparison with Kiowa testimony and original military and civilian records.

sections.title: Later land loss as a local historical question
sections.text: Palmer’s 2011 study examines later Kiowa allotment sales through land-tenure applications and geographic comparison. He describes economic needs, relocation and divided inheritance as factors within his case-study area. He also notes difficulty separating relocation policy’s effects. This attributed local analysis is not a current ownership assessment or a single explanation for every Kiowa family’s history.

sections.title: Reading path and unfinished coverage
sections.text: Read community publications alongside the actual 1865 and 1867 agreements, keeping promises, interpretation and implementation separate. The newsletter offers a dated route into remembrance; Palmer’s partially accessible study extends the land-history questions. Nine substantive works form a reviewed foundation, with substantial gaps in Texas primary evidence, community-authored historical depth and later history. No completion or community endorsement is claimed.
