name: Kootenai (Ktunaxa)
overview: Kootenai/Ktunaxa communities have distinct governments across the U.S.–Canada border. This reading path includes the Kootenai Tribe of Idaho and keeps community histories, language work and political relationships in their stated scope.

sections.title: Homelands across a later international border
sections.text: The Ktunaxa Nation Council describes homelands along the Kootenay and Columbia rivers and Arrow Lakes, extending historically beyond British Columbia into neighboring provinces and U.S. states, including Idaho. Its accompanying map expressly warns that its boundaries are not comprehensive or exhaustive. This community account connects land, seasonal livelihoods and stewardship without defining a single modern government or final legal boundary.

sections.title: Language work and distinct participating communities
sections.text: The Council's public language article describes work with speakers from four Canadian First Nations, the Kootenai Tribe of Idaho and Montana's Ksanka Band of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes. It connects classes, curriculum and community activities with intergenerational relationships. This is an institutional account of language work, without a verified speaker census or proof that every participating community operates identical programs.

sections.title: An Idaho community's history of remaining and organizing
sections.text: The Kootenai Tribe of Idaho describes a separately governed community within the broader Ktunaxa world. Its history recounts pressure to relocate to Montana, remaining near Bonners Ferry, and peaceful protest in 1974 against neglect and inadequate living conditions. This is the Idaho Tribe's own account of dispossession and self-determination, not a single political history for all Ktunaxa communities.

sections.title: Reading a dated constitutional publication
sections.text: The Tribe-hosted Constitution and Bylaws records adoption on April 10, 1947, followed by federal approval on June 16. The compilation labels its latest amendment 1996. Its framework assigns a Tribal Council powers to represent the Tribe, manage affairs and establish a court and law code. This is a dated institutional text, without independently verifying all current amendments or rules.

sections.title: River restoration as a Tribal priority
sections.text: The Kootenai Tribe’s restoration materials connect changes to the Kootenai River with habitat and subsistence concerns. In 2003 testimony, then-chairman Gary Aitken described the Tribe-created Kootenai Valley Resource Initiative around Bonners Ferry and concerns for white sturgeon and burbot, speaking on behalf of the Upper Columbia United Tribes. A later USGS study, prepared in cooperation with the Tribe, examines one reach of the Tribe-led restoration project: it reports increased pool and depth measures after construction, while noting that the tested conditions fell short of the project’s stated depth target and that the measured sediment declines were more consistent with reduced incoming sediment than an effect of the treatments. The study recommends continued monitoring. These dated sources show specific institutional priorities and technical findings; neither establishes overall species recovery or represents all Ktunaxa communities.

sections.title: Canadian Council work and community-driven planning
sections.text: The Council's 2026 annual report describes education outreach, tutoring, training support and youth engagement in its Canadian member communities. Its governance chapter discusses data sovereignty and community-driven decision making. These are dated institutional reports and proposals, distinct from the Idaho Tribe's government. The report's draft governance goals do not establish completed agreements or verified outcomes.

sections.title: An education access point in Idaho
sections.text: The Idaho Tribe's short education page describes school support, adult learning and assistance for higher education. It is a useful access point; the undated description does not establish current eligibility, availability or outcomes.

sources.title: Effects of Restoration Work on Kootenai River White Sturgeon Critical Habitat, 2011–22
sources.author: Megan K. Kenworthy and Taylor J. Dudunake
sources.publisher: U.S. Geological Survey, prepared in cooperation with the Kootenai Tribe of Idaho
sources.annotation: A technical evaluation of a Kootenai Tribe-led, interagency restoration program in the Kootenai River’s Braided and Straight Reaches. Selected findings report improved pool and depth metrics after construction, but the tested conditions did not meet the stated channel-depth target, and sediment trends did not show that the treatments themselves reduced suspended-sediment transport. The study is geographically and methodologically bounded; it does not evaluate the Tribe’s overall stewardship or establish species recovery.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual 46-page PDF read selectively: abstract; introduction, printed pp. 3–5; discussion, p. 28; and summary/conclusions, p. 30. Title, acknowledgments and contents were checked. Methods, complete results, references, data release and associated figures were not reviewed. The official publication record returned 403 to one automated page fetch, but the linked USGS PDF downloaded successfully; this is not described as a reader paywall.

inspectedSubresources.scope: Actual report PDF, selected sections noted above; publication landing page and PDF are one work.

sources.countReason: Substantive government technical report, prepared in cooperation with the Tribe and focused on the Tribe-led river restoration project; counts once, not as an independent cultural history.

initialAdequacy.rationale: Eight substantive works now support a clearer Idaho-centered introduction, including direct Kootenai Tribe history and governance, a dated chairman’s testimony, and a USGS technical study produced in cooperation with the Tribe. This remains unfinished as a profile titled Kootenai (Ktunaxa): the evidence is uneven across the distinct U.S. and Canadian communities, and an environmental report cannot supply the missing community histories or language perspectives.
remainingLimits: Independent Montana-community perspectives are limited to explicit peer identification in these sources.
The Canadian Council’s work is not a substitute for the four member First Nations’ own detailed histories.
The 2003 hearing is a dated coalition policy statement, not a full Kootenai history; the 2025 USGS study covers one restoration reach and selected physical indicators.
Current law, broader program outcomes and quantitative language conditions remain outside the review.

researchGaps: Further Idaho-community oral-history/public interview perspectives, and original historical records, would broaden the institutional accounts without substituting a colonial author's voice for the Tribe's own.
Separate substantive Ksanka/Kootenai community sources in Montana remain a priority; Salish and Upper Pend d'Oreille people are not interchangeable with Kootenai people within CSKT.
The Canadian Council report and map are situated institutional perspectives, not exhaustive research into each member Nation, boundary, title claim or land declaration.
An actual specialist language-learning publication and dated evaluation would strengthen the public program descriptions. No current speaker census or tested fluency outcome was established.

The Kootenai Tribe’s 2009 restoration master plan, complete technical methods/results, data release and other monitoring studies remain to be read. The 2025 USGS report is a bounded assessment of one reach and selected river-habitat indicators; it does not establish overall ecological recovery.
evidenceNotes: Substantive works and supporting access routes are counted separately. Actual selected inspection scope and dates appear on the cards; unread references and source media are not counted.
This regional batch is an initial educational review, not a complete history or community endorsement. Governmental, historical and language labels retain their specific community and period.

Reviewed 2026-10-23: added one 2003 oral congressional statement by Kootenai Tribe of Idaho chairman Gary Aitken, delivered for the five-government Upper Columbia United Tribes coalition, and one 2025 USGS report prepared in cooperation with the Tribe. Neither source adds a historical-map route or substitutes for distinct Ktunaxa community histories.

name: Lenape
region: Delaware Valley / displaced and continuing communities in Oklahoma, Ontario and elsewhere; scoped Texas history
overview: Lenape histories connect an eastern homeland with distinct present communities and different displacement routes. This reading foundation includes community accounts, a primary treaty, language education and critical scholarship. Its Texas coverage is introductory and specifically scoped.

sections.title: Names and distinct present communities
sections.text: Lenape is broader than any one government. Delaware Nation’s history distinguishes its Anadarko community from Delaware Tribe of Indians and other Lenape governments. Similar names do not make these institutions interchangeable.

sections.title: An eastern homeland and overlapping reading labels
sections.text: The Tribe’s introduction locates Lenape history in the Delaware Valley. This people-level route overlaps the preserved Delaware (Lenape) entry; both labels remain available. Individual governments and language communities need their own specifically supported identities.

sections.title: Reading the Walking Purchase critically
sections.text: Jennings examines the 1737 Walking Purchase through land papers and competing testimony. He argues that proprietary manipulation affected both dispossession and the records used to describe it. Read this as an attributed historical argument: the original manuscripts have not been independently checked here.

sections.title: What the 1778 treaty actually says
sections.text: The Fort Pitt treaty addresses peace, military passage, trade and territorial guarantees. Article VI proposes a state headed by the Delaware nation with congressional representation, expressly subject to congressional approval. A proposed arrangement is not proof that a state or seat was created. The document’s terms also do not demonstrate their fulfillment.

sections.title: A specifically scoped Texas connection
sections.text: Delaware Nation connects its Absentee Delaware history with movement toward Texas and the Brazos reservation. Lipscomb’s Texas reference adds diplomacy, scouting and reserve-removal context. These accounts describe particular groups and stages; they do not place every Lenape community in Texas or establish all present families’ descent. Detailed migration and relocation chronology remains unfinished.

sections.title: An Ontario community’s own account
sections.text: Eelünaapéewi Lahkéewiit’s Our Story follows a Moravian-connected community through displacement and rebuilding at Fairfield and New Fairfield. This is an Ontario community’s retrospective, distinct from the Oklahoma government also called Delaware Nation. Its wider historical claims and battle interpretation require comparison rather than automatic adoption.

sections.title: Learning through the Talking Dictionary
sections.text: The Lenape Talking Dictionary identifies its main language scope as Southern Unami. Its introductory lesson explains spelling and everyday greetings, while documentation identifies speakers and other contributors. Selected entry text was read; audio playback was not tested. This resource does not stand for every Lenape language variety, and recordings retain their individual provenance.

sections.title: Language programs in a dated account
sections.text: Writing in 2002, Rementer and Pearson describe several generations of Oklahoma language classes, learning materials and the early dictionary project. Their different community relationships are explicit. The paper is useful program history, not a current speaker census or proof of learning outcomes. Language loss must not be read as disappearance of a people.

sections.title: Reading path and remaining work
sections.text: Start with community accounts, compare the treaty’s actual terms, and use the language resources within their stated scope. Jennings provides a focused example of archival criticism. This is a reviewed first reading foundation. Texas primary records, broader community perspectives and later histories still need substantial work; no completion or community endorsement is claimed.

name: Lipan Apache
overview: Lipan Apache is a living people whose community histories cross Texas, northern Mexico, and neighboring regions. Lipan Apache accounts and historical scholarship describe multiple bands, settlements, and routes; present-day communities should not be collapsed into one historical movement or equated with every Apache community.

sections.title: A living people and a present-day community
sections.text: The Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas describes a united Lipan Apache community today while preserving the names and histories of distinct historical bands. Its account places families in Texas and across the border in northern Mexico and also describes later Lipan participation in the Mescalero Apache community. These records do not make every Lipan family’s history identical or make the Tribe interchangeable with other Apache governments.

sections.title: Place, movement, and regional history
sections.text: The Tribe-hosted homeland essay and its community-contributed timeline describe relationships with the upper Brazos, Colorado, Concho, San Antonio, Rio Grande and northern Mexican communities across different periods. Brandon Seale’s Handbook of Texas account offers a broader scholarly narrative. Anthony K. Webster’s linguistic study examines place names in Augustina Zuazua’s 1938 narrative to Harry Hoijer; the article gives different totals in its main text and notes, leaves some locations unidentified, and cautions against broad conclusions from this small sample. These accounts offer historically situated evidence, not a surveyed boundary or proof that all places were occupied at the same time.

sections.title: Diplomacy across Spanish, Mexican, and Texas governments
sections.text: Community-authored histories discuss Lipan diplomacy with Mexican and Republic of Texas authorities, including the Bustamante agreement and the 1838 Treaty of Live Oak Point. The Tribe-reproduced 1846 Council Springs treaty is a multination U.S. instrument that names Lipan alongside other Native parties; its articles address U.S.-directed trade regulation, prisoners, legal arrangements, and other terms. The Indigenous Digital Archive/National Archives catalogue gives a March 8, 1847 ratification date, though its normalized named-nations field omits Lipan. This record does not establish implementation or a single Lipan response. The 1838 and 1844 treaty scans remain unread, so their terms are not independently summarized here.

sections.title: Displacement, borderlands, and community continuity
sections.text: The Tribe-hosted account of nineteenth-century campaigns describes Lipan communities in Coahuila and cross-border military attacks; its language and interpretation are attributed to the author. The TSHA entry supplies a related scholarly synthesis and describes later Lipan communities in Texas and northern Mexico. Neither sparse government records nor movement into Mexico or another Apache community establish that Lipan people disappeared.

sections.title: Different paths during the reservation era
sections.text: The Tribe-hosted reservation-era essay describes different Lipan groups moving to Mescalero, Tonkawa, Mexican, and Texas communities. The Mescalero Apache Tribe’s own history says Lipan survivors joined its community in about 1903; the Lipan Tribe-hosted essay dates one group’s joining to 1904. These accounts concern related but not necessarily identical events, and the one-year difference remains unresolved. A 2021 Fort Davis National Historic Site page says Lipan had no longer a “discernible presence” in their homeland after some families joined Mescalero. Later community and scholarly accounts document continuing Lipan communities and institutions, so the NPS phrase is not used here as evidence that Lipan people disappeared. Its stated 1936 Mescalero incorporation date also differs from the Mescalero Tribe’s 1934 date. A 1876 federal compilation adds a separate Fort Griffin strand: officials reported that a small Lipan group moved there from Fort Sill in 1874, and the 1875 Interior Department commissioner described intermarriage with Tonkawa people and considered several possible relocation arrangements. This is administrative correspondence, not a Lipan account; it does not show that the proposed consolidation or removal occurred and cannot stand for all Lipan groups.

sections.title: Present-day institutions and public historical work
sections.text: The Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas describes its Tribal Council and unified community, and it documents a 2021 transfer of a Presidio cemetery to the Tribe and a later collaboration around site protection and interpretation. A 2026 congressional bill proposing federal recognition was introduced and referred to committee; that proposed legislation is not an enacted law. This page makes no current population claim and does not substitute for the Tribe’s own legal or membership information. A 2024 local report follows the completion of a Presidio cemetery protection project, documenting participation by descendants and Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas leadership. It describes a historical-marker text drafted by an enrolled member in collaboration with the Texas Historical Commission and public historical interpretation developed for the site. These interviews document one dated local project and its participants, not all Lipan communities or a comprehensive account of Lipan history.

sections.title: Lipan people at Fort Griffin in federal records, 1874–1876
sections.text: An eight-page 1876 congressional document reproduces federal and military correspondence about Lipan people at Fort Griffin alongside Tonkawa people. Officials report authorizing a small Lipan group to move from Fort Sill in 1874, ending regular ration issues in 1875, and seeking help for both communities. An Interior Department letter describes the Lipans as related to Tonkawa people by intermarriage and considers possible destinations, including Mescalero or Hot Springs agencies. This is a colonial administrative record: its labels, descriptions, and policy proposals reflect federal officials. It does not establish a general Lipan-Tonkawa political merger, prove any proposed move occurred, or represent every Lipan community.

Its account says a group led by Magoosh joined the Mescalero community in 1904; the Mescalero Apache Tribe’s own public history gives 1903 for Lipan survivors arriving. The one-year difference is recorded as unresolved rather than reconciled here.

sources.title: Mellon Foundation Monuments Project Awards Support for Cementerio del Barrio de los Lipanes
sources.annotation: A 2023 Tribe-published project account documents collaboration with Big Bend Conservation Alliance, family descendants, and named Lipan Apache researchers on cemetery protection, interpretation, and a regional land-reclamation study. It reports project plans at publication, not present-day completion status.
sources.contentReviewScope: The complete article body and named project roles were read. Grant terms, construction completion, the land-reclamation study’s findings, and any culturally restricted cemetery details were not reviewed or reproduced.

sources.title: Lipan Apache Indians
sources.publisher: Handbook of Texas Online / Texas State Historical Association; Brandon Seale
sources.annotation: A long-form state historical reference with sections on early colonial relations, diplomacy, displacement, diaspora, enclave communities, legal history, and present-day organizations. The article is valuable for its bibliography and chronology, but its claims about continuity, boundaries, peyote history, and present institutions remain the author’s synthesis and should be compared with community records and primary sources.
sources.contentReviewScope: The complete main article body, sections and bibliography were read. The bibliography identifies additional work by Lipan Apache scholars and historians, but those cited books and archival records were not inspected in this pass. No population estimate or sensitive religious content is carried into the profile.

sources.title: Our Culture — Tribal History and Reservation History
sources.annotation: The Mescalero Apache Tribe’s own account identifies Mescalero, Lipan, and Chiricahua as constituent subtribes and describes Lipan arrivals in the early twentieth century. This is relevant to one historical community connection, not a complete Lipan history or a claim that all Lipan people are Mescalero.
sources.contentReviewScope: The page’s relevant history and reservation-history paragraphs were read. It dates Lipan arrivals to about 1903, differing by one year from the Lipan Tribe-hosted reservation essay; this discrepancy remains open.

sources.title: Treaty Between Texas and the Lipan Tribe (1838) — document page
sources.annotation: A Tribe-hosted document route to the 1838 Treaty of Live Oak Point. Retained for further primary-source reading; it does not count as an inspected treaty text in this profile.
sources.contentReviewScope: Only the document landing page and title were inspected. The linked scan was not readable through the source-review tool in this pass, so its terms, signatures, manuscript lineage, and later implementation are not summarized.

sources.title: Tehuacana Creek Treaty (1844) — document page
sources.annotation: A Tribe-hosted document route to the 1844 Tehuacana Creek treaty. The treaty is important for following territory, negotiations and political relationships, but the surviving text and later record have not yet been reviewed.
sources.contentReviewScope: Only the document landing page and title were inspected. The linked seven-page scan was not readable through the source-review tool in this pass; it is retained as a lead and excluded from the substantive count.

sources.title: We Are Still Lipan: Identity Erasure, Settler Colonialism, Historical Memory and the Persistence of the Non-Reservation Lipan Apache
sources.publisher: Freddy Cabral, University of Texas at El Paso
sources.annotation: A 2026 doctoral dissertation whose repository abstract outlines an argument about non-reservation Lipan continuity and describes archival, oral-history, family-interview and community-memory methods. The abstract represents the author’s thesis, not independently verified chapter-level evidence; the full 230-page work remains a high-priority reading lead.
sources.contentReviewScope: Repository metadata and abstract were read. The linked full-text request returned HTTP 403 to the available reader; that response does not establish a reader paywall. No access control was bypassed, the dissertation remains unread, and this lead is excluded from the substantive-source count.

sources.title: Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas: Ethnic and Racial Identity
sources.publisher: Ashley S. Leal, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
sources.annotation: A 2016 master’s thesis whose abstract describes semi-structured interviews with 20 registered members of the Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas. It is an important direct-research lead, but the full text was not available to inspect in this pass.
sources.contentReviewScope: Repository metadata and abstract only. The full PDF request returned HTTP 403 to the available reader; this is not evidence of a reader paywall and no access control was bypassed. Excluded from the substantive source count.

sources.title: H.R. 10435 — Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas Recognition Act (introduced text)
sources.publisher: United States Congress / Government Publishing Office
sources.annotation: The introduced September 16, 2026 bill proposes federal recognition and contains legislative findings about the Tribe. Its introduction and committee referral do not make it law; statements in bill findings are attributed to Congress as proposed text and are not treated here as independently established historical findings. Retained as a dated supporting legislative reference, not a substantive historical work.
sources.contentReviewScope: The complete introduced bill text and front matter were read, including its proposed recognition and services provisions. It was introduced and referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources on September 16, 2026. This record does not establish later action or enacted status and remains excluded from the substantive research count.

sources.title: Lipan Apache Placenames of Augustina Zuazua: Some Structural and Discursive Features
sources.publisher: Anthony K. Webster, Names: A Journal of Onomastics 55(2)
sources.annotation: A linguistic and ethnohistorical analysis centered on Augustina Zuazua’s 1938 narrative to Harry Hoijer. Webster examines how place names work in that account and cautions that a small sample from one narrator cannot support broad claims about all Lipan Apache naming practices. The article’s abstract and main text refer to 22 names, while a note identifies a twenty-third; several locations remain unidentified. These names are not a surveyed boundary or a statement of present-day territorial extent.
sources.contentReviewScope: The full 20-page article was read, including its discussion of the 1938 narrative, place-name forms and discourse, comparative analysis, conclusion and notes. The author explicitly limits generalization because the corpus is small and centered on one narrator. Some locations are unidentified; no new boundary geometry is inferred.

sources.title: Treaty with the Comanche, Ioni, Anadaco, Caddo, Lipan, Longwa, Keechi, Tawakoni, Tonkawa, Wichita, and Waco (Council Springs, 1846)
sources.publisher: United States commissioners and named Native parties; treaty text reproduced by the Lipan Apache Tribe
sources.annotation: A multination treaty text that names Lipan among its parties. Its articles describe U.S.-directed trade regulation, prisoner return, law-enforcement arrangements and other terms. Read as a government-recorded instrument and not as proof of implementation, uniform Lipan consent or response, or a boundary. The parallel Indigenous Digital Archive/National Archives record identifies ratification on March 8, 1847; its normalized “Named Native nations” tags omit Lipan despite Lipan appearing in the catalog title and treaty preamble.
sources.publicationDate: Concluded May 15, 1846; ratified March 8, 1847 (archival catalogue date)
sources.contentReviewScope: The full six-page treaty text was read, including its preamble, articles, amendments/stricken clauses and signatures page. The Indigenous Digital Archive/National Archives Treaty 246 catalogue record was also inspected for title, date, ratification metadata and named-nation indexing. No claim is made about implementation or the Lipan parties’ interpretation.

sources.title: Ratified Indian Treaty 246 — Council Springs, 1846 (catalogue and related archival copies)
sources.publisher: Indigenous Digital Archive Treaties Explorer / National Archives partnership
sources.annotation: Supporting catalogue record for the multination 1846 treaty, including related National Archives file units and the March 8, 1847 ratification date. Its “Named Native nations” indexing does not list Lipan even though the catalogue title and treaty text do; this is recorded as a catalogue scope/indexing issue, not an inference about the treaty parties. Excluded from the substantive-work count because the treaty itself is counted once.
sources.contentReviewScope: The full visible catalogue record and its named-nation/present-day-nation fields were inspected. Related copies are not counted as separate works.

sources.title: Tonkawa Indians at Fort Griffin, Texas — H. Ex. Doc. 44-102
sources.author: U.S. House of Representatives; correspondence by War Department, Interior Department, and Army officers
sources.publisher: U.S. Government Publishing Office, Congressional Serial Set; digitized by the Law Library of Congress
sources.type: Primary government correspondence / Congressional Serial Set document
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the full searchable text of the eight-page public PDF, including its letters and reports dated 1872–1876. The OCR text was inspected; the page images, handwriting, signatures, and original correspondence files were not independently inspected. The authors write from federal and military administrative positions, not as Tonkawa or Lipan narrators. No reader access restriction was encountered.
sources.annotation: The congressional document records federal officials’ accounts of a small Lipan group moving from Fort Sill to Fort Griffin in 1874, subsequent ration decisions affecting Tonkawa and Lipan people there, and proposed removal options. The 1875 Interior Department letter reports kinship through intermarriage and discusses a possible consolidation; it is an official’s account and recommendation, not a Lipan-authored history or evidence that the proposal was implemented. It must not be generalized to all Lipan people or treated as proof of incorporation into Mescalero Apache.

sources.title: In Presidio, the effort to preserve an Indigenous cemetery is finally complete
sources.author: Annie Rosenthal
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the complete visible article text (approximately six-minute audio story) and captions on October 23, 2026, paragraphs covering the 2024 completion of the Presidio cemetery protection project, local descendant participation, Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas leadership, and the collaboratively drafted historical-marker interpretation. The audio itself was not played and the article photographs were not used. This is local reporting based on attributed interviews, not a comprehensive Tribe-authored history; no access restriction interrupted reading.
sources.annotation: Annie Rosenthal reports on the completion of a community-led protection and interpretation project at a Presidio cemetery. Interviewed descendants, an anthropologist, the Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas vice-chairman, local conservation partners, and the project architect describe their different roles. The story reports that a descendant drafted historical-marker text in collaboration with the Texas Historical Commission and that the completed site includes public historical and cultural interpretation. Use it as a dated local case study of contemporary community stewardship, not as a complete account of the Tribe or of Lipan communities generally. The profile summarizes the public-history work and omits sensitive burial details.

initialAdequacy.rationale: This Texas-focused collection now contains fourteen substantive inspected works, including Tribe-hosted history and treaty records, a full scholarly place-name study, the text of a ratified multination treaty, federal correspondence about a small Lipan group at Fort Griffin, and local reporting on a contemporary Presidio historical-stewardship project. The numerical target is exceeded, but the collection remains unfinished: direct community-source depth and coverage of related Lipan communities remain uneven; treaty implementation and party-specific responses are unverified; two earlier treaty scans and two full theses/dissertations remain unread; and legal and chronology questions remain open. The 1876 federal report describes one group and government proposals, while the 2024 news report documents one local project through attributed interviews; neither should be generalized to all Lipan people. No community review is recorded.
remainingLimits: The 1838 and 1844 treaty scans linked by the Tribe were not readable in the available reader; do not treat the landing pages as inspected treaty text. The 1846 multination treaty was read, but it does not establish implementation or a uniform Lipan response.
The 2026 UTEP dissertation and 2016 UTRGV thesis were inspected only through repository abstracts; full texts returned automated HTTP 403 responses and remain unread and uncounted.
The TSHA article is an outside historical synthesis; its bibliography points to community historians, archival records and scholarship that require separate review.
The 1903/1904 difference for Lipan arrivals at the Mescalero community and the 1934/1936 reorganization dates need source-level resolution.
The Texas State Library and Archives map 01413 remains metadata-only; the image was not inspected and no map-to-profile association has been made.

The Webster place-name article is based primarily on one narrator’s 1938 account, includes some unidentified locations, and should not be used to draw a fixed homeland boundary or generalize beyond its own small sample.
Current legal status, enrollment, population, language use and relationships among Lipan communities in Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma and northern Mexico require further, carefully scoped research.
No community review or endorsement has been recorded.

The 1876 Fort Griffin report is a federal administrative compilation. Its statements concern one Lipan group and federal policy; underlying records, a Lipan-authored interpretation, and whether recommendations were implemented remain unverified.

The 2024 Marfa Public Radio report is a useful dated local case study, not a comprehensive history written by the Tribe; the audio was not played, and its accounts should remain attributed to the interviewees.
initialAdequacy.searchScope: On October 23, 2026, read all eight pages of the searchable text of H. Ex. Doc. 44-102 for 1872–1876 correspondence on a small Lipan group at Fort Griffin, ration policy, and relocation proposals; scan images and original correspondence were not inspected. On October 23, 2026, also read the full visible text and captions of the April 19, 2024 Marfa Public Radio report on the Presidio cemetery protection project; audio was not played, photographs were not used, and claims remain attributed to interviewees.

researchGaps: The 1838 and 1844 treaty scans linked by the Tribe were not readable in the available reader; do not treat the landing pages as inspected treaty text. The 1846 multination treaty was read, but its implementation and Lipan-specific response remain unverified.
The 2026 UTEP dissertation and 2016 UTRGV thesis were inspected only through repository abstracts; full texts returned automated HTTP 403 responses and remain unread and uncounted.
The TSHA article is an outside historical synthesis; its bibliography points to community historians, archival records and scholarship that require separate review.
The 1903/1904 difference for Lipan arrivals at the Mescalero community and the 1934/1936 reorganization dates need source-level resolution.
The Texas State Library and Archives map 01413 remains metadata-only; the image was not inspected and no map-to-profile association has been made.

The Webster place-name article is based primarily on one narrator’s 1938 account and includes unidentified locations; it cannot support a fixed homeland boundary or broad conclusions about all Lipan place-naming practices.
Current legal status, enrollment, population, language use and relationships among Lipan communities in Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma and northern Mexico require further, carefully scoped research.
No community review or endorsement has been recorded.
evidenceNotes: October 22, 2026 follow-up: the collection now has twelve substantive inspected works (ten previously counted, plus Webster’s 2007 article and the 1846 Council Springs treaty text), seven supporting records excluded from the count, and six cited sections. Reaching the numerical target does not complete the research or establish adequacy/community endorsement.

Webster’s full article analyzes place names centered on Augustina Zuazua’s 1938 narrative. The article cautions that broad claims cannot be made from its small sample; the abstract/main discussion mention 22 names while a note mentions a twenty-third, and some places are unidentified. The Atlas uses it as attributed linguistic/ethnohistorical interpretation, not as a boundary source.

The full six-page 1846 Council Springs treaty text was read. It is a multination instrument naming Lipan among other Native parties and was ratified in 1847 according to the Indigenous Digital Archive/National Archives catalogue. The catalogue’s normalized “Named Native nations” field omits Lipan despite its title and the treaty preamble; this indexing discrepancy is preserved. Treaty text is not evidence by itself of implementation, a uniform Lipan response, or a modern homeland boundary.

The 2026 H.R. 10435 text and UTEP dissertation abstract were rechecked as supporting records only. Proposed legislative findings and a dissertation abstract are attributed positions, not independently corroborated findings; the full dissertation and the UTRGV thesis remain unread after automated HTTP 403 responses.

The earlier Lipan source review remains valid for its original eight-source addition and other inspection limits. The current initial adequacy is Still unfinished because substantive gaps remain despite reaching twelve inspected works. No historical map was added or assigned.

name: Mescalero Apache
region: Southern New Mexico / Texas / northern Mexico
overview: The Mescalero Apache Tribe’s public sources describe a contemporary community that includes Mescalero, Lipan, and Chiricahua people. This reading path brings together the Tribe’s public history, language-program goals and a dated 2024 education update, its posted constitution, Texas-focused historical research, and a peer-reviewed account of a Tribe-requested family-program pilot. It is an initial introduction, not a complete history or a substitute for distinct community accounts from Mescalero, Lipan, and Chiricahua people.

sections.title: A present-day Tribe and its own public history
sections.text: The Mescalero Apache Tribe’s official pages describe a contemporary community that includes Mescalero, Lipan, and Chiricahua people. Its 2023 anniversary account presents these as three bands working together to preserve ancestral homelands, traditions, and culture. The Tribe’s public constitution, in its posted version amended through 1988, defines membership irrespective of Apache band and sets out a formal government framework. This dated constitutional text is useful for institutional history; it is not a substitute for current codes or a community-reviewed explanation of each band’s distinct history. A 2017 peer-reviewed article by University of New Mexico and Mescalero Apache program staff describes a Tribe-requested research partnership, a Tribal Council resolution to co-write and co-submit the project, and a Mescalero Apache Tribal Research Team that adapted and piloted a family program. The article says the publication was approved by the Tribal Council and Southwest Tribal IRB. This documents a dated community-based research process, not current program delivery or a universal description of Mescalero family life.

sections.title: Language-program goals and education
sections.text: The Tribe’s Ndé Bizaa’ Language Program says its mission is to support Apache language and culture and describes language as important to identity and community well-being. Its stated goals include increasing the number of fluent speakers, Apache use across age groups and settings, literacy, knowledge of history, and participation in cultural activities. The undated page lists documentation, curriculum updates at the Language Program, immersion school and K–12 schools, language materials, and development of future language teachers; later items are possible approaches, not confirmed policy. A September 2024 program update reports that two immersion teachers had been hired for early-childhood settings, with classes planned to begin at specified sites, and describes efforts to recruit mentor–apprentices and learn from other language programs. Those are dated reports and plans, not confirmation that classes began as scheduled or remain active. Neither page supplies present fluency figures or measured outcomes. Ceremony-specific material is not repeated.

sections.title: Texas connections across a wide homeland
sections.text: The Tribe’s undated Our Culture page describes historical Mescalero movement through Texas and neighboring parts of the Southwest and northern Mexico. TxDOT’s 2020 report focuses specifically on the locations and periods of Mescalero Apache presence in Texas. Its introduction says its source set was recommended and approved by the Tribe’s Historic Preservation Officer and that her draft comments were addressed. The report remains a government synthesis, and it sometimes uses Apache as an inclusive label for several historical bands. Its regional account does not define the present Tribe’s boundaries or imply that every Apache group in Texas was Mescalero. The collaborative study also describes Mescalero homelands across the current reservation and broader Southwest regions of Texas, Arizona and Mexico. This is the article’s broad historical framing, not a boundary survey; its underlying historical sources were not independently checked here.

sections.title: Historical names and changing political conditions
sections.text: Spanish and later writers applied changing names to Apache communities, sometimes based on outsiders’ descriptions rather than names used within the communities. The TxDOT report lays out this problem while tracing a broad chronology from Spanish Texas through the nineteenth century; the Fort Davis National Park Service page adds a shorter Trans-Pecos chronology. Read their group labels and accounts of conflict as period-specific descriptions, not as a single timeless Apache identity. NPS’s wording about a historical end to free-roaming Mescalero presence in the Trans-Pecos does not mean the people disappeared. The study provides a dated background on the three bands brought together at the reservation and on family connections to ancestral bands, while noting that the present institutional community formed through reorganization. These statements are attributed to the authors and are read alongside the Tribe’s own public account and dated constitution.

sections.title: Reservation history and the Tribe’s commemorative perspective
sections.text: The Tribe’s 2023 article commemorates the May 1873 designation of the present reservation and quotes then-President Edward Martinez describing the event as a return to homeland and a point of resilience. Those statements convey the Tribe’s public interpretation and are attributed to its speaker. The same article dates Lipan arrival at the reservation to 1905, while the undated Our Culture page says “about 1903.” The available pages do not resolve that difference, so this guide preserves both formulations rather than selecting one.

sections.title: Reading path and open questions
sections.text: Begin with the Tribe’s own public history and its 2023 reservation-anniversary account, then compare the posted constitution’s dated framework with the 2020 TxDOT report and the Fort Davis NPS page. Keep community statements, government research, and park interpretation distinct. The TxDOT report contains maps that were not inspected as images, and it separately marks culturally sensitive planning resources; that section was not opened. More work is needed on community-authored accounts from Mescalero, Lipan, and Chiricahua people, the primary records behind the historical chronology, current legal materials, and differences among historical labels. Read the 2017 Mescalero Apache–University of New Mexico study as a specific example of Tribal-directed, co-produced research and a family curriculum pilot, not as a current program directory. The pilot ran in 2013–2014 with a small participant group and short follow-up; the article itself says its long-term impact required further evaluation. Its broader homeland statements should be checked against the Tribe’s own sources and the underlying historical evidence.

sources.title: Mescalero Apaches
sources.annotation: The National Park Service’s Fort Davis page offers a brief regional historical interpretation of Mescalero Apache geography and nineteenth-century events in the Trans-Pecos. Its author and supporting record citations are not shown on the page, and its broad use of Apache labels and statement that Mescaleros had “disappeared” from the Trans-Pecos must not be read as the disappearance of a people or as a description of present identity. Use the site’s dated chronology alongside the Tribe’s own accounts and the consulted TxDOT report.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the complete visible page body (lines 21–30), including the range description, selected named events, the 1871/1875 timeline and the site’s 1881–1882 narrative. The page says it was last updated October 30, 2021. No underlying archival records or associated image were inspected.

sources.title: Our Culture
sources.annotation: The Tribe’s public Our Culture page is a first-party institutional account. This review uses only its statements about the present Tribe’s three named constituent bands, its account of broad historical travel through Texas and neighboring regions, and its reservation chronology. The page is undated and also contains broad older descriptions; detailed ceremonial material and animal protocols are deliberately not reproduced or treated as unrestricted cultural instruction.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the visible body at lines 14–26 and 43–56 for the Tribe’s identity, reservation chronology, homeland and foodways account. The dedicated puberty-rite description and animal protocol sections (lines 59–89) were intentionally excluded from this synthesis. Linked photographs were not inspected or reused.

sources.title: Mescalero Apache Tribe commemorates reservation boundaries created 150 years ago
sources.author: Mescalero Apache Tribe; institutional byline
sources.annotation: The Tribe’s own 2023 commemoration describes its communitywide anniversary event for the present reservation boundaries and quotes then-President Edward Martinez explaining the Tribe’s interpretation of the 1873 designation. The article describes the contemporary Tribe as comprising Mescalero, Lipan, and Chiricahua bands and gives a Lipan arrival date of 1905, while the Tribe’s undated Our Culture page says “about 1903”; that discrepancy is left open. Statements about time immemorial and ancestry are attributed to the Tribe or its president, not independently established by this article.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the full visible article body, especially the Tribe’s account of the 1873 anniversary, the quoted statement from President Edward Martinez, its description of three constituent bands, and the 1905 Lipan / 1913 Chiricahua chronology (lines 13–34). The linked resolution and parade video were not opened; ceremonial activity is not described beyond the article’s public event summary.

The page states that the text is amended through 1988. It is not used as a complete statement of current ordinances or present policy; current legal amendments were not checked, and period-specific membership wording is not repeated in this profile.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the title, revision history, preamble, Articles I–III and VII–VIII, including the Council composition/election provisions (visible lines 13–215). Selected Tribal Council powers in Article XI were read (lines 357–435). Remaining articles and current ordinances were not reviewed.

sources.title: Mescalero Apache Tribe Research Report — TxDOT Tribal Histories
sources.author: Texas Department of Transportation research team; title page gives no individual author byline
sources.publisher: Texas Department of Transportation, TxDOT Tribal Histories Project
sources.type: Government historical research report developed in consultation with the Tribe’s Historic Preservation Office
sources.annotation: This 54-page government report specifically studies locations and periods of Mescalero Apache presence in Texas. Its introduction says the sources were recommended and approved by Mescalero Apache Tribe Historic Preservation Officer Holly Houghton, who also commented on the draft; the report itself remains a TxDOT synthesis, not a Tribe-authored work. It combines historical, archaeological, linguistic, oral-history, and contemporary sources and says its broad contextual narrative is inclusive of Apache bands. Older names such as Querecho, Natage, and Lipan should therefore remain attributed and should not be collapsed into present-day government identities. Findings and colonial descriptions are attributed to the report and its cited authors.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read PDF pages 3–4 (method, consultation and scope), 7–8 and 10–12 (selected early records and historical-name table), 35–40 (Texas-era chronology and reservation context), and selected lines on pages 41 and 48–49. The 54-page report was not read cover to cover. Page 50’s section explicitly labeled culturally sensitive for future planning was not opened. Maps and figures were not visually inspected or used as map evidence; most cited underlying records were not independently checked.

sources.title: The piloting of a culturally centered American Indian family prevention program: a CBPR partnership between Mescalero Apache and the University of New Mexico
sources.author: Lorenda Belone, Ardena Orosco, Eloise Damon, Willymae Smith-McNeal, Rebecca Rae, Mingma L. Sherpa, Orrin B. Myers, Anslem O. Omeh, and Nina Wallerstein; coauthors include Mescalero Apache Prevention Program and System of Care staff
sources.publisher: Public Health Reviews 38 (2017), article 30; University of New Mexico and Mescalero Apache community partnership; PubMed Central open-access copy
sources.annotation: A peer-reviewed article coauthored by University of New Mexico researchers and staff affiliated with the Mescalero Apache Prevention Program and System of Care. It reports that the Tribe requested the partnership, that a Tribal Council resolution supported co-writing and co-submission, and that a Mescalero Apache Tribal Research Team adapted and piloted a family program. The authors state the manuscript received Tribal Council and Southwest Tribal IRB approval. The study concerns a specific 2013–2014 pilot, not current program availability, all Mescalero families, or long-term outcomes. Its brief historical statements—including a broad homeland context spanning parts of Texas, Arizona and Mexico—remain attributed to the article; the underlying historical records were not checked here. The Atlas does not reproduce curriculum materials, participant data, images, or private content.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the open-access article body: publication metadata, abstract, research-partnership and historical-background sections, team formation and curriculum adaptation, pilot design and sample, selected results, discussion/conclusion, acknowledgments, approval statement and data-availability note (visible sections around lines 33–160, 176–215, 224–300 and 373). The pilot is discussed only as a dated collaborative research project; small sample, incomplete follow-up, short duration, and the authors’ statement that no difference in substance use was observed are kept in view. No participant-level data, session materials, images or follow-up study results were accessed. Cited historical works were not independently reviewed.

sources.title: Ndé Bizaa’ — The Mescalero Apache Tribe Language Program
sources.annotation: The Tribe’s first-party language-program page states a mission to support Apache language and culture and sets goals for increasing fluent speakers, language use across ages and settings, literacy, knowledge of history, and participation in cultural activities. It outlines documentation, curriculum development at Tribal schools/programs, language materials, and teacher development. Later items on the page are framed as possible strategies, not current commitments. The page is undated and does not report current schedules, fluency counts, or outcomes. Sacred and animal-specific guidance on the same page is not reproduced or elaborated.
sources.contentReviewScope: Complete visible Ndé Bizaa’ page read. The mission, stated goals, current strategy headings, teaching settings, teacher-development goals, and proposed future approaches were reviewed. Sacred/culturally sensitive details were excluded from the synthesis; linked images and curriculum materials were not reviewed.
sources.accessNotes: Public page on the official Mescalero Apache Tribe website; undated. The atlas links to the page and does not reproduce text or images.

sources.title: Update on the Mescalero Apache Tribe Language & Cultural Program
sources.publisher: Mescalero Apache Tribe Language & Culture Program
sources.annotation: A two-page program update linked from the Tribe’s September 9, 2024 news post. It reports that two immersion teachers had been hired for early-childhood settings, describes intended start dates for classes, and reports recruitment and peer-learning activity for a mentor–apprentice program. These are statements in a dated program snapshot; its plans are not confirmation that classes began as scheduled or remain active, and the report provides no later outcome data. Ceremony-specific material is not summarized.
sources.contentReviewScope: Visually inspected both pages of the complete two-page scanned PDF after rendering; the PDF has no searchable text. Read the program update, including reported immersion-teacher hiring, planned early-childhood classes, mentor–apprentice recruitment and program visits. Used only language-education details. Ceremony-specific content was deliberately excluded. No linked curricula, lesson materials, current program schedule, or subsequent outcome reports were reviewed.
sources.accessNotes: Public PDF linked from the Mescalero Apache Tribe website. The page was an image scan and required visual rendering to inspect; the atlas links to the original PDF and does not reproduce it.

initialAdequacy.rationale: Eight substantive works provide an initial path across the Tribe’s public identity and reservation history, a dated posted constitution, the Tribe’s language-program goals and a September 2024 program snapshot, a Texas-focused government synthesis whose source pool and draft received Historic Preservation Officer input, an NPS regional interpretation, and a peer-reviewed Mescalero Apache–University of New Mexico participatory-research article coauthored with Mescalero program staff. The 2024 update reports hiring and plans at that time but does not confirm subsequent delivery or outcomes. The research article concerns a specific 2013–2014 pilot rather than current service delivery. This remains an initial introduction—not a complete history, community endorsement, or claim that the broader research target has been met.

name: Native Hawaiian (Kānaka Maoli)
region: Hawaiian archipelago / Pacific; US-HI used as a geographic navigation region
kind: Indigenous people / language / diverse communities and institutions
overview: Begin with annotated public sources on Native Hawaiian identity, language education, land and water care, institutional roles and the 1993 federal apology. This initial source guide supports a Hawaiʻi map connection while keeping its limited coverage visible.

sections.title: An Indigenous people and a Hawaiian name
sections.text: Native Hawaiian and Kānaka Maoli identify the Indigenous people of Hawaiʻi. The university naming reference provides an attributed introduction. The 1993 resolution uses an ancestry-based definition specific to that instrument; it is not a universal enrollment rule.

sections.title: A homeland connection for the map
sections.text: The resolution connects Native Hawaiian ancestors with the islands now indexed as Hawaiʻi. This state route is a finding aid, not a parcel map or a decision on territorial rights. Island-specific histories need further research.

sections.title: The Kingdom, overthrow and a dated apology
sections.text: Congress’s 1993 resolution acknowledges United States involvement in the 1893 overthrow and apologizes to Native Hawaiians. It explicitly does not settle claims. Original Kingdom documents and Hawaiian scholarship are needed for a fuller history.

sections.title: Rebuilding everyday language education
sections.text: ʻAha Pūnana Leo traces its work to Hawaiian language educators who organized in 1983. Its account describes the first preschool at Kekaha, Kauaʻi, in 1984, followed by schools on other islands. Elders’ advice about children learning through everyday interaction shaped that work. The history also acknowledges inspiration from Māori language nests. This is a community institution’s account of rebuilding education; the page does not establish current proficiency outcomes for all Native Hawaiians.

sections.title: Learning through care for land and water
sections.text: Paepae o Heʻeia’s public collection explains how a coastal fishpond on Oʻahu uses a wall and managed water exchange to support aquatic life. Its education page describes students investigating water quality and other ecological questions while helping inform the organization’s management decisions. These accounts connect inherited environmental knowledge with contemporary learning at one place. Heʻeia’s story should not be generalized to every island, family or fishpond.

sections.title: Understanding OHA as a particular institution
sections.text: The Office of Hawaiian Affairs describes itself as a semi-autonomous state agency. Its account connects its creation with 1970s Native Hawaiian activism and the 1978 constitutional convention. It identifies advocacy, research, land management and support for community programs among its roles. Reading its own description helps distinguish a service and advocacy institution from the people as a whole. Its remit does not establish consensus on political futures or make OHA a sovereign Native Hawaiian government.

sources.title: Our History
sources.author: ʻAha Pūnana Leo
sources.annotation: Educators’ institutional account of rebuilding Hawaiian-medium education, beginning with organizing in 1983 and the first preschool in 1984. A valuable program history; historical policy claims and present outcomes still need independent comparison.
sources.documentDate: Undated live page; timeline extends through 2023
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual HTML history and timeline, lines 79–114. Photographs, linked courses, videos and private portals were not inspected.

sources.title: The Fishpond and Education — Heʻeia public learning collection
sources.author: Paepae o Heʻeia
sources.annotation: The community organization explains a coastal fishpond and connects its care with place-based ecological learning. The history and education pages are counted together as one public collection. Undated teaching schedules, output figures and ownership statements are not treated as verified current conditions.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual Fishpond body, lines 54–76; Education introduction and charter-school learning account, lines 53–61. No restricted material, oral recordings, site geometry or photographs reused.

inspectedSubresources.title: Education
inspectedSubresources.scope: Public introduction and charter-school learning paragraphs, lines 53–61

sources.title: About the Office of Hawaiian Affairs
sources.author: Office of Hawaiian Affairs
sources.annotation: OHA describes its state-agency role, origins in 1970s activism and work supporting Native Hawaiian wellbeing. Useful for understanding this particular institution; it is not a sovereign government speaking for every Native Hawaiian perspective. Staff totals and financial claims are omitted.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual substantive About, vision, mission and overview text, lines 99–118. Linked film, program reports and current administrative rules were not reviewed.

sources.title: Public Law 103–150: acknowledgment and apology for the overthrow of the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi
sources.author: United States Congress
sources.publisher: United States Statutes at Large, 107 Stat. 1510–1514; Government Publishing Office / GovInfo
sources.annotation: Original 1993 federal resolution: historical recitals, apology, instrument-specific definition and non-settlement disclaimer. A dated primary instrument, not a complete history or determination of contemporary citizenship, sovereignty or remedies.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual five-page PDF text/OCR read: 107 Stat. 1510–1514, all recitals and sections 1–3. This records text inspection, not a claimed page-image transcription audit.

sources.title: Hawaiian Word of the Week: Maoli
sources.author: University of Hawaiʻi News; attributed reflection by Diamond Badajos
sources.annotation: Brief university publication identifies Kānaka Maoli as the Indigenous people of Hawaiʻi through an attributed alumna’s reflection. Included for naming and orientation only; its brevity makes it supporting material rather than a substantive research-target source.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual definition and attributed reflection, lines 34–49. Embedded video and linked dictionary were not reviewed.

relationshipNote: Native Hawaiian / Kānaka Maoli is a people-level access point, distinct from the population of the modern state and from any single agency or organization. OHA is a state agency; ʻAha Pūnana Leo and Paepae o Heʻeia are specific community institutions. The historical Kingdom, its subjects, Indigenous identity, ancestry-based program categories and contemporary political proposals require their own contexts. The state-index connection does not decide recognition, citizenship or territorial claims.
researchGaps: A fuller account needs Hawaiian-authored historical scholarship and original Kingdom-era documents, with island-specific histories.
Contemporary family voices, diaspora experiences, health and housing, and the diversity of political positions need stronger representation.
Legal program definitions, current law and recognition debates require separately dated specialist research; the 1993 resolution does not answer them all.
Learning outcomes, restoration results and present program availability have not been independently assessed.
evidenceNotes: Four substantive works/collections and one short supporting naming reference were inspected within recorded scopes on October 21, 2026. Paepae o Heʻeia pages count once. The guide is not promoted to a developed profile or an adequate initial introduction; no community review is implied.
No generated images, copied photographs, restricted cultural content or precise site coordinates were used. The 1993 law was reviewed as text/OCR, not asserted as a full image-transcription audit.

name: Ojibwe
overview: Ojibwe, Chippewa, and Anishinaabe are names used in different contexts for a wider people, while Minnesota includes distinct Ojibwe governments and communities. Six separately sovereign Bands form the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe and share its constitution; Red Lake Nation follows a separate governmental history. This Minnesota-focused guide brings together community accounts, Leech Lake Band treaty and co-management history, dated federal and state court opinions, a Smithsonian Leech Lake lesson, and place-specific historical research. The sources describe different nations and periods rather than one uniform community.

sections.title: Names, peoples, and distinct governments
sections.text: Sources use Ojibwe, Chippewa, and Anishinaabe in overlapping but context-dependent ways. The White Earth Nation and Sault Tribe explain their naming and language choices from their own community perspectives. The Bureau of Indian Affairs lists six member Bands of the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe, and Mille Lacs states that those Bands are separately sovereign with distinct laws and systems. Red Lake Nation’s history says its leaders maintained a separate political path rather than joining that six-Band organization. These records describe present governments and source usage; they do not make every local identity interchangeable.

sections.title: Migration accounts and local histories
sections.text: Bois Forte’s government and Heritage Center preserve a community migration account centered on an elder’s prophecy and a westward route around the Great Lakes. The Red Lake Nation’s timeline offers its own chronology of Ojibwe movement into northern Minnesota. Mille Lacs’ illustrated guide also presents a migration teaching and seasonal food history. These accounts are attributed to their publishers; older archaeological and colonial records cannot replace them, and one community’s route is not treated as a uniform timeline for all Ojibwe communities.

sections.title: Treaties, homelands, and changing land tenure
sections.text: Mille Lacs’ treaty reading path connects the 1837 cession and reserved harvesting rights with later litigation, and identifies the 1855 treaty as establishing its reservation. Its historical guide describes the Sandy Lake tragedy, later pressure to remove the Band, and allotment policy. Bois Forte’s history outlines separate 1854 and 1866 treaty arrangements and an 1881 executive order. Grand Portage’s government identifies its 1854 Treaty of La Pointe relationship, while the National Park Service places the monument within Grand Portage Anishinaabe homeland. These are distinct community and place-specific histories, not statewide boundary definitions. The Leech Lake Band’s resource-management booklet supplies a direct Band account of the 1837, 1854, 1855, 1864, and 1867 treaty sequence, followed by the Nelson Act, allotment, and logging. It describes the 1864 consolidation and the later creation of White Earth while Leech Lake lands were retained, and explains the effects of these policies from the Band’s perspective. The booklet also records differing Pillager and military accounts of how the 1898 Sugar Point conflict began. Its legal conclusions and chronology are attributed to the Band; the treaty texts and underlying court and archival records require separate review. Two later reported opinions help distinguish the historical stages of the Leech Lake dispute. In 1971, the U.S. District Court held that treaty rights had not been ended by the Nelson Act and protected hunting, fishing, and wild-rice gathering on public lands and waters within the reservation, while declining to grant the Band the exclusive regulatory authority it sought. In 1977, the Minnesota Supreme Court upheld the 1973 settlement and fishing-stamp statute as a compromise that recognized retained treaty rights while also allowing state regulation of fishing by nonmembers under that arrangement. These are specific historical holdings; current rules, later law, and the underlying treaty texts remain separate research questions. A 2023 federal district-court order in Fond du Lac Band v. Cummins concerned the Band’s challenge to a Forest Service land exchange for a proposed NorthMet mine. At the motion-to-dismiss stage, the court accepted the complaint’s allegation that the exchange could remove access to 6,650 acres used for treaty rights and held that the Band could assert its own 1854 Treaty usufructuary interests; the rights were not exclusively individual-member rights. The court denied dismissal, but did not decide the land-exchange claim on its merits or the project’s ultimate outcome. A 2026 Grand Portage Band news release reports the return of three parcels to Band ownership and describes different routes by which they had left Band ownership: treaty cession, transfer into state school-trust lands, and allotment. This is the Band account of one present-day land return; the underlying treaty and title records were not independently examined, and this case does not define all Ojibwe homelands or imply that all Bands experienced the same history.

sections.title: Language, foodways, and community continuity
sections.text: Fond du Lac records its 2010 decision to make Ojibwe its official language and describes a language program established in 2015. White Earth’s cultural division describes ongoing work in language, schools, gatherings, and cultural activities. The Smithsonian Leech Lake lesson explains manoomin as a food and teaching relationship and includes educator contributions; it is a broad school resource rather than a substitute for community-specific teaching. Each account has a distinct publisher and scope.

sections.title: Place-based research and public interpretation
sections.text: A National Park Service study of Voyageurs combines archaeology, photographs, historic maps, records, and oral histories to document Bois Forte occupation in and near the park, especially during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Its author marks the limit of the evidence and does not claim to trace the groups to their beginning. Grand Portage National Monument describes a separate portage corridor and identifies the Grand Portage Band as a present community connected to that place. Such local studies are useful precisely because their place and time limits are explicit.

sections.title: Contemporary community priorities
sections.text: White Earth’s 2025 Climate Action Plan was co-authored through a community planning process and links seasonal cycles, wild rice, food sovereignty, and climate resilience to White Earth’s current priorities. Its survey and modeled outcomes are dated to the plan and its respondents; they are not current population statistics or a universal Ojibwe position. Bois Forte’s current natural-resources page and public statement describe the Band’s own work and treaty concerns in its 1854 treaty area. These sources show living governments and current community priorities alongside historical accounts. A Leech Lake Band resource-management booklet describes the Reservation Business Committee’s assignment of natural-resource law and planning to the Band’s Division of Resource Management, and presents the 2019 co-management agreement with the Chippewa National Forest as a government-to-government framework. This is the Band’s own institutional explanation, based on a compilation that includes dated 2019–2020 materials; it is not a current status audit of every agreement or program.

sections.title: Fond du Lac food access and community education
sections.text: Fond du Lac’s Food Sovereignty Assessment 2019–2022 describes Gitigaaning as a community farm and training site, with demonstration gardens and a kitchen/cannery. These are the Band’s dated descriptions, not verified current schedules or evidence of outcomes. Its December 2018–May 2019 survey received 342 responses; most analysis used 223 responses from Band members, descendants or elders, while some questions included broader groups. Voluntary online and paper participation and the report’s explicit limits on representativeness mean its results should not be generalized to every Band member or other Ojibwe governments.

sections.title: Scope and gaps in this Minnesota reading path
sections.text: This is a reviewed initial source guide, not a complete history of Ojibwe peoples. It gives distinct starting points for all seven Minnesota governments named in the regional inventory: the six Minnesota Chippewa Tribe member Bands and the separate Red Lake Nation. Direct, deeper histories remain uneven: Leech Lake now has a Band-published treaty, land, and co-management overview as well as a Smithsonian educational module; Fond du Lac still needs more direct public history and treaty material; the other communities have varying mixes of government and place-based evidence. Wisconsin and Canadian communities, specialist language scholarship, primary treaty scans, oral-history transcripts, and community review remain open work. Short listings and background references are labeled as support rather than counted as substantive works.
