sources.author: Bois Forte Band Natural Resources Department
sources.annotation: The Band describes stewardship on its reservation sectors and within the 1854 Treaty Area, including its cooperation with the 1854 Treaty Authority and current programs. It is a present-day institutional account; land-return and harvest-right assertions are attributed and not independently adjudicated here.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the mission and 2026 highlights (lines 136–158), including the climate plan partnership and current ecological/resource projects. Linked plans and video were not opened.

sources.title: Bois Forte Band statement on H.J. Resolution 140 and treaty-reserved rights
sources.author: Bois Forte Band of Chippewa; statement quotes Chairperson Carlos Hernandez
sources.sourceKind: Dated tribal government statement about a current federal policy action
sources.annotation: A dated Band statement explains the Band’s view of treaty-protected harvesting, ancestral homelands and environmental risk related to proposed mining. Its estimates of access and policy impacts remain attributed to the Band; the source is a community position statement, not an independent environmental or legal assessment.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the full statement (lines 18–30). It distinguishes Congressional action from later permitting; underlying legislation and environmental analyses were not reviewed in this profile pass. Counts as supporting context only.

sources.title: Materials Related to the Co-Management of the Chippewa National Forest: The Right to Self-Governance — Historical and Current Overview of the Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe
sources.author: Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe, Division of Resource Management
sources.publicationDate: Undated compilation; contains a 2019 Memorandum of Understanding and a 2020 briefing presentation
sources.annotation: A first-party Leech Lake Band educational and resource-management account, created to explain historical events, treaties, the Band’s government, and its agency relationships to Band staff and citizens. The historical overview narrates the 1837, 1854, 1855, 1864, and 1867 treaty sequence, later allotment and logging, the 1898 Sugar Point conflict, and the Band’s resource-governance work. Treaty-right and legal conclusions are presented as the Band’s institutional interpretation; the underlying treaty instruments, court opinions, and cited historical records were not independently checked in this source review. The booklet also includes later co-management materials that should be read as dated documents, not assumed to describe every current policy.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the complete first 20-page “Right to Self-Governance: Historical and Current Overview” (PDF pages 4–23), including its preface, treaty chronology, Nelson Act/allotment and timber discussion, Sugar Point account, present governance and federal/state-agency relationships. The complete PDF has 133 pages; later slide decks, the 2019 MOU, appendices, management letters, implementation guide, and species list were not inspected as separate works. No map or sensitive site information was reused.

sources.title: Leech Lake Band of Chippewa Indians v. Herbst, 334 F. Supp. 1001 (D. Minn. 1971)
sources.author: U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota, Chief Judge Edward J. Devitt
sources.publisher: Justia, reproducing a reported federal district-court opinion
sources.sourceKind: Reported U.S. District Court memorandum and order
topics: Treaty fishing, hunting, and wild-rice rights
sources.annotation: The complete reported opinion addresses whether Leech Lake Band members could fish, hunt, and gather wild rice on public lands and waters within the Leech Lake Reservation free from Minnesota game and fish laws. The court held that treaty rights had not been abrogated by the Nelson Act and declared those activities protected on the specified public lands and waters. The opinion did not accept the Band’s claim to exclusive regulatory authority over all fishing, hunting, and ricing. This is a dated judicial holding in a particular case, not a statement of current regulations or a substitute for later law.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the full opinion and notes (reported text at pages 1001–1010; Justia lines 38–143). The opinion recounts the litigants’ positions, testimony, treaty/legal analysis, and the court’s narrow declaratory judgment. The 1855/1864/1867 treaty originals, trial exhibits, and later proceedings were not independently inspected in this entry.

sources.title: State v. Forge, 262 N.W.2d 341 (Minn. 1977)
sources.author: Supreme Court of Minnesota
sources.publisher: Justia, reproducing a reported Minnesota Supreme Court opinion
sources.annotation: The full opinion recounts the Leech Lake Band’s 1969 federal lawsuit, the 1971 Herbst decision, the 1973 settlement and consent judgment, and challenges to Minnesota’s reservation fishing stamp. The Minnesota Supreme Court held that Minnesota Chippewa Tribe members retained treaty rights and upheld the 1973 statutory compromise and the convictions of nonmembers who fished without the stamp. This later ruling supplies important historical context for the 1971 opinion; it does not establish every present-day regulation or decide all treaty-right questions.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the full reported opinion and notes (262 N.W.2d 341–349; Justia lines 38–163), including its description of the 1971 federal case, the 1973 settlement and consent judgment, statutory terms, holding, and express limits on what issues the appeal decided. The settlement document, current statute and later court cases were not separately reviewed.

sources.title: Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa v. Cummins et al., Document 48 (D. Minn. Feb. 24, 2023)
sources.author: United States District Court for the District of Minnesota; Chief Judge Patrick J. Schiltz
sources.publisher: Justia, reproducing the federal district-court order
sources.sourceKind: District-court order denying a motion to dismiss
sources.annotation: In a challenge to a Forest Service land exchange for the proposed NorthMet mine, the District Court denied PolyMet’s motion to dismiss. At this pleading-stage ruling, it accepted the complaint’s allegation that the exchange could remove access to 6,650 acres used for the Band’s treaty rights and held that the Band had standing to assert its own 1854 Treaty usufructuary interests; those rights were not exclusively individual member rights. This is not a decision on the merits of the land exchange or the ultimate project outcome. The alleged access loss is described as a complaint allegation, not a factual finding.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the full 18-page opinion as reproduced on Justia, including the docket/date and disposition (lines 38–50), the complaint’s background and stated alleged injury (lines 51–63), the treaty and tribal-right analysis (lines 64–98), and the order denying dismissal (lines 103–110). The complaint and docket exhibits, Forest Service Record of Decision, environmental review, and later case history were not independently inspected.

sources.title: Grand Portage Band Regains Historic Tribal Land
sources.author: Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa
sources.publisher: Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa
sources.type: Tribal news release / contemporary land stewardship
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the full 83-line public Band news release on October 23, 2026. It reports the February 16, 2026 acquisition of three parcels through a Band/Foundation partnership, describes the Band account of different land-loss mechanisms, and quotes the Band chair and partner representatives. Its linked map/images were not opened or used. The Band statements about federal policy and the parcels past ownership are attributed community interpretation; underlying treaty, land-title and allotment records were not independently inspected.
sources.annotation: A Grand Portage Band news release reports that a February 2026 acquisition restored three parcels totaling about 87 acres to Band ownership through a partnership with the Lloyd K. Johnson Foundation and Minnesota Land Trust. The Band describes three distinct routes by which those parcels left Band ownership: 1854 treaty cession, state school-trust transfer, and allotment. This is a direct community source for the Bands current action and its historical interpretation; the underlying treaty, land-title chain, tax records, and allotment documents were not independently checked. The Bands broad discussion of allotment policy remains attributed to the release and is not generalized to every Ojibwe Band. A linked map/images package is not included.

sources.title: Food Sovereignty Assessment 2019–2022
sources.publisher: Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa
sources.author: Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa
sources.annotation: A dated community assessment linking food access and gardening education. Its voluntary survey is a bounded community snapshot, not a representative measurement of every Band member or all Ojibwe peoples. Read the program descriptions alongside the methodology; present operations and outcomes were not verified.
sources.contentReviewScope: Searchable text of printed pp.5–8,16–20,22–31 reviewed on October 23, 2026. Page images, maps and charts were not visually inspected. Medical claims, eligibility advice and numerical chart labels are excluded from synthesis; no image is reproduced.

initialAdequacy.rationale: Nineteen substantive works have now been inspected, including direct sources from several Minnesota Ojibwe governments, a Leech Lake Band resource-management and treaty-history booklet, two full reported court opinions about Leech Lake treaty rights and a 1973 settlement, a 2023 federal order addressing Fond du Lac tribal standing and communal treaty interest in a land-exchange challenge, a Band-authored Grand Portage land-return report, the Bois Forte community museum, a White Earth community planning document, and National Park Service place-based research. The guide distinguishes community accounts from specific legal holdings and names all seven Minnesota government routes in the reviewed inventory. Quantity exceeds the twelve-work target, but community-specific depth remains uneven; the Grand Portage release is a dated Band account, not an independently checked title history or comprehensive Ojibwe history; the Fond du Lac litigation source concerns a preliminary standing ruling, not the merits or a complete Band history; and the wider Ojibwe peoples across Canada and the United States are not comprehensively covered. No community review is recorded. The Fond du Lac food-sovereignty assessment adds dated community-program and survey-method evidence; it does not establish current outcomes.
remainingLimits: The seven Minnesota governments have not all received equally deep, direct source review. Leech Lake now has a Band-published historical overview and two reported court opinions, but the underlying treaty texts, 1973 settlement document, current rules, and later legal history still need review; Fond du Lac now has a directly relevant 2023 federal standing order in addition to its language and official-source coverage, but still needs more direct community history, treaty material, and review of the case merits and later docket; separate institutional and community voices should be deepened for every Band and Red Lake Nation.

The Minnesota Chippewa Tribe website’s linked History of the Tribe page did not expose substantive text through the inspection tool, and the direct 2015 Leech Lake annual report exceeded the source tool’s document-size limit. The Leech Lake Band’s 20-page overview inside its 133-page co-management booklet and the full reported opinions in Leech Lake Band v. Herbst (1971) and State v. Forge (1977) were inspected; the booklet’s later MOU, appendices, and implementation materials, underlying treaties, settlement document, and later legal history were not reviewed. These are inspection constraints, not evidence that readers face a paywall; no limit was bypassed.

The full Bois Forte oral-history transcripts listed by its museum, the Smithsonian video transcript, and the Mille Lacs Band’s linked Social History book were not read. They are not represented as inspected sources.

Specialist Ojibwe language scholarship, treaty originals and legal decisions, more community-authored records from Grand Portage, White Earth and Red Lake, and relevant communities in Wisconsin and Canada remain to be reviewed.

The Minnesota Indian Affairs Council’s older Fond du Lac sketch includes broad, dated ethnographic descriptions; it is retained only as supporting context and those generalizations are not carried into the synthesis.
No Ojibwe community review or endorsement is recorded.

The 2026 Grand Portage land-return release documents a specific Band action and presents the Band historical interpretation; its underlying treaty, title, state-transfer and allotment records were not independently inspected. It cannot stand for other Ojibwe Bands or a single homeland boundary.
initialAdequacy.searchScope: On October 23, 2026, read the complete public text of the March 16, 2026 Grand Portage Band news release about the completed land acquisition; its linked map/images and underlying land-title records were not inspected.

researchGaps: The seven Minnesota governments have not all received equally deep, direct source review. Leech Lake now has a Band-published historical overview and two reported court opinions, but the underlying treaty texts, 1973 settlement document, current rules, and later legal history still need review; Fond du Lac needs more direct public history and treaty material; separate institutional and community voices should be deepened for every Band and Red Lake Nation.

The Minnesota Chippewa Tribe website’s linked History of the Tribe page did not expose substantive text through the inspection tool, and the direct 2015 Leech Lake annual report exceeded the source tool’s document-size limit. The Leech Lake Band’s historical overview and the full reported opinions in Leech Lake Band v. Herbst (1971) and State v. Forge (1977) were inspected; the booklet’s later MOU, appendices, implementation materials, underlying treaties, and settlement document were not independently reviewed.

The full Bois Forte oral-history transcripts listed by its museum, the Smithsonian video transcript, and the Mille Lacs Band’s linked Social History book were not read. They are not represented as inspected sources.

Specialist Ojibwe language scholarship, treaty originals and legal decisions, more community-authored records from Grand Portage, White Earth and Red Lake, and relevant communities in Wisconsin and Canada remain to be reviewed.

The Minnesota Indian Affairs Council’s older Fond du Lac sketch includes broad, dated ethnographic descriptions; it is retained only as supporting context and those generalizations are not carried into the synthesis.
No Ojibwe community review or endorsement is recorded.
evidenceNotes: 19 substantive inspected works are counted separately from supporting resources. Quantity remains distinct from adequacy, completion and community review.
The six Minnesota Chippewa Tribe Bands and Red Lake Nation are treated as distinct governments. Minnesota’s state lines and the regional map are navigation aids, not Indigenous homeland boundaries.
Community histories, government pages, educational modules, a state-hosted historical page and NPS research answer different questions. Claims stay attributed to source, community, time and place.
The 2025 White Earth Climate Action Plan is a contemporary planning source; its survey and modeled future outcomes are not population measurements or evidence of an all-Ojibwe consensus.
The existing Grand Portage map-profile association remains linked with its prior evidence; this source pass did not inspect a map object or create a new association.

Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe’s 133-page co-management compilation was counted once, based on its complete 20-page historical/current overview (PDF pages 4–23). Its treaty and legal claims remain explicitly attributed; the later included MOU, appendices, and implementation materials are not separately counted as inspected works.

Leech Lake Band v. Herbst (1971) and State v. Forge (1977) are counted as two distinct full judicial opinions. The synthesis records their historical holdings and sequence; neither is presented as current regulatory advice. The 1971 court declined the Band’s claim to exclusive regulatory authority, and the 1977 Minnesota Supreme Court discussed and upheld a 1973 legislative/settlement compromise. Underlying instruments and later law remain open.

Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa v. Cummins (2023) is a full federal order on standing at the motion-to-dismiss stage. It holds that the Band may assert its 1854 Treaty usufructuary interest; it does not resolve the merits of the land exchange or later project status. The 6,650-acre access loss is a complaint allegation accepted at that procedural stage, not a final factual finding.

Fond du Lac Food Sovereignty Assessment 2019–2022 counted once after selected-text inspection. Voluntary respondent selection and question-specific denominators limit interpretation. Maps, photographs and charts were not visually reviewed, and medical claims are not used.

sections.text: Pensacola/Panzacola is a historical people-name associated with Pensacola Bay in West Florida. The initial reading path now points to original people-specific research and distinguishes this name from the later city and the broader archaeological Pensacola culture.

sections.title: A focused source, with limits
sections.text: DeRoche’s thesis examines documentary and archaeological evidence for the historical Panzacola. The introduction and selected pages support this initial orientation; they do not establish a positively identified excavated village. The remaining thesis, contemporary descendant connections and other original accounts need further review.

sources.title: Patrick Anthony DeRoche — In Pursuit of the Panzacola: A Historical Documentary and Archaeological Investigation
sources.publisher: University of West Florida — Patrick Anthony DeRoche
sources.annotation: DeRoche’s introduction explicitly places the historical Panzacola people around present-day Pensacola Bay in West Florida using seventeenth-century documentary accounts. His discussion distinguishes this people from the archaeological Pensacola culture; the test excavation did not establish a positive Panzacola site identification. Inspection: Actual university public download, valid-TLS HTTP 200, 2,675,875 bytes, 100 PDF pages including added cover. Cover/title; abstract printed p.viii / PDF p.9; introduction printed pp.1–3 / PDF pp.10–12; and printed p.8 / PDF p.17 were read as text/OCR. Not a complete thesis or excavation-data review. Limits: The canonical name Pensacola is retained; Panzacola is the historical people-label used by the thesis. The later city and archaeological culture are separate referents. No definitive excavated Panzacola village, coordinates, ethnicity-from-ceramics inference, contemporary recognition status or disappearance claim is adopted. This is an original student thesis with committee oversight, not a statement of consensus on every historical identification.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual university public download, valid-TLS HTTP 200, 2,675,875 bytes, 100 PDF pages including added cover. Cover/title; abstract printed p.viii / PDF p.9; introduction printed pp.1–3 / PDF pp.10–12; and printed p.8 / PDF p.17 were read as text/OCR. Not a complete thesis or excavation-data review.

name: Shoshone
overview: Shoshone is a broad name for distinct regional peoples and communities, not one single government or uniform history. This reviewed introduction centers publicly documented histories connected to Idaho, including the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes at Fort Hall and the Shoshone-Paiute Tribes of Duck Valley, while also placing Eastern and Northwestern Shoshone sources in view. It is a selected reading guide, not an exhaustive account of all Shoshone communities.

sections.title: Names, communities, and scope
sections.text: “Shoshone” is used for related peoples whose histories span a large area of the inland West; the name does not identify one government or one community. The Shoshone-Bannock Tribes describe their Fort Hall government as comprising Northern Shoshone and Bannock bands, while their account distinguishes the peoples’ languages. The Shoshone-Paiute Tribes’ Duck Valley history describes a separate community formed from Western Shoshone and Northern Paiute bands whose reservation crosses today’s Idaho–Nevada border. The Eastern Shoshone Tribe and Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation are distinct governments with their own public historical accounts. The NPS wayside exhibit’s term “Newenee” and its “Shoshonean” language grouping belong to a specific Shoshone-Bannock collaboration and should not be treated as universal names for every Shoshone community.

sections.title: Idaho homelands and seasonal movement
sections.text: For the Fort Hall community, the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes describe ancestral lands extending beyond present reservation and state borders, and document seasonal use of southern Idaho’s river, camas, salmon, and high-country areas. The National Park Service’s Craters of the Moon account outlines a seasonal round through Fort Hall, Camas Prairie, the Boise and Snake Rivers, and hunting areas farther north and east. That is a place-based NPS interpretation, not a complete account of all Shoshone families or a present-day territorial boundary. Northwestern Shoshone historian Mae Parry’s chapter separately describes seasonal gathering and travel in northern Utah, southern Idaho, and adjoining regions; her account helps show why present state lines and reservation maps cannot stand in for community history.

sections.title: Language, cultural work, and public knowledge
sections.text: The Shoshone-Bannock Language and Cultural Preservation Department describes teaching both Shoshone and Bannock, maintaining archives and family-history materials, recording oral histories, and protecting information it considers confidential or sensitive. The NPS Newenee exhibit was prepared with Shoshone-Bannock representatives and includes artwork by Shoshone-Bannock artist Derek No-Sun Brown; its welcome and language examples should be read as a specific community contribution to a public park exhibit. These sources document programs and public interpretation, not language-use totals or outcomes. This guide does not reproduce restricted material.

sections.title: Treaties, reservation formation, and distinct governments
sections.text: The 1868 Fort Bridger treaty names the Eastern Shoshone and Bannock parties separately. Its text set aside the Wind River reservation for named Shoshone signatories and promised a later reservation for the Bannacks in the Portneuf and “Kansas Prairie” countries. The Shoshone-Bannock Tribes’ Treaty Day account says the separate Bannock reservation was never established and that Bannock people were relocated to Fort Hall in 1869. WyoHistory’s timeline describes later Bannock moves in 1873 and the arrival of Pocatello’s band in 1876. These accounts differ in how they date the move and do not make the treaty’s promise identical to its later implementation. The Fort Hall Constitution and Bylaws, approved in 1936 and amended through 2013 in the published copy, describe that government’s own jurisdiction and council structure; they should not be generalized to other Shoshone governments.

sections.title: Duck Valley and Shoshone-Paiute history
sections.text: The Shoshone-Paiute Tribes’ cultural department locates Duck Valley across Idaho and Nevada and describes the community as including Western Shoshone and Northern Paiute bands. Its historical account covers executive orders, movement on and off the reservation, resistance to a proposed relocation to Fort Hall, the 1936 constitution, and schooling. The page’s acreage and membership figures are undated and are not repeated here. A 2021 Department of the Interior statement for the record explains the Duck Valley water-rights settlement and the federal trust funds for irrigation infrastructure; it is a narrow legal and administrative source, not a full account of the Tribes’ history or water knowledge.

sections.title: Northwestern and Eastern Shoshone histories
sections.text: Mae Parry’s chapter, written by a Northwestern Shoshone historian for a Utah history volume proposed by Utah Indian leaders, combines family oral history, written records, and tribal history. The selected pages discuss the Bear River Massacre of 1863, survivors’ accounts, the settlement of Washakie, testimony about homes burned in 1960, and the Northwestern Band’s later legal history. Utah Humanities’ 2024 account, produced for the Northwestern Band, describes Mae Parry’s archival and oral-history work and continuing community efforts. These sources provide Northwestern-specific context; their accounts do not represent every Shoshone community. The Eastern Shoshone government’s About page is also retained as its own public account, while its deep-time and treaty-area figures are left unattributed in the synthesis because they need closer comparison with community and archaeological sources.

sections.title: What this collection can and cannot establish
sections.text: This source set supports an introductory comparison of several living Shoshone communities and particular treaty, language, place, and government records. Its coverage remains uneven: Fort Hall, Duck Valley, Wind River, and the Northwestern Band have different kinds and depths of documentation here, while many other Shoshone communities, family histories, languages, and contemporary priorities are not represented. Some historical sources use old collective labels or compress distinct bands into one timeline. The collection has twelve substantive works with actual content inspected, but that count is separate from adequacy, completeness, or community review. No community endorsement is recorded, no population total is offered, and no map is assigned by geographic inference.

sources.title: About — Shoshone-Bannock Tribes
sources.annotation: Read the actual Culture and History body (especially paragraphs on bands, homelands, language distinctions, seasonal foodways and reservation geography). This is the Fort Hall Tribes’ own public summary; its expansive ancestral-land description is not a boundary survey, and its dated account is not universal to all Shoshone peoples.

sources.title: Shoshone - Gateway Arch National Park (U.S. National Park Service)
sources.annotation: Retained as a relevant National Park Service reading lead. Its page body was not inspected in this review, so it is not cited as evidence and does not count as a substantive content check.

sources.publisher: Shoshone-Bannock Tribes Language and Cultural Preservation Department
sources.annotation: Read the department’s sections on language teaching, archival stewardship, Original Territories research, family histories, oral-history recording and museum work. The page itself identifies confidential or sensitive information; no such material is reproduced. Current class schedules and changing program details are not repeated.

sources.title: Newenee: The Shoshonean Peoples of Southern Idaho
sources.publisher: National Park Service, with Shoshone-Bannock Tribes representatives
sources.annotation: Read the complete public exhibit article, including the Shoshone-Bannock welcome, the exhibit panel, and its attributed elder quotation. The page states NPS collaborated with Shoshone-Bannock representatives and identifies artist Derek No-Sun Brown as a Shoshone-Bannock artist. “Newenee” and “Shoshonean” are used in this exhibit’s context, not asserted as universal labels.

sources.title: History — Craters of the Moon National Monument and Preserve
sources.annotation: Read the complete Shoshone-Bannock and Goodale’s Cutoff sections. Useful as an NPS place-based account of seasonal routes and the later use of those routes by emigrants. Its “limited resources” framing and settler-centered account of the 1862 wagon-train incident are attributed to the NPS page rather than adopted as a comprehensive tribal interpretation; the two public oral narratives on the page are not retold here.

sources.title: Our History — Cultural Department
sources.publisher: Shoshone-Paiute Tribes of the Duck Valley Indian Reservation
sources.annotation: Read the full Our History section. It describes Duck Valley as a shared Western Shoshone and Northern Paiute community, the reservation’s executive orders, movement and resistance, schools, and the Tribe’s 1936 constitution. The page’s undated acreage, membership and current-governance figures are not reused; its account is identified as the Tribe’s own historical narrative.

sources.title: H.R. 1869: Technical Correction to the Shoshone-Paiute Tribes of the Duck Valley Reservation Water Rights Settlement Act of 2021
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of the Interior, Office of the Secretary
sources.annotation: Read the complete Secretary’s statement for the record, especially the Duck Valley settlement background and trust-fund explanation. This is a 2021 federal legislative position on one technical correction, not the Tribe’s own full water history or a neutral summary of all parties’ views.

sources.title: Fort Bridger Treaty of 1868 — treaty text reproduced by the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes
sources.publisher: Treaty with the Eastern Band Shoshoni and Bannock, 1868; compiled by Charles J. Kappler (1904)
sources.annotation: Read the treaty heading and Articles 1–2 in the Tribe’s hosted reproduction of the 1904 Kappler compilation. The text distinguishes Eastern Shoshone and Bannock parties and promises a later Bannock reservation; it is primary treaty text, not evidence by itself of how each provision was later implemented.

sources.title: Constitution and Bylaws for the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes of the Fort Hall Reservation
sources.publisher: Shoshone-Bannock Tribes; U.S. Office of Indian Affairs edition, approved 1936 and amended 2013
sources.annotation: Read the preamble and the territory, membership and council provisions in the published copy. It documents the Fort Hall government’s constitutional structure in this dated edition; later amendments or current practice should be checked against current tribal law before making present-day claims.

sources.title: About the Shoshone Tribe
sources.annotation: Read the complete public About page and its sections on the Wind River reservation, Washakie and Sacajawea. This is the Eastern Shoshone government’s own public account; some archaeological, treaty-area and historical totals are not independently assessed here and are not repeated as established fact.

sources.title: Coming to Wind River: The Eastern Shoshone Treaties of 1863 and 1868
sources.annotation: Read the full article’s 1863 treaty, migration and 1868 treaty sections, plus its notes and bibliography. A cited secondary narrative useful for treaty chronology and comparisons; it distinguishes Eastern Shoshone and Bannock groups but is not a substitute for treaty text or the involved governments’ accounts. Its dates for later Bannock moves differ from the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes’ public account.

sources.title: The Northwestern Shoshone — A History of Utah’s American Indians
sources.publisher: Mae Parry; edited by Forrest S. Cuch; Utah State Division of Indian Affairs and Utah State Division of History, 2000
sources.type: Indigenous-authored historical interpretation / selected book excerpt
sources.annotation: Read selected pages of Mae Parry’s 48-page chapter in the digitized book viewer: pp. 25–26 on regional seasonal life; pp. 34–42 on the Bear River Massacre and survivor accounts; pp. 59–61 on Washakie testimony; and pp. 69–72 on the Box Elder treaty and Northwestern Band legal history. The book introduction identifies this as a Utah Indian leaders’ project; Parry’s family and oral-history sources are attributed as such. This selected-page review is not a reading of every page in the chapter.

sources.title: Lessons in Resilience
sources.publisher: Nate Housley, Megan van Frank, and Megan Weiss for the Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation; The Beehive Archive / Utah Humanities, 2024-12-30
sources.annotation: Read the full article and metadata/source notes. The authors describe the Band’s public history and archive work and Mae Parry’s oral-history role; it is a dated public-history synthesis produced for the Northwestern Band, not an exhaustive tribal account. The article uses a different death toll estimate than some other public histories, so no single figure is asserted here.

sources.title: History — Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation
sources.publisher: Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation
sources.annotation: Read the page’s timeline and historical sections. Retained as a current Band-published perspective, but its compressed treaty and relocation chronology conflicts with the 1868 treaty text and other histories; those unverified details are not used as settled facts. It is excluded from the substantive count pending closer comparison.

initialAdequacy.rationale: Twelve distinct substantive works have actual-content inspection records: community publications from Fort Hall, Duck Valley, Eastern Shoshone and the Northwestern Band; a community–NPS exhibit; two place-based NPS histories; a Northwestern Shoshone historian’s selected chapter pages; a cited Wyoming history article; primary treaty and constitutional texts; and a federal Duck Valley water-settlement statement. These support a carefully scoped introduction across several regional communities, but the entry is a broad umbrella and evidence depth remains uneven. Reaching the source target does not make the collection complete or community-reviewed.
remainingLimits: The entry’s broad “Shoshone” access point cannot stand in for separate studies of the many Shoshone governments, communities, bands, and family histories. The current sample is uneven across Fort Hall, Duck Valley, Wind River, the Northwestern Band, and other Shoshone communities.

More community-authored histories, language materials, and contemporary accounts from Shoshone governments in Nevada, Utah, Idaho, and Wyoming remain to be inspected; no single source represents all communities.

The Fort Bridger Treaty text, the Shoshone-Bannock Treaty Day account, and WyoHistory describe the separate Bannock reservation and later move using different chronology. The relationship between reservation promises, relocation, and later Fort Hall governance needs further original-record review.

Mae Parry’s 2000 chapter was reviewed at selected pages only. Its family and oral-history evidence is attributed, while its historical interpretations are not treated as universal community consensus.

The Shoshone-Paiute cultural page and Eastern Shoshone About page contain undated or broad totals and historical claims that require independent checking; no current population, acreage, or deep-time claim is reused.

The Shoshone-Bannock and Shoshone-Paiute language evidence here is introductory. Comparative specialist work on Shoshone varieties, Bannock, and Northern Paiute, with each community’s terminology and stewardship preferences, remains needed.
No community review or endorsement is recorded. No historical map was independently inspected for this batch and none has been newly assigned.

name: Tittabawassee Ojibwe communities
region: Great Lakes / Michigan / Tittabawassee River and Saginaw watershed
overview: Explore the Tittabawassee River communities through Michigan treaty records, an attributed nineteenth-century account, and Saginaw Chippewa community sources. This regional reading route is placed in Ojibwe context and does not identify a separate present-day tribal government.

sections.title: A river-community name and its scope
sections.text: This is a historical and regional reading route for Indigenous communities associated with the Tittabawassee River in Michigan’s Saginaw watershed. It is not the name of a separate contemporary government established by this review. The Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe describes itself through three Ojibway bands: Saginaw, Black River and Swan Creek. That broader community history should not be reduced to a fourth band called Tittabawassee, or an exclusive descent claim for every river settlement.

sections.title: The river and historical place-names
sections.text: The 1819 treaty names Little Forks and Black Bird’s town on the river printed as Tetabawasink. The January 1837 text uses Tetabwasing. Clarke Historical Library’s Houghton exhibit connects Black Bird Reservation and the 1819 treaty with the Tittabawassee–Chippewa river landscape near Midland. These records help orient the reading, but do not supply a complete settlement inventory or justify drawing precise community boundaries.

sections.title: Reading the 1819 and January 1837 treaties
sections.text: The September 24, 1819 agreement identifies Chippewa parties and reserves two 6,000-acre tracts at Little Forks and Black Bird’s town. The January 14, 1837 agreement, made at Detroit with Saganaw/Chippewa parties, lists those tracts among the lands ceded and prescribes relocation. Treaty wording is evidence of the instrument and its terms; individual experiences, enforcement and later rights require separate study.

sections.title: Why the December 1837 supplement matters
sections.text: The December 20 agreement at Flint River modifies the January treaty, including relocation and financial provisions. The two supplied 1837 links therefore represent different, related Michigan agreements. Their listed proclamation date in 1838 should not replace their treaty dates. A proposed destination does not demonstrate that all local people relocated or that their communities disappeared.

sections.title: An attributed account of river travel
sections.text: In his 1887 book, Andrew J. Blackbird recalls a winter journey seeking support for Native citizenship. He describes following the frozen Tittabawassee, finding one camp deserted and receiving food at another where women and children remained while men hunted. This is his personal recollection of a particular encounter. He does not name every host or establish a genealogy for the camps, so the episode should not become a universal description of river life.

sections.title: Continuing communities, education and watershed care
sections.text: The Ziibiwing Center shares the Saginaw Chippewa Tribe’s account of continuing community institutions. A U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service restoration story, framed around the 2020 settlement, describes the Tribe’s cultural use of wetlands and planned habitat work in the wider Saginaw Bay area. The Tribal College’s history offers a further community-led educational route. These sources concern particular institutions and projects, rather than one unchanging river community or a claim that planned restoration is complete.

sections.title: Language and further reading
sections.text: Ojibwe language resources provide broader context, but their regional coverage matters. The Ojibwe People’s Dictionary identifies its main variety as Central Southwestern Ojibwe from Minnesota, Wisconsin and border-lakes communities. It should not be treated as a record of historical Tittabawassee pronunciation. The owner-supplied study and all 19 contributed links are retained below; only the sources with explicit inspection notes have been checked for this guide.

sources.title: History — Ziibiwing Center
sources.publisher: Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe of Michigan, Ziibiwing Center
sources.annotation: The Tribe’s own historical account identifies its three Ojibway bands and describes reservation history, reorganization and the cultural center. It supplies present-community context, not an exclusive descent chart for river settlements.
sources.contentReviewScope: Complete visible chronology and prose read, especially the three-band statement and reservation/reorganization paragraphs. Ancient chronology, numerical land-loss claims and broad legal assertions are not independently corroborated here.

sources.title: Treaty with the Chippewa, September 24, 1819 (7 Stat. 203)
sources.publisher: Oklahoma State University Libraries, Tribal Treaties Database; primary treaty transcription
sources.annotation: The treaty describes named Chippewa tracts, including Little Forks and Black Bird’s town. Read as a dated legal instrument, not a complete community history or current-rights opinion.
sources.contentReviewScope: Readable transcription: date/preamble and articles 1–9, web-extracted lines 25–112, plus displayed signatures/witness headings. Original manuscript scans were not opened. Main evidence is preamble and article 2. No signed manuscript or implementation files inspected.

sources.title: Treaty with the Chippewa, January 14, 1837 (7 Stat. 528)
sources.publisher: Oklahoma State University Libraries, Tribal Treaties Database; primary treaty transcription
sources.annotation: A Michigan/Saganaw treaty lists river tracts among lands ceded and prescribes relocation. Its terms are not proof that every person moved; read the December supplement alongside it.
sources.contentReviewScope: Readable transcription, date/preamble and articles 1–7, web-extracted lines 25–100. Original scan, later articles, schedules and signature pages were not inspected in this bounded pass. Main evidence is preamble, article 1 and article 6. No signed manuscript or implementation files inspected.

sources.title: Treaty with the Chippewa, December 20, 1837 (7 Stat. 547)
sources.publisher: Oklahoma State University Libraries, Tribal Treaties Database; primary treaty transcription
sources.annotation: This Flint River supplement changes parts of the January arrangement. It concerns Michigan Saganaw/Chippewa parties, rather than another treaty with the same generic Chippewa title.
sources.contentReviewScope: Entire readable treaty transcription, date/preamble, articles 1–7, signatures and witness lines, web-extracted lines 21–80. Original manuscript scan not opened. No signed manuscript or implementation files inspected.

sources.title: History of the Ottawa and Chippewa Indians of Michigan (1887), selected Tittabawassee passage
sources.publisher: Andrew J. Blackbird; University of Wisconsin–Madison-hosted transcription
sources.annotation: Blackbird’s first-person recollection describes winter travel and hospitality at a Tittabawassee riverside camp. It is a named Odawa author’s retrospective account, not an ethnic census of every camp.
sources.contentReviewScope: Title/front matter and selected citizenship-journey passage on PDF pages 42–43, marked printed pages 60–61, read. The rest of the 140-page PDF and its language material were not reviewed for this entry.

sources.title: Tittabawassee River Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe Restoration
sources.annotation: An agency account connects Saginaw Chippewa wetland use with restoration planning after the 2020 settlement. It records planned work and cultural values, not verified project completion or historical village locations.
sources.contentReviewScope: Complete story body, restoration overview and Tribe-specific paragraphs read. Linked restoration plan, settlement files and preserve pages not inspected. No present project-outcome, health or current legal-rights claim made.

sources.title: About the Ojibwe Language
sources.publisher: Ojibwe People’s Dictionary, University of Minnesota
sources.annotation: Useful language orientation, with an explicit Minnesota/Wisconsin/border-lakes variety scope. It does not independently document historical Tittabawassee speech.
sources.contentReviewScope: Visible orientation, orthography explanation and regional-scope note read; audio, individual entries and cultural galleries not inspected. Dated speaker estimates not repeated.

sources.title: Our History — Saginaw Chippewa Tribal College
sources.annotation: The college recounts its 1998 establishment and educational purpose. This is a present institutional reading route, not a direct history of the river communities.
sources.contentReviewScope: Complete visible college history read. Degree offerings, enrollment, operating schedules and language outcomes not verified as current.

sources.title: Douglass Houghton Field Notes — Volume 3 exhibition summary
sources.publisher: Clarke Historical Library, Central Michigan University
sources.annotation: The library’s curatorial summary relates Black Bird Reservation and the 1819 treaty to the Tittabawassee–Chippewa river landscape. It helps orient the historical place-names; the handwritten journal remains unread.
sources.contentReviewScope: Complete short exhibition page read; the Black Bird Reservation paragraph provides the geographic bridge. Linked handwritten volume and map images not inspected. Precise site directions omitted.

relationshipNote: Related to the broader Ojibwe reading collection and Saginaw Chippewa historical context. Historical river communities and the present Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe are not interchangeable labels; no exclusive descent or separate sovereign-government claim is made.

Inspect the 1855 and 1864 treaty texts, later policy and community testimony before extending the removal, reservation or current-rights account.

The historical name is a regional access point, not proof of a distinct present government, a fourth constituent band or an exclusive genealogy.
The Houghton manuscript, full Blackbird book, other study URLs and project outcomes have not all been reviewed. No community review or endorsement is recorded.

name: Tonkawa
overview: The Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma is a contemporary sovereign community. The Tribe’s public history centers the 1884–1885 forced removal from Fort Griffin, Texas, to Oakland in present-day Oklahoma. Historical records describe Tonkawa-speaking communities and named groups across Texas and the southern plains, but their composition, earlier locations, and relationships remain debated. This guide puts the Tribe’s present account beside archival and scholarly records, including a treaty, federal reports, and a later Tonkawa memorial challenging a land cession.

sections.title: A contemporary Tribe and the scope of this entry
sections.text: The Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma’s public profile places its headquarters and community in Kay County and describes an elected Tribal Committee and a constitution adopted in 1938 with amendments listed through 2014. The same undated page lists population, enrollment, and acreage totals; those figures are omitted as current statistics. This entry centers the present-day Tribe while examining older Tonkawa and Tonkawa-associated names as historical records use them.

sections.title: Names and language
sections.text: The Tribe’s public history gives “Tickanwa-tic” as its self-name and identifies “Tonkaweya” as a Waco/Wichita name. Spellings in older records vary. Don Paterson’s introductory language outline was prepared for the Tribe’s language-restoration program; it includes a pronunciation guide and a first lesson, and explains its intended learning context. It documents a public educational resource, not the current reach of language programs or a count of speakers.

sections.title: Texas histories and changing geography
sections.text: TxDOT’s 2021 report follows references from the seventeenth century through the nineteenth, including mission activity around the San Xavier/San Gabriel rivers and later locations across central Texas. Jones’s 1969 Smithsonian study assembles older colonial and American accounts. These records are uneven and mediated; their named bands and locations do not form a precise boundary map. TxDOT describes the statewide project as collaborative with participating Tribes, but this specific Tonkawa report does not identify a Tribal reviewer or approval.

sections.title: Diplomacy and written agreements
sections.text: A November 1837 treaty records terms negotiated by Tonkawa head chiefs and a Republic of Texas commissioner, including mutual peace language and a Republic-appointed trading agent. The 1846 Council Springs treaty text names Long-wha among ten participating Native groups; a signatory page separately labels a group of marks “Tonkaways.” Its articles describe U.S. control of trade, prisoner exchanges, rules for movement and criminal complaints, and proposed blacksmiths and schoolteachers. The archival title gives a March 1847 ratification date, but the linked advice-and-consent and ratification instruments, implementation, and Tonkawa interpretations were not inspected. The archive’s normalized nation fields omit Tonkawa even though the title and treaty pages name the group. These documents show what governments recorded in particular proceedings; they do not establish a modern boundary or one Tonkawa view of every agreement.

sections.title: Removal and the Tribe’s own commemoration
sections.text: The Tribe dates removal from Fort Griffin to October 1884 and describes travel through the Sac and Fox and Ponca agencies before arrival at Oakland on June 30, 1885. It calls this forced journey its “Trail of Tears” and connects the date with its annual powwow. TxDOT’s later government chronology adds federal-policy context. The Tribe’s commemorative language is presented in its own voice; details are not extended beyond the sources.

sections.title: The 1862 Fort Cobb attack and Texas’s request for relief
sections.text: Joseph Connole’s 2019 scholarly article reviews several explanations for the 1862 Fort Cobb attack and massacre, including accusations about cannibalism, the wider assault on the agency, and accumulated intertribal and political conflicts. Connole argues that changing alliances and the failure of U.S. and Confederate authorities to protect the Tonkawa were central to their exposure; he also states that the immediate instigation remains uncertain and that only one first-hand account of the agency attack is known. A September 1866 letter from Texas Governor J. W. Throckmorton asks the federal commissioner for food, land and an agent for Tonkawa survivors who had returned to Texas. The letter describes events from the governor’s perspective and links relief to state frontier policy. Neither work supplies a Tonkawa-authored narrative of the massacre, and the article’s interpretation and numbers remain attributed. A separate 1876 congressional document prints earlier federal correspondence on Tonkawa people at Fort Griffin. Army officers discuss ration stoppages, brief relief, and possible reservation placement; these statements show the government’s administrative record and proposals, not a Tonkawa account or proof that a proposed relocation occurred.

sections.title: A 1866 Texas act and the Tribe’s later land claim
sections.text: An 1866 Texas law provided for a league of unappropriated state land to be used as a Tonkawa home while the Tribe lived there; the governor was to select the site and the fee remained with the state. In a corrected 1996 opinion, the Fifth Circuit reviewed the Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma’s later suit against Texas officials and affirmed summary judgment for the State. The court held that the act did not itself perfect a vested land grant because the State had not designated a site and the Tribe had not used the designated land as a homeland. This is the panel’s interpretation of a specific Texas statute and claim, not a ruling on the full extent of Tonkawa homelands or on the Tribe’s present existence. Later treatment of the case was not reviewed.

sections.title: The 1891 land cession in two records
sections.text: A 1892 federal Senate document transmits the 1891 agreement and reproduces agency and commission reports about allotments, the land involved, compensation, and the commissioners’ view of Tonkawa title. A memorial adopted by the Tonkawa Tribe in council in 1907 and presented to Congress in 1908 challenges the agreement’s terms and describes members’ understandings and absences. The memorial and affidavits are primary evidence of the Tribe’s later claim and testimony, not a judicial ruling; the federal reports are evidence of government reasoning, not a neutral account of consent. Reading both makes the disagreement visible without deciding it. Individual allotment schedules and burial-location details are not reproduced.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.text: Historical sources disagree about the timing and direction of Tonkawa movement, which named bands became associated with the Tonkawa, and possible archaeological links. The proposed Toyah connection in Jones is explicitly uncertain. Secondary accounts give differing casualty estimates for the 1862 massacre; underlying records and community accounts need more direct comparison. A 1996 Handbook entry’s statement that the Tonkawa were no longer distinguishable as a tribe is contradicted by the present-day Tonkawa Tribe and is not used to describe current identity.

sections.title: Reading path and remaining work
sections.text: Start with the Tribe’s own history and government pages, then read its public language-learning outline. Compare the complete visible 1837 treaty transcription and selected 1846 Council Springs treaty pages with the 1891 federal agreement record and the council-adopted 1907 memorial, noting their different authors, purposes, and limits. The 1846 archive page links the main scan and separate ratification records; only treaty text through the signatory pages was inspected. The corrected Fifth Circuit opinion is useful for understanding the Tribe’s later 1866-law claim and its narrow legal disposition; it is not a general homeland history or current legal advice. Connole’s scholarly account and Throckmorton’s 1866 letter add a secondary interpretation and a contemporary state-government response to the 1862 violence; read both with their perspectives and limits visible. TxDOT’s chronology and Jones’s Smithsonian study offer historical syntheses whose cited records and assumptions should be checked. This remains an initial source guide rather than a full history or a community-reviewed account. The documentary is a lead for future work; the film and its interviews were not viewed. The 1876 Fort Griffin correspondence offers a government-side record of ration decisions and proposed placement for Tonkawa and Lipan people; read it as administrative evidence and distinguish recommendations from completed action.

The page is undated and contains older stereotypes and generalized language; this guide avoids those passages and attributes its historical account to the Tribe.

This statement is the production company’s account of its process, not independent verification. The full film and trailer have not been viewed, so their contents are not used as evidence and this card remains outside the substantive count. The project is a promising lead for future review of public oral-history and contemporary community material; do not assume that all filmed ceremonies are intended for unrestricted circulation.

sources.contentReviewScope: Read the complete visible body, especially the location/land-status and government sections (lines 23–49). Undated population and acreage figures are excluded from synthesis; the linked elder interview was not played.

sources.title: Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma Research Report — TxDOT Tribal Histories
sources.author: Texas Department of Transportation; individual report author not identified in the inspected text
sources.annotation: This 30-page chronological research report compiles scholarship and records for Texas transportation planning and public education. TxDOT describes its broader Tribal Histories project as collaborative with participating Tribes, but the Tonkawa report itself does not identify a specific Tribal reviewer or approval; it is therefore treated as a government synthesis, not as a Tonkawa-authored account. Its reconstructions of early bands, locations, and 1862 casualty totals remain attributed to the report and cited literature.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the report introduction and selected chronology: PDF pages 3–10, 15–29, including bibliography entries at pages 29–30. Pages 11–14 and most bibliography entries were not reviewed. Figures/maps were not visually inspected and are not used as map evidence.

sources.title: Notes on the History and Material Culture of the Tonkawa Indians
sources.publisher: Smithsonian Institution, Smithsonian Contributions to Anthropology 2(5)
sources.author: William K. Jones
sources.annotation: Jones places a historical sketch alongside a study of objects collected by U.S. Army surgeon Henry McElderry at Fort Griffin in 1868. The work is valuable for its named documents and the history of the collection, but it reflects a 1969 museum and ethnological framework and relies on older colonial and scholarly accounts. Its proposed archaeological links and broad identity/language classifications are uncertain or dated and are not treated as settled evidence. Object descriptions and images are not reproduced here.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the title/contents, introduction, selected historical-sketch pages (printed pp. 65–71), the conclusion section (printed p. 77), and selected bibliography/context passages. The full object catalogue on printed pp. 74–76 was not reviewed; maps listed by the work were not inspected as images.

sources.title: Beginning to Learn Tonkawa: An Elementary Outline of Tonkawa Grammar
sources.publisher: Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma, Language Restoration and Preservation Program Series
sources.author: Don Paterson
sources.type: Indigenous-led language-learning resource prepared for the Tribe
sources.publicationDate: 2015 program series; PDF does not provide a more precise release date
sources.annotation: Paterson prepared this 24-page learning outline for the Tonkawa Tribe’s language-restoration and preservation program. Its introduction describes an educational goal of renewed use and bilingual community life, and the text includes a pronunciation guide, teaching guidance, and a first lesson. This is a language-learning resource, not a substitute for a current account of community language programs; the instructor guidance should be understood in its stated classroom context.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the cover and introduction, pronunciation guide, teaching goals/methods, and the first lesson’s question-and-answer material (PDF pages 1–15 and 18–22). Remaining pages and any associated audio were not reviewed.

sources.title: Tonkawa Indians — Handbook of Texas Online
sources.author: Jeffrey D. Carlisle
sources.publicationDate: 1996; accessed through current Handbook of Texas Online page
sources.annotation: A concise older synthesis that can be compared with the Tribe’s account, TxDOT’s 2021 report, and Jones’s 1969 study. The article includes unsourced or broad claims, dated cultural generalizations, and a 1951 statement implying the Tonkawa were no longer a distinct tribe; that last claim conflicts with the contemporary Tonkawa Tribe government and must not be repeated as a fact about present-day identity. Kept as a contextual reference, not counted toward the substantive target.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the complete visible article body and its “Learn More” bibliography (lines 6–47). No linked books or underlying works were read as part of this review.

sources.title: Language — Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma
