sources.publicationDate: Undated; site footer 2025 does not date the page
sources.annotation: The Tribe’s public language page provides a sound guide and points learners to a series of lessons, a dictionary, and other materials. The linked dictionary was too large for the normal content reader and a direct ordinary request returned 403; neither event establishes a reader paywall, and no restriction was bypassed. The dictionary remains unread and uncounted. This index is supporting-only; the inspected Lesson 1 is catalogued separately.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the complete visible page body, including the sound guide, learning-resource descriptions, and language references (lines 18–128). Lesson 1 was reviewed separately; linked dictionary, audio, other lessons, coloring book, and story were not counted as inspected.

sources.title: Agreement with the Tonkawa Tribe for cession of lands in Oklahoma Territory — S. Ex. Doc. 52-13
sources.publisher: United States Congress, Senate, Congressional Serial Set
sources.author: President Benjamin Harrison; Secretary of the Interior John W. Noble; Commissioner of Indian Affairs T. J. Morgan; Cherokee Commission report and agreement reproduced
sources.type: Primary federal executive document and agreement
sources.annotation: This federal document transmits the 1891 Tonkawa land agreement and reproduces reports from the Department of the Interior and the Cherokee Commission. It states aggregate acreage and compensation and records the commissioners’ own description of the transaction and their view of Tonkawa land rights. It is strong evidence of the government’s position and the document sent to Congress, not a neutral account of the negotiation or proof that Tonkawa participants shared the commissioners’ understanding. The individual allotment schedule and burial-location details are not reproduced in this guide.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the full 16-page public PDF’s transmittal, agency/commission reports, agreement articles, and selected contextual pages (PDF pages 1–6). The individualized land schedule was not reviewed in detail or reproduced; the Senate document is a government record of the agreement, not an independent account of consent or implementation.

sources.title: 1837 Treaty between Texas and the Tonkawa — Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, vol. I, pp. 28–29
sources.publisher: Texas State Library and Archives Commission / Texas History Trust digital edition
sources.author: Tonkawa head chiefs and Republic of Texas commissioner Henry W. Karnes; reproduced in the edited volume by Dorman H. Winfrey and James M. Day
sources.type: Primary treaty text in a scholarly archival compilation
sources.annotation: This transcribed treaty records an agreement between Tonkawa head chiefs and the Republic of Texas. Its articles describe reciprocal promises of peace and a state-appointed trading agent with a controlling role in trade. The document captures the contracting governments’ written terms and the language of its period; it does not establish how each provision worked in practice or provide a complete account of Tonkawa political decision-making. The digitized pages are part of an edited compilation of Texas Indian papers.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the complete treaty transcription across printed pp. 28–29 (digital pages 34–35), including the articles, signatures/marks, and ratification note. The surrounding volume is not counted as read.

sources.title: Memorial of the Tonkawa Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma relating to claims against the United States — S. Doc. 60-206
sources.publisher: Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma; printed by the U.S. Senate in the Congressional Serial Set
sources.author: Memorial adopted by the Tonkawa Tribe at Oakland Agency on January 2, 1907; member affidavits and historical extracts appended
sources.type: Primary community petition and member testimony in a congressional record
sources.publicationDate: Memorial adopted January 2, 1907; presented to Senate January 28, 1908
sources.annotation: This six-page Senate document reproduces a memorial adopted by the Tonkawa Tribe in council and affidavits from members contesting the 1891 cession’s terms and the way it was negotiated. Their claims are direct evidence of the Tribe’s later position and named members’ recollections, not a judicial finding or independent valuation. The memorial’s account should be read alongside the 1892 federal document, which records commissioners’ contrasting assessment. It also reprints older federal agent reports with their own colonial and comparative framing; those passages are attributed rather than adopted.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read all six PDF pages, including the council memorial, affidavits by Frank E. Mason, John Rush Buffalo, and John Allen, and appended excerpts from federal agents’ reports. Claims about the negotiation are attributed to the memorialists and affiants; the appended agent language is not treated as Tonkawa testimony. No individualized allotment or burial site details were published.

sources.title: Ratified Indian Treaty 246: Council Springs, May 15, 1846 — treaty text and archival record
sources.publisher: National Archives and Records Administration and Indigenous Digital Archive (Museum of Indian Arts and Culture)
sources.author: Catalog metadata and transcription project; treaty signatories are multiple nations
sources.type: Primary treaty text and archival record
topics: Tonkawa under the recorded name Longwha
sources.annotation: The National Archives / Indigenous Digital Archive record supplies the treaty title, a scan viewer with transcribed text, and links to separate Senate and presidential ratification records. The treaty preamble and signatory pages name the Tonkawa as “Long-wha” / “Tonkaways” among multiple Native parties. Its articles record the U.S. government’s terms on trade, prisoners, criminal complaints, and proposed services. This is a federal treaty text in its own period language, not a Tonkawa-authored interpretation or proof of implementation. The archive’s normalized named-nation fields omit Tonkawa despite the title and treaty pages; that indexing discrepancy is retained.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the complete visible metadata and the scan viewer’s transcribed/OCR text for viewer pages 2–10: treaty preamble and articles (pages 2–7) plus signatory lists, including the Tonkawa/Tonkaways page (page 10). The 22-page archival object’s linked Senate advice-and-consent and presidential ratification instruments, other duplicate copies, and later implementation records were not inspected. No signatory marks were individually identified or interpreted.

sources.title: A Terrible Truth: The Tonkawa Massacre of 1862
sources.author: Joseph Connole
sources.publisher: Chronicles of Oklahoma, 97(4), Winter 2019–2020, pp. 450–467; Oklahoma Historical Society / Gateway to Oklahoma History, UNT Libraries
sources.annotation: An 18-page article in the Oklahoma Historical Society’s scholarly journal. Connole compares explanations for the 1862 attack and argues that long-running political alliances and failures of federal and Confederate protection shaped the Tonkawa’s vulnerability. This is the author’s secondary interpretation, not a Tonkawa-authored account or a settled consensus; his own opening discussion says the instigators and immediate reasons remain unclear.
sources.contentReviewScope: Complete article body, printed pp. 450–465, and selected endnotes pp. 466–467 inspected from the UNT/Oklahoma Historical Society digital copy. The author relies on cited historical scholarship and government reports; most cited underlying records were not independently re-read in this pass. The article notes one known first-hand account of the Fort Cobb attack. Its casualty estimate and causal interpretation remain attributed. The map and archival photograph were not separately inspected.

sources.title: Letter from J. W. Throckmorton to the U.S. Commissioner of Indian Affairs, September 20, 1866
sources.author: James W. Throckmorton, Governor of Texas
sources.publisher: Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, vol. IV, no. 80, printed pp. 110–112; Texas History Trust / University of North Texas Libraries
sources.annotation: A contemporary state-executive letter asking federal officials to provide Tonkawa survivors with food, land, an agent and other assistance after their return to Texas. Throckmorton gives one official explanation for the attack and presents the survivors’ needs alongside frontier-security concerns. The language, reported figures and causal account are the governor’s claims, not a Tonkawa voice, a neutral count, or proof that the requests were implemented.
sources.contentReviewScope: Full transcribed letter read across printed pp. 110–112 in the edited volume. The archive page OCR and displayed text were inspected; the original Executive Record Book manuscript, federal response and any later appropriation or land transfer were not checked. The unrelated next letter beginning on p. 112 was excluded.
sources.publicationDate: September 20, 1866 (document); edited volume publication date not established in this review

sources.title: Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma v. Richards, No. 94-50369 (corrected opinion following rehearing)
sources.author: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit; opinion by Judge Robert M. Parker
sources.publisher: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
sources.type: Federal appellate opinion / primary legal record
sources.annotation: The corrected February 9, 1996 appellate opinion recounts the Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma’s suit over the 1866 Texas act, which provided for a one-league home site selected by the Governor. The Fifth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Texas and held that the act did not create a perfected, self-executing grant under the record and statutory language before the panel. The decision addresses that statute and case; it is not a general historical-homeland survey, a statement about present Tonkawa identity, or current legal advice. The court states that the opinion replaced its October 1995 version after rehearing to correct a factual error; only the corrected text is used here.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the official 20-page opinion’s opening and procedural history, its reproduction of the 1864 resolution and 1866 act, the background to the Tribe’s later claim, the statutory and Nonintercourse Act analysis, the court’s conclusion, and the rehearing correction (PDF pp. 1–5, 8–10, 12–17, 20). The underlying 1866 legislative record, district-court docket, original 1992–1994 correspondence, and later treatment of the ruling were not independently checked. Historical facts recounted by the opinion remain attributed to the court and cited sources.
sources.publicationDate: Corrected opinion filed February 9, 1996; substituted after rehearing for the October 23, 1995 opinion

sources.title: Tonkawa Indians at Fort Griffin, Texas — H. Ex. Doc. 44-102
sources.author: U.S. House of Representatives; correspondence by War Department, Interior Department, and Army officers
sources.publisher: U.S. Government Publishing Office, Congressional Serial Set; digitized by the Law Library of Congress
sources.type: Primary government correspondence / Congressional Serial Set document
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the full searchable text of the eight-page public PDF, including its letters and reports dated 1872–1876. The OCR text was inspected; the page images, handwriting, signatures, and original correspondence files were not independently inspected. The authors write from federal and military administrative positions, not as Tonkawa or Lipan narrators. No reader access restriction was encountered.
sources.annotation: This 1876 federal compilation reproduces correspondence about Tonkawa people at Fort Griffin. Army officers describe the cessation and temporary resumption of rations and recommend a reservation or other assistance; the Interior Department discusses possible destinations. These records document government decision-making and administrative language, not Tonkawa testimony or the community’s own understanding. Proposed transfers are not treated as completed events, and no current status is inferred from the period’s categories.

initialAdequacy.rationale: Twelve substantive inspected works support a careful initial guide: the Tribe’s public history and language materials, TxDOT’s 2021 historical synthesis, Jones’s 1969 Smithsonian study, the 1837 Texas treaty, the 1846 multination Council Springs treaty, the 1891 federal agreement record, a council-adopted Tonkawa memorial with member affidavits, the corrected Fifth Circuit opinion on the 1866 Texas act, a scholarly study of the 1862 massacre, an 1866 Texas governor’s letter, and an 1876 federal compilation on Tonkawa and Lipan people at Fort Griffin. Five supporting access/context references remain excluded. The new congressional document adds government correspondence about ration decisions and proposed relocation; it is not Tonkawa testimony and does not show that proposals were implemented. The collection still relies heavily on government and outside written records and does not provide a full Tonkawa-authored account of the massacre. It remains unfinished and does not settle the causes of the 1862 attack, consent to the 1891 cession, or all questions about historical Texas relationships.
remainingLimits: The 1862 massacre article is a secondary interpretation. Tonkawa-authored or community-held public accounts of the event and the original underlying government records need further review; no single-cause explanation is adopted.
The timing/direction of earlier movement, composition of named bands, language classification, and archaeological associations remain contested or uncertain.

The 1837 treaty, 1891 agreement, and 1907 memorial have been read, but related federal/Republic records, ratification/implementation documentation, and later claim disposition still require systematic review.
The 1846 Council Springs treaty scan’s transcribed text and signatory pages were read; separate ratification instruments, later implementation, and Tonkawa-specific interpretations remain unreviewed.

Current community-authored cultural, language-program, and historical publications need broader review. The 2020 museum booklet and large dictionary were not fully inspected; failed automated access is not treated as a paywall.
The documentary site describes collaboration and an oral-history film project, but neither film nor interviews were viewed; culturally sensitive footage may require limits on public use.
Current population, enrollment, acreage, and program-status figures are not claimed from undated pages.
This review did not inspect or add maps.

The 1996 appellate decision addresses a specific claim under the 1866 Texas act; the underlying legislative record and later case treatment were not reviewed, and the ruling is not extended to broad homeland or present-identity questions.
initialAdequacy.searchScope: Reviewed Tonkawa Tribe public history, government-profile and language pages; Don Paterson’s language lesson; selected pages of TxDOT’s 2021 report and Jones’s 1969 Smithsonian study; full visible Handbook of Texas entry; the 1837 treaty text, 1891 federal agreement document, and full 1907 Tonkawa memorial with member affidavits; and the 1846 NARA / Indigenous Digital Archive Treaty 246 record. It also reviewed the corrected 1996 Fifth Circuit opinion on the Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma’s suit under the 1866 Texas act. On October 23, 2026, read Joseph Connole’s full 18-page article, the full three-page 1866 Throckmorton letter, and the 1846 treaty viewer’s text through the signatory pages. The 1846 source’s separate ratification instruments and later implementation remain unread. The underlying 1866 legislative and district-court records and later treatment of the Fifth Circuit opinion remain unchecked. The article’s cited primary sources were not all independently checked; the Governor’s original manuscript and federal reply remain unread. Direct web searches prioritized community and archival materials. Large PDFs and the 2020 booklet were not bypassed when normal requests failed. On October 23, 2026, the full eight-page searchable text of H. Ex. Doc. 44-102 was read for its 1872–1876 federal and military correspondence; OCR artifacts and the uninspected scan images are noted.
initialAdequacy.assessmentNote: Adequacy is a dated editorial assessment, not community endorsement or research completion.

evidenceNotes: Review supplemented 2026-10-23. Eleven works count toward the substantive inspected-source target; five supporting/context references remain excluded. Each source card records authorship, actual inspection scope, review date, access limits and perspective.

The 1837 treaty records terms negotiated with the Republic of Texas; it does not prove implementation. The 1891 federal Senate document records agency and commission positions. The 1907 Tonkawa memorial and affidavits are direct evidence of the later community claim and named testimony, not a legal finding. The two land-cession perspectives are cited together.
The Tribe’s history and language pages are community-government publications. Older stereotyping and any page descriptions that the Tribe’s site itself identifies as secret are not reproduced.
TxDOT describes its statewide Tribal Histories project as collaborative; the individual Tonkawa report does not name a specific Tonkawa reviewer.
Jones’s Smithsonian work is a dated scholarly publication based on historical records and museum objects. The archaeology and broad historical classifications are not treated as settled.
No undated population or enrollment figure is stated as current. The individual allotment schedules and burial location in the federal records are not copied into the narrative.

Connole’s full article adds a scholarly interpretation of 1862 while acknowledging uncertain immediate causes and a limited firsthand record. Its casualty figures and conclusions remain attributed; the underlying cited records were not all independently reviewed.

Throckmorton’s full 1866 letter is a contemporary state-government appeal for relief after Tonkawa survivors returned to Texas. It also frames state interests and frontier policy; it is not the Tonkawa community’s account, and requested aid is not proof of implementation.
The owner-supplied Jumano-study URLs remain in the distinct reading-lead catalogue and are not treated as Tonkawa research or completed content checks. No map was inspected or added.

The 1846 Council Springs scan viewer’s treaty text was read through the signatory pages. It names Long-wha / Tonkaways in the treaty text and signature roster while the archive’s normalized named-nation field omits Tonkawa. The record’s ratification date is catalogued as March 8, 1847, but the separate Senate and Presidential instruments and later implementation were not inspected; no acceptance or implementation claim is inferred.

The corrected 1996 Fifth Circuit opinion is used for its narrow interpretation of the 1866 Texas act and the Tribe’s later lawsuit. The court affirmed summary judgment for the State, holding that the statutory one-league land provision was not a self-executing vested grant under the conditions before it. This is not a determination of the whole Tonkawa homeland history or present identity; underlying records and later case treatment remain unchecked.
researchGaps: The 1862 massacre article is a secondary interpretation; seek further public Tonkawa-authored or community-held accounts and compare more of the original government records. Do not force a single-cause explanation from the present evidence.
The timing/direction of earlier movement, composition of named bands, language classification, and archaeological associations remain contested or uncertain.

The 1837 treaty, 1891 agreement, and 1907 memorial have been read, but related federal/Republic records, ratification/implementation documentation, and later claim disposition still require systematic review.

The 1846 Council Springs treaty text and signatory pages have been inspected, but its separate 1847 advice-and-consent and presidential ratification instruments, implementation record, and Tonkawa-specific interpretations remain unread.

Current community-authored cultural, language-program, and historical publications need broader review. The 2020 museum booklet and large dictionary were not fully inspected; failed automated access is not treated as a paywall.
The documentary site describes collaboration and an oral-history film project, but neither film nor interviews were viewed; culturally sensitive footage may require limits on public use.
Current population, enrollment, acreage, and program-status figures are not claimed from undated pages.
This review did not inspect or add maps.

The 1996 Fifth Circuit opinion resolves a narrow dispute over the Texas 1866 act on the record before that court; its underlying legislative/administrative materials and later treatment have not been surveyed. Do not extend its holding to broader Tonkawa homeland history or current identity.

overview: Wichita is a broader people-level reading route, while Wichita and Affiliated Tribes is the name of a present government centered at Anadarko, Oklahoma. Its institutional history includes Wichita Proper, Waco, Taovaya, Tawakoni and Kichai, whose names and histories should remain individually identified. This community-source foundation follows the Tribe’s account of Plains village life, displacement, continuing community and educational resources; it does not make the historical labels interchangeable or establish every present affiliation.

sections.title: Named peoples and a present government
sections.text: The Tribe’s history identifies Wichita Proper, Waco, Taovaya, Tawakoni and Kichai within its account. Its later chapter describes the organized Wichita and Affiliated Tribes community at Anadarko. Keep those two levels clear: related historical peoples are not simply alternate spellings, and this institutional account does not make every historical group one timeless government. Other historical and community sources should be read with their dates and named scope. The dated Elam and Harper accounts also distinguish narrower and broader uses of Wichita; their historical terminology must be read in context.

sections.title: Farming, hunting and the seasonal village
sections.text: The People of the Grass House chapter describes a seasonal pattern combining gardens and buffalo hunting. It follows food preservation and storage alongside the work of maintaining grass houses. Read this as a historical account of particular Plains village practices, including cooperative household work, rather than a picture of how every Wichita person lives today. Cultural and ceremonial narratives in the original remain with their publisher.

sections.title: Red River trade and changing villages
sections.text: Harper places Taovaya settlements on both sides of the Red River and discusses related villages sharing trade centers. Her interpretation supports historical Texas connections while retaining separate names; it does not establish a fixed territory. The underlying colonial records remain unread here.

sections.title: Reading the 1846 Council Springs treaty
sections.text: The May 15, 1846 treaty names Wichita, Waco and other participating groups separately. Its text addresses trade, prisoners, violence, peace, and proposed blacksmith and teaching services. The printed signatory list also retains distinct period headings. Readers can examine a primary agreement here while keeping its limits clear: stated promises are not proof of implementation, and historical names or signatures alone do not settle present identity, jurisdiction or treaty rights.

sections.title: Texas displacement and wartime refuge
sections.text: The Tribe’s August 2012 history distinguishes Waco and Tawakoni removal from the Brazos Reserve from the Wichita and Keechi journey through the Fort Arbuckle area. Neighbors’s September 3, 1859 report, reprinted in 1883, dates his Texas-reserve party’s arrival to August 16 and the administrative handover to September 1. He also reports that people were unwilling to occupy new homes without protection. Those official dates do not establish safety, voluntary migration or one identical journey for every named people. Individual registers and fuller route records remain unreviewed. The Tribe’s account later describes wartime flight to Kansas and a return to Indian Territory.

sections.title: A later petition and the limits of official records
sections.text: The collection also prints an April 1882 petition by delegates identifying Wichita, Caddo and “Pannatakees,” using that period wording. They ask Congress to confirm land held in common. This preserves their stated claim, not a finding that the claim was accepted or proof of every community’s position. Keeping the petition separate from officials’ interpretations helps readers compare whose account each record presents.

sections.title: Continuity through family and community
sections.text: A New Beginning emphasizes continuing community after the loss of grass-house village life. The account describes older and younger generations sharing memories while people pursue education, employment and family gatherings. Its language of endurance is the institution’s interpretation of its history; it is not a statistical survey or a claim that every member has the same experience or practice.

sections.title: Community memory beyond a story of disappearance
sections.text: Bethke, Trabert and Gary McAdams’s collaborative research with Wichita and Affiliated Tribes brings community memories together with archives and low-impact archaeology. The authors describe how twentieth-century gathering places in Oklahoma helped sustain relationships through and after allotment. Their account connects older history with living Wichita people. It remains a specific community-based study: its published recollections and academic interpretation should be attributed, rather than treated as a survey of every community or a current legal boundary.

sections.title: A public route into the language
sections.text: The Tribe’s online dictionary pairs English vocabulary and phrases with Wichita forms and links many entries for pronunciation. Readers can follow this community-published resource directly. The listing was inspected, but recordings and apps were not tested. Resource availability alone does not establish current speaker totals, proficiency or learning outcomes.

sections.title: Language learning and community-controlled archives
sections.text: Sapphire Hodges’s 2018 thesis examines archives and language-learning possibilities in a Wichita community setting. Her account describes Tribal direction of an archive project and argues for community control over learning priorities. The survey was largely voluntary at a local event, included people with different community relationships, and used self-assessed language ability. It is a dated case study, not a census or a test of present proficiency. The Tribe’s Department of Preservation separately describes its History Center, archives, library and language projects; listing a resource does not make all its materials public or establish learning outcomes.

sections.title: Education as a contemporary institution
sections.text: The Education Services Department describes support ranging from adult and vocational learning to undergraduate and graduate study. Its program account also discusses lending equipment for coursework. These are the publisher’s stated activities and aims. Funding, eligibility and application requirements vary; this guide does not promise assistance or report measured outcomes. The original pages remain the route to current details.

sections.title: Reading path and the scope of this foundation
sections.text: Begin with the Tribe’s connected history exhibit, then compare its more specific newsletter account of removal with the 1846 treaty text and the later federal compilation of the 1859 report and 1882 petition. Use the public dictionary and education pages as direct community-published routes. Harper’s trade-history pages, the collaborative twentieth-century study and Hodges’s language/archive case study ask different questions and should retain their dates, methods and perspectives. Further primary records, separately scoped affiliated histories and governing-text review remain open. This is a developing cited source guide, not a completed or community-endorsed history.

name: Yaqui
overview: Yaqui or Yoeme people have homelands in Sonora’s Yaqui River valley and continuing communities across the modern U.S.–Mexico border. This guide begins with the Texas Band’s own account and keeps it distinct from Pascua Yaqui institutions in Arizona and the Sonora-focused works.

sections.title: A Texas community account
sections.text: The Texas Band of Yaqui Indians describes its community through Yoeme family histories of displacement from Sonora and continuing relationships with Yaqui pueblos there. Its longer institutional account places a Presidio/Fort Davis connection in the 1870s. These details are attributed to this publisher; the underlying family and archival records were not inspected. The two pages form one institutional account, not two independent historical confirmations.

sections.title: Read the 2015 Texas resolution directly
sections.text: Texas Senate Resolution 989 was adopted on May 27, 2015. Its operative clauses honor the Band’s members and request a commemorative copy. The historical recitals should be read alongside the community account rather than treated as an independent archival investigation. This review does not determine broader legal effects or equate the resolution with federal acknowledgment.

sections.title: Keep the Arizona statute in its own scope
sections.text: Public Law 95-375, enacted September 18, 1978, addresses the named Pascua Yaqui association and Tribe in Arizona. It provides for federal-service eligibility and includes trust-land, governing-document and membership provisions. This is an historical enactment, not a statement of every Yaqui community’s status or of current membership rules. Later amendments were not reviewed.

sections.title: Language teaching and individual experience
sections.text: The Pascua Yaqui Teacher Language Institute describes goals for preparing language instructors, curriculum and family language use. These are stated educational aims, not measured outcomes. On the same page, instructor Graciela Garcia describes growing up with Yaqui as a first language and facing difficulties learning English at school. Her account is an individual experience, not a generalization about all Yaqui speakers or Texas education.

sections.title: A dictionary shaped with Yaqui educators
sections.text: The 2016 Diccionario yaqui de bolsillo presents Yaqui–Spanish and Spanish–Yaqui material. Its acknowledgments credit Yaqui-speaking teachers, and its teacher-written foreword explains educational and intergenerational purposes. The inspected front matter supports that collaborative context; it does not establish present fluency, universal dialect coverage or a full review of the entries.

sections.title: A community reading route
sections.text: The Pascua Yaqui Tribal Library describes Hiaki special collections, literacy support and family programming. Its page links readers to books, catalogues and digital services. The library account is useful educational context; each linked book still needs its own review. Availability and account requirements of the individual services were not checked.

sections.title: Reading a 1930s research encounter
sections.text: In the selected introduction to the 1936 Texas Technological College study, Holden describes how intermediaries and translation shaped the expedition’s access to Sonora communities in 1934. This helps readers examine who recorded an account and how. The excerpt is not direct evidence of Texas settlement. The later chapters and illustrations were not reviewed, and hosting by a present-day Tribal library is not blanket endorsement.

sections.title: Scope and the next reading steps
sections.text: This is a foundational source guide, not an adequate wider Yaqui history. The selected river-history and Pótam oral-history works add Sonora perspectives but do not settle the Texas migration account. Continue with community-directed history, documented migration records and language scholarship. The museum sheet is brief orientation; the retained INPI route remains unread. Follow cultural materials through the relevant community publisher and stated scope.

sections.title: A river landscape that changed over time
sections.text: Historian Esther Padilla Calderón explains how the Yaqui River’s floods supported cultivation while sometimes damaging or relocating settlements. Her selected historical account describes a major channel change in 1833 and later attempts to control the river through irrigation works and dams. This helps readers see the Sonora homeland as a changing lived landscape. Her explanation combines archival material with earlier scholarship; the underlying archival files were not inspected for this guide. It does not establish present water allocations or Texas settlement history.

sections.title: Listening to women’s memories in Pótam
sections.text: Edna Lucía García Rivera’s 2023 study follows the memories of two older women living in Pótam. They recall ancestors’ displacement, survival and return, and connect those memories with responsibilities to family and community. García Rivera interprets their accounts through oral history and postcolonial feminist scholarship. These are named individual perspectives shaped by remembrance and the research encounter. They enrich the history without standing for every Yaqui woman or independently confirming each event recalled.

name: Ysleta del Sur Pueblo
region: El Paso / West Texas / Southern Tiwa-Pueblo history
overview: Ysleta del Sur Pueblo is a distinct living Pueblo nation and tribal government in the El Paso area of Texas. The Pueblo identifies its community as Tigua and describes histories linking Quarai, Isleta in New Mexico, and Ysleta del Sur. Federal law redesignated the earlier Tiwa Indians of Ysleta, Texas, as Ysleta del Sur Pueblo in 1987. These names and histories connect communities without making their governments interchangeable.

sections.title: A distinct Pueblo and tribal government in Texas
sections.text: The Pueblo identifies itself as a federally recognized sovereign nation in Texas and describes the Tigua as the community that established Ysleta del Sur. Congress used a separate title for Ysleta del Sur in the 1987 Restoration Act, redesignating the people previously called the Tiwa Indians of Ysleta, Texas, by the 1968 Tiwa Indians Act. The same 1987 law restored a federal trust relationship and defined the reservation through specified land categories in El Paso and Hudspeth Counties. These are distinct legal and community records; the statute does not collapse Ysleta del Sur into the Pueblo of Isleta in New Mexico, or make the broad Tiwa grouping a single government.

sections.title: Connected histories of Isleta, Quarai, and Ysleta
sections.text: The Pueblo’s public history describes a route from Quarai to refuge at Isleta and then south to Ysleta during the upheavals of the Pueblo Revolt period. National Park Service accounts and the TxDOT report describe Spanish retreat, relocation, and the establishment of Ysleta del Sur, while noting that some Isletans remained in New Mexico and that some descendants later returned. These accounts give different emphases to the sequence and circumstances of movement. Older historical summaries also report different population counts for people who went south. This profile therefore avoids adopting a single number or turning a complex history into a claim that all Isleta people relocated or that the two present-day Pueblos share one government.

sections.title: Land, settlement, and a changing cultural landscape
sections.text: The Pueblo’s 2016 planning report and its current historical account place the community in the El Paso area and describe the importance of farming and acequia irrigation in the early settlement. The 2021 TxDOT report adds a longer, source-cited account of settlement and land tenure, developed for transportation planning with the Pueblo’s Department of Cultural Preservation. Its colonial and state-era accounts remain interpretations of cited historical sources, not a complete map of Tigua homelands. The National Park Service’s account of Ysleta Mission situates the Pueblo within a wider lower Rio Grande landscape shaped by Indigenous movement, Spanish colonial roads, missions, and later urban development. Each publication has a different purpose: the 2016 report records a dated community planning snapshot, TxDOT synthesizes historical and cultural-landscape sources, and the Park Service describes a historic place and trail. Present administrative boundaries and mission locations should not be read as limits on historical relationships or contemporary community connections.

sections.title: Governance, oral tradition, and federal law
sections.text: The 2025 Year-End Report describes the Pueblo’s elected Tribal Council alongside traditional leadership roles, and explains that governance draws on oral tradition and the Tribal Code of Laws. The 1987 federal statute records a dated legal framework for the tribe, its land, federal services, and the relationship with the United States. The accompanying Senate committee report records the bill’s stated purpose, background, and amendments; it is evidence of legislative process and congressional framing, not an independent community history or current legal interpretation. Its colonial-era and land-loss summary is attributed to that committee. The TxDOT report also summarizes earlier land-grant records and later federal recognition, with claims tied to the sources it cites. Neither the statute nor the reports supplies a complete account of later court decisions, present jurisdiction in every circumstance, or the Pueblo’s own full constitutional history. Current governmental details should be checked against the Pueblo’s own dated reports and official publications.

sections.title: Tiwa language and publicly shared cultural work
sections.text: The Pueblo’s 2025 report describes Tiwa classes and language-learning materials as part of its own cultural and educational work. Its Cultural Development Division separately describes Southern Tiwa language-preservation classes, the use of Miromaa software for archiving and teaching materials, collaboration with linguists and fluent speakers, and Traditional Council review intended to prevent teaching materials from sharing sacred or traditional information. These are the Pueblo’s own descriptions of program design; this guide does not reproduce restricted content or claim measured learning outcomes, current fluency, or a comprehensive account of Southern Tiwa. The Department of Cultural Preservation also distinguishes public-facing exhibits, tours and demonstrations from some member- and family-restricted classes. Shared language connections with Isleta are evidence of relationship, not proof that every community or variety is identical.

sections.title: A dated community study and the limits of current figures
sections.text: Ysleta del Sur Pueblo’s 2016 Socioeconomic Profile was prepared under tribal direction to describe members’ geographic and economic circumstances for planning. Its methods and tables offer a substantial look at the questions the Pueblo was studying at that time, including member residence beyond the El Paso area. The figures are a 2016 snapshot, not present-day population or migration estimates. The Pueblo’s current webpages display differing, undated membership totals, so no such total is repeated here. The 2025 Year-End Report offers a newer institutional view of programs and priorities but likewise should be read as the Pueblo’s own annual account, not an independent evaluation of outcomes.

relationshipNote: Ysleta del Sur Pueblo is a distinct Pueblo nation and tribal government in Texas; Tigua is the community name used by the Pueblo. The 1987 statute links the present name to the earlier legal designation Tiwa Indians of Ysleta, Texas. NPS sources describe historical movement connecting Ysleta del Sur with Isleta Pueblo in New Mexico, and the 2025 report documents Tiwa language teaching with Isleta consultants. These are historical and linguistic relationships, not grounds to merge the two present governments, treat all Tiwa speakers as Ysleta citizens, or make the broad Pueblo label a single people.
researchGaps: Read further Pueblo-authored historical essays and publicly released educational material, while respecting community-controlled archival access.

Compare the Pueblo’s oral-history framing with relevant Spanish-language colonial records and independent historical scholarship; preserve disagreement over the chronology and number of people who moved south.
Review later federal laws, court opinions, and current Pueblo legal materials before making claims about present jurisdiction, land status, or implementation of the 1987 Act.

The 2016 socioeconomic study is a dated community planning snapshot. Present-day member distribution and demographics have not been independently established; undated membership totals on Pueblo webpages conflict and are not repeated.
The Cultural Center lists some programming for Tribal Members only. No private archive, sensitive site, ceremonial detail, or community review is included in this public guide.

A Pueblo-published language-preservation page now describes program methods and safeguards. Inspect publicly released Southern Tiwa learning materials only when clearly authorized; the page does not supply a grammar, audio sample, fluency count, measured outcomes or dated current schedule.
evidenceNotes: Initial focused review completed 2026-10-22. Follow-ups on 2026-10-23 inspected the substantive first nine pages of the 1987 Senate committee report accompanying the Restoration Act and selected non-sensitive sections of TxDOT’s 2021 Ysleta del Sur Pueblo research report. They are counted as distinct works with different purposes: legislative process and a community-consulted cultural-landscape synthesis. The first follow-up had eight substantive works; the 2026-10-23 Southern Tiwa language-preservation page raises the profile to nine substantive works. Later Senate-report pages remain unread and OCR errors are disclosed. The TxDOT report’s identified culturally sensitive planning section was excluded from profile synthesis.

The Pueblo’s 2016 report is limited to its actual inspected pages and dated purpose; the 2025 report is an institutional annual report, not an independent evaluation. Migration accounts differ in emphasis and older headcounts conflict; no single number is adopted.

No historical map association was added. The Texas map connection records the present-day Pueblo/community location only; it is not a homeland boundary. No private cultural materials or generated imagery were used.

initialAdequacy.rationale: Nine substantive inspected works provide a clearly bounded introduction grounded in the Pueblo’s own history, current reporting and public language-preservation description, community-directed planning, federal legal texts and National Park Service accounts of the related Isleta/Ysleta landscape. The directly inspected Cultural Development Division page adds specific account of the Pueblo’s Southern Tiwa teaching and archival safeguards; a separate brief Cultural Preservation page remains supporting-only. This supports an adequate starting guide, not a full deep dive, current legal opinion, comprehensive linguistic study or community-reviewed account.
remainingLimits: Further Pueblo-authored and community-controlled public historical scholarship is needed; the 2016 report and 2025 annual report each have limited purposes, and TxDOT’s consulted synthesis does not replace a Pueblo-authored monograph.
Primary Spanish records and additional independent scholarship are needed to compare the chronology, route, and differing historical counts associated with movement to Ysleta.
No community review or endorsement is recorded, and protected digital archive materials were not accessed.

The Pueblo’s undated online language-program description was inspected, but the actual curriculum, materials, audio, language-variety details, teaching outcomes and present class schedule were not; future claims should be limited to what the Tribe publicly describes.
